label: Authored wave 2 (NGN formats + Client Needs gaps)

items.stem: Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A resident in long-term care receives continuous enteral feeding through a gastrostomy tube at 60 mL/hr. To reduce the risk of aspiration and keep the tube patent, the nurse keeps the head of the bed at {{1}} throughout the feeding and flushes the tube with {{2}} every 4 hours.

options: flat with one pillow
10 degrees
90 degrees only during bag changes
at least 30 degrees
5 mL of normal saline
30 mL of water
120 mL of apple juice
10 mL of air

items.rationale: Keeping the head of the bed elevated at least 30 degrees during continuous feeding limits reflux of formula into the pharynx and lowers aspiration risk; a flat or 10-degree position allows pooling. Routine flushes with about 30 mL of water every 4 hours keep the tube patent and supply free water. Saline adds unnecessary sodium, juice is acidic and clogs tubes, and air is used only to check placement, not to flush.

items.stem: A nurse reviews the lunchtime note for a client on a rehabilitation unit. Click to highlight the findings that require immediate follow-up.

highlightSegments.text: 1230 rehab unit: 74-year-old client 9 days after a left-hemisphere stroke, on a minced and moist diet with mildly thick liquids.
Sitting upright in the chair for lunch with chin tucked as taught.
Wet, gurgly voice quality noted after swallowing sips of water from the bedside pitcher.
Client states, 'My daughter brought me a bottle of water; it goes down easier.'
Ate 75% of the meal tray.
Temperature 37.2 C (99.0 F), SpO2 96% on room air.
No coughing during pudding or minced foods.
Client pockets food in the left cheek and needs cueing to clear it.
Oral care completed after the meal.
Client rests in the chair for 30 minutes after the meal.

items.rationale: A wet, gurgly voice after sips of thin water, a family member supplying thin liquids that are not on the diet order, and pocketing of food are aspiration cues that call for stopping the unsafe intake, cueing the client to clear the mouth, reinforcing liquid restrictions with the family, and updating speech-language pathology. Upright positioning, chin tuck, adequate intake, normal temperature and saturation, post-meal oral care and resting upright are appropriate findings.

items.stem: A nurse in a long-term care facility reviews the 3-day fluid record of an 84-year-old resident who has been refusing most of the beverages offered. Which conclusion should the nurse draw?
options: The values are expected for an older adult and need only routine monitoring
The resident is becoming dehydrated and needs a scheduled fluid plan and provider notification
The resident is retaining fluid and needs a fluid restriction
The weight loss reflects appropriate diuresis after a change in diet
items.rationale: Falling intake with falling output, weight loss of more than 1 kg in 2 days and urine that has darkened to amber together show developing dehydration in an older adult, who has a blunted thirst response. The nurse starts a plan of preferred beverages offered every 1 to 2 hours and notifies the provider. Fluid retention would show weight gain, diet-related diuresis does not explain the falling intake, and these changes are not a normal part of aging.

items.stem: Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A home health nurse visits a 79-year-old client who reports no bowel movement for 4 days, hard stool, and straining. Before recommending a laxative, the nurse should first assess for {{1}} and then teach the client to {{2}}.

options: lactose intolerance by reviewing dairy intake
urinary retention with a bladder scan
fecal impaction by asking about liquid stool leakage and checking for abdominal distention
hemorrhoids by inspecting the perianal skin
take a stimulant laxative every day for the next month
drink about 2 L of fluid daily unless restricted and add dietary fiber gradually
limit walking until the bowel is empty
use a sodium phosphate enema every morning

items.rationale: Four days without stool plus hard stool and straining raise concern for fecal impaction; liquid stool leaking around a hard mass and abdominal distention are the classic cues, and impaction must be ruled out before stimulant laxatives or bulk agents are used. Adequate fluids, gradual fiber and regular activity are the first-line measures. Daily enemas and long-term stimulant laxatives cause dependence and electrolyte loss, and reducing activity slows peristalsis.

items.stem: A nurse is planning care for a bed-bound resident in long-term care whose Braden score is 12. For each intervention, click to specify whether it is indicated or contraindicated.
matrixRows: Reposition at least every 2 hours using a 30-degree lateral tilt
Massage reddened bony prominences to improve circulation
Use a ring cushion under the sacrum while sitting
Apply a moisture barrier cream after each incontinence episode
Keep the head of the bed at 45 degrees at all times
Place a pillow under the calves so the heels float off the mattress
items.rationale: Repositioning at least every 2 hours with a 30-degree tilt, floating the heels and protecting skin from moisture reduce pressure, shear and maceration. Massaging bony prominences damages fragile tissue over already compromised capillaries, ring cushions concentrate pressure around the rim and impair circulation, and keeping the head of the bed at 45 degrees continuously increases shear on the sacrum; 30 degrees or less is used except during meals and tube feedings.

items.stem: A nurse is teaching a 16-year-old client with a right ankle fracture how to use axillary crutches at home. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: Keep the crutch pads 2 to 3 finger-widths below the armpits
Wear socks or slippers so the floor is not scuffed
Remove throw rugs and keep walkways clear at home
Support body weight on the hands, not the armpits
Rest the armpits on the crutch pads when tired
Go down stairs by moving the crutches and the injured leg down first
Go up stairs by moving the crutches and the injured leg first
items.rationale: Crutch pads must sit 2 to 3 finger-widths below the axillae and weight is carried on the hands, because pressure on the axillae damages the brachial plexus. Stairs are climbed with the unaffected leg first and descended with the crutches and injured leg first ('up with the good, down with the bad'). Clear floors and supportive nonskid shoes prevent falls; resting on the pads and wearing socks or slippers are unsafe.

items.stem: Click to highlight the findings in the handoff report that require the oncoming nurse to follow up immediately.

highlightSegments.text: 1900 handoff: 58-year-old client, postoperative day 2 after abdominal hysterectomy.
Indwelling urinary catheter placed in surgery is still in place; no removal order noted.
Drainage bag was hung from the side rail above the level of the bladder during transport back from x-ray.
Urine clear and amber, 300 mL over the last 4 hours.
Client reports lower abdominal cramping rated 3/10.
Catheter tubing secured to the thigh with a securement device.
Temperature 37.0 C (98.6 F) at 1800.
Client ambulated in the hall twice with assistance.
Sediment noted in the tubing and the client says the catheter 'burns' when moving.
Perineal care last documented yesterday at 0800.

items.rationale: A drainage bag raised above the bladder lets urine reflux toward the bladder, a catheter still in place on postoperative day 2 without a removal plan raises the daily risk of catheter-associated urinary tract infection, sediment with burning suggests infection or irritation, and perineal care that is more than a day overdue breaches the CAUTI bundle. Adequate clear output, mild cramping, thigh securement, normal temperature and ambulation are expected findings.

items.stem: The nurse reviews the pain log for a client 1 day after total knee arthroplasty. Which conclusion should the nurse draw about the non-pharmacologic comfort measures?
options: No conclusion can be drawn until the nurse rates the pain rather than the client
The measures are ineffective and only the analgesic dose should be increased
Guided imagery is the most effective measure and should replace cold therapy
Cold application with repositioning consistently lowers pain and should be scheduled as part of the plan
trendRows: Repositioned with pillow between knees, cold pack to the knee
'That is the best it has been'
items.rationale: Each time cold and repositioning were used the client's pain fell by 2 to 3 points and the client reported clear relief, so the nurse builds these measures into the scheduled plan alongside analgesics. Guided imagery produced no change and the client could not engage with it, so it is not the most effective choice. The data show that non-drug measures are working, and the client's self-report is the most reliable pain measure.

items.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A 70-year-old client with left knee osteoarthritis is learning to use a single-point cane. The nurse teaches the client to hold the cane in the {{1}} hand and, when walking, to move the cane forward {{2}}. When the client stands with the arm relaxed at the side, the cane handle should be level with the {{3}}.

options: dominant
left
whichever has the stronger grip
right
after both legs have advanced
together with the right leg
only when climbing stairs
together with the left leg
wrist crease, allowing 15 to 30 degrees of elbow flexion
waist
elbow when the arm is bent to 90 degrees
mid-thigh

items.rationale: A cane is held on the side opposite the affected knee, so a client with left knee arthritis holds it in the right hand; the cane and the weak leg then move forward together to share the load while the strong leg bears weight. The handle should reach the wrist crease when the arm hangs at the side, giving about 15 to 30 degrees of elbow flexion. Holding the cane on the weak side or at waist height makes gait unstable.

items.stem: Click to highlight the findings in the admission note that increase the client's risk for pressure injury.

highlightSegments.text: Admission note, skilled nursing facility: 88-year-old client transferred from the hospital after treatment for pneumonia.
Client is alert but needs the assistance of two staff to move up in bed and slides down frequently.
Eats about 25% of meals and has lost 4 kg in the past month.
Incontinent of urine at night; brief changed on rounds.
Skin over the sacrum is intact with blanchable redness that fades within 20 minutes of turning.
Heels are soft, pink and warm.
Uses a walker to go to the bathroom during the day with one-person assist.
Denies pain in the hips or back.
Blood pressure 128/74, pulse 82.
Serum albumin 2.6 g/dL on hospital labs.

items.rationale: Needing two people to move and sliding down in bed create friction and shear, eating a quarter of meals with 4 kg weight loss and an albumin of 2.6 g/dL indicate poor nutrition for tissue repair, and nighttime urinary incontinence keeps the skin moist; each of these lowers the Braden score. Blanchable redness that fades after turning is normal reactive hyperemia, and soft pink heels, daytime walking, absence of pain and normal vital signs do not add risk.

items.stem: A nurse reviews the Braden scale trend for a hospitalized client with a heart failure exacerbation. Which conclusion should the nurse draw?
options: Risk has progressed to high and a stage 1 pressure injury is present, so the prevention plan must be intensified now
The client remains at mild risk and the current plan is adequate
Nutrition is the only factor that has changed, so a dietitian referral is sufficient
The redness is reactive hyperemia that will resolve with the current turning schedule
items.rationale: The total Braden score has dropped from 18 (mild risk) to 12 (high risk) as the mobility, moisture and nutrition subscores worsened, and nonblanchable sacral redness on intact skin is a stage 1 pressure injury. The nurse intensifies prevention now: pressure-redistribution surface, more frequent turning, moisture management, nutrition consult and offloading the sacrum. Nonblanchable redness is not reactive hyperemia, the risk is no longer mild, and more than nutrition has changed.

items.stem: A nurse is positioning a client who has returned to the unit after a total hip arthroplasty through a posterior approach. Which position should the nurse maintain?
options: Sitting in a low recliner with the hips flexed past 90 degrees
Supine with the legs crossed at the ankles
Supine with an abduction pillow between the legs
Side-lying on the operative side with the knees flexed
items.rationale: After a posterior-approach hip replacement the joint dislocates with adduction, internal rotation and hip flexion beyond 90 degrees, so the client is kept supine or turned only with an abduction pillow or wedge between the legs. Lying on the operative side, sitting in a low chair with the hips flexed past 90 degrees, and crossing the legs all move the new joint toward the dislocation position.

items.stem: Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A nurse provides oral care to an unconscious client who is not intubated. The nurse positions the client {{1}} and cleans the teeth, gums and tongue with {{2}}, using only a small amount of fluid and oral suction as needed.

options: prone with a pillow under the chest
supine with the head of the bed flat
in high Fowler position with the neck extended
side-lying with the head turned toward the mattress
a soft toothbrush or foam swab moistened with water or an alcohol-free rinse
lemon-glycerin swabs
a firm-bristled toothbrush and an alcohol-based mouthwash
a gauze pad soaked in hydrogen peroxide

items.rationale: An unconscious client cannot protect the airway, so oral care is done side-lying with the head turned toward the mattress so fluid drains out of the mouth, with oral suction ready. A soft toothbrush or foam swab moistened with water or an alcohol-free rinse cleans without injuring the mucosa. Supine or neck-extended positions let fluid pool in the pharynx, lemon-glycerin swabs dry the mucosa and erode enamel, and peroxide and alcohol-based rinses irritate oral tissue.

items.stem: Click to highlight the findings in the night shift note that the nurse can modify to promote the client's sleep.

highlightSegments.text: 2300 note: 81-year-old client admitted with cellulitis, hospital day 3.
Client states, 'I have not slept more than an hour at a time since I got here.'
Vital signs were taken at 0000 and 0400 last night per unit routine.
Hallway lights on and door open; the monitor alarm from the next room is audible.
Client drank two cups of coffee with dinner at 1800.
Napped from 1300 to 1600 this afternoon.
Temperature 37.1 C (98.8 F), IV antibiotic infusing on schedule.
Leg elevated on two pillows; states the leg 'feels better tonight.'
Reports being 'a night owl' at home and usually going to bed at midnight.
Reading glasses and hearing aid at the bedside.

items.rationale: Routine vital signs at midnight and 0400 for a stable client, hallway light and noise, evening caffeine and a 3-hour afternoon nap are all modifiable causes of poor sleep: the nurse asks the provider to reduce overnight vital signs, closes the door and dims the lights, moves caffeine to the morning and limits naps to 30 minutes early in the afternoon. The complaint, normal temperature, scheduled antibiotic, leg elevation and usual bedtime are context, not factors the nurse can change.

items.stem: A nurse evaluates the bowel log of a long-term care resident 4 weeks after starting a program of scheduled toileting after breakfast, increased fluids and fiber, and daily walking. Which conclusion should the nurse draw?
options: Fluid intake is excessive for an older adult and should be reduced
The program is effective and should be continued as planned
The resident now has diarrhea and the fiber should be stopped
The program is ineffective and a daily stimulant laxative is needed
items.rationale: Bowel movements have increased from 2 to 6 per week, consistency has moved from hard Bristol type 1-2 stools to soft formed type 4, straining has stopped and fluid intake has reached a healthy level, so the program is meeting its goals and continues unchanged. Type 4 stool is normal, not diarrhea, so fiber stays; a daily stimulant laxative is unnecessary and risks dependence; and 1,800 mL daily is appropriate for an older adult without a fluid restriction.

items.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A client with a new descending colostomy is learning pouch care. The nurse teaches the client to empty the pouch when it is {{1}} full and to cut the skin barrier opening {{2}} larger than the stoma. The nurse explains that a healthy stoma looks {{3}}.

options: one-third to one-half
three-quarters
one-quarter
completely
10 mm (3/8 inch)
exactly the size of the stoma with no gap
the width of a fingertip
about 1.5 to 3 mm (1/16 to 1/8 inch)
dark purple
pink to red and moist
pale and dry
gray with a black edge

items.rationale: Emptying the pouch at one-third to one-half full prevents the weight of stool from breaking the seal and causing leakage. The barrier opening is cut just 1.5 to 3 mm larger than the stoma so that stool does not reach the peristomal skin while the stoma is not constricted. A healthy stoma is pink to red and moist because it is bowel mucosa; pale, purple, gray or black color indicates impaired blood flow and must be reported.

items.stem: A nurse cares for a confused 86-year-old client on a medical unit who repeatedly tries to climb out of bed and pulls at the IV line. Which alternatives to restraints should the nurse implement? Select all that apply.
options: Raise all four side rails to keep the client in bed
Move the client to a room near the nurses' station
Ask the family to bring familiar photographs and to stay at the bedside when possible
Check for pain, hunger, thirst and the need to toilet at regular intervals
Cover the IV site with a sleeve so it is out of sight
Keep the room dark and quiet during the day to reduce stimulation
Apply a soft wrist restraint whenever the client is alone
items.rationale: Placing the client near the nurses' station allows frequent observation, regular checks for pain, hunger, thirst and toileting remove common triggers for climbing out of bed, familiar objects and family presence reduce confusion, and covering the IV site removes the visual cue that prompts pulling. Four raised side rails and a soft wrist restraint are restraints, not alternatives, and a dark, quiet room during the day worsens day-night confusion.

items.stem: Click to highlight the findings in the nurses' note that require immediate follow-up.

highlightSegments.text: 1000 note: 66-year-old client receiving bolus feedings of 240 mL every 4 hours through a gastrostomy tube.
Head of bed at 40 degrees during and for 1 hour after each feeding.
Abdomen firm and distended; client reports nausea since the 0600 feeding.
External tube marking at 22 cm; documented at 18 cm on admission.
Skin around the insertion site clean and dry with no redness.
Formula at room temperature, container labeled with date and time.
Coughing and wheezing began about 20 minutes into the 1000 feeding, which was continued to completion.
Tube flushed with 30 mL of water before and after the feeding.
Blood glucose 146 mg/dL at 0730.
Client asks when a family member can be taught to give the feedings.

items.rationale: A firm, distended abdomen with nausea indicates intolerance or delayed emptying, a 4 cm change in the external tube marking suggests migration that must be verified before any further feeding, and coughing and wheezing that began during a feeding are aspiration cues, so continuing the bolus was unsafe; the nurse holds feedings, assesses the client and notifies the provider. Head-of-bed elevation, a clean site, labeled formula, routine flushes and a mildly elevated glucose are not urgent.

items.stem: A home health nurse reviews the measurements of a stage 3 sacral pressure injury over 5 weeks of care. Which conclusion should the nurse draw?
options: The wound is healing as expected and the current plan of care should continue
The wound is infected and a culture is needed
The wound should now be documented as a stage 2 pressure injury
Healing has stalled and the dressing should be changed to wet-to-dry gauze
items.rationale: Over 5 weeks the wound has shrunk in length, width and depth, slough has been replaced by red granulation tissue, the edges are contracting and drainage has decreased to scant serous fluid, all signs of expected healing, so the plan continues. Infection would show increasing drainage, odor, erythema or pain. Pressure injuries are never reverse-staged as they heal; this is documented as a healing stage 3 injury. Wet-to-dry gauze strips new granulation tissue.

items.stem: Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A client with right-sided weakness after a stroke is being transferred from the bed to a wheelchair. The nurse places the wheelchair on the client's {{1}} side, {{2}}, and applies a gait belt before helping the client stand.

options: right (weaker)
side facing the window
side closest to the door
left (stronger)
angled about 45 degrees to the bed with the brakes locked and footrests raised
facing the bed with the footrests lowered
directly at the foot of the bed
parallel to the bed with the brakes unlocked so it can be pulled closer

items.rationale: The wheelchair is placed on the client's stronger side so the client can lead with the strong leg and reach the armrest with the strong arm, angled about 45 degrees to the bed with the brakes locked and the footrests raised out of the way. A gait belt gives the nurse a secure grip. Placing the chair on the weak side, leaving the brakes unlocked, keeping the footrests down or positioning it at the foot of the bed increases the pivot distance and the risk of a fall.

items.stem: A nurse is choosing a comfort measure for each situation. For each situation, click to specify whether heat, cold, or neither is appropriate.
matrixRows: Acute ankle sprain that occurred 2 hours ago
Chronic low back stiffness on waking
Numb area over the sacrum with impaired sensation
Muscle spasm in the neck after a long day at a computer
Bruising and swelling around a new venipuncture hematoma
Perineal swelling in the first 24 hours after childbirth
items.rationale: Cold is used for the first 24 to 48 hours after acute injuries, hematomas and perineal swelling because vasoconstriction limits bleeding, edema and pain. Heat relaxes muscles and improves circulation, so it suits chronic stiffness and muscle spasm. Neither modality is applied to skin with impaired sensation, such as a numb sacral area, because the client cannot feel a developing burn or cold injury and tissue damage can occur unnoticed.

items.stem: Click to highlight the findings in the hospice nurse's visit note that indicate the client needs additional comfort measures.

highlightSegments.text: 1400 home hospice visit: 72-year-old client with end-stage lung cancer receiving comfort-focused care.
Family reports the client has been sleeping most of the day.
Respirations 24 with loud rattling secretions in the throat on each breath.
Lips cracked; tongue dry with crusted secretions.
Client grimaces and moans when turned and pulls away when the left hip is touched.
Skin cool and mottled over both knees.
Urine output about 200 mL, dark, over the last 24 hours.
Daughter has been giving sips of water with a spoon when the client is awake.
No bowel movement in 6 days; abdomen firm.
Family has the hospice contact numbers and the comfort kit is in the refrigerator.

items.rationale: Rattling secretions distress the family and are eased by side-lying positioning, raising the head and limiting fluids; cracked lips and a crusted tongue need mouth care every 1 to 2 hours; grimacing and guarding on movement indicate pain that needs assessment and analgesia; and 6 days without a bowel movement with a firm abdomen suggests constipation or impaction causing discomfort. Sleeping most of the day, cool mottled skin and low dark urine output are expected in the dying process.

items.stem: A nurse in a long-term care facility reviews the meal intake record for a resident with dysphagia after a diet texture change. Which conclusion should the nurse draw?
options: The resident can return to a regular diet because intake has improved
The increase in intake shows the dysphagia has resolved
The resident needs enteral feeding because intake is still below 100%
The texture-modified diet is meeting the resident's needs better and should continue
trendRows: Minced and moist, mildly thick liquids (after SLP evaluation)
Minced and moist, mildly thick liquids
items.rationale: After speech-language pathology recommended minced and moist foods with mildly thick liquids, intake rose from about 25% to 75 to 80% of meals and coughing during meals stopped, showing that the texture matches the resident's swallowing ability. Returning to a regular diet would restore the aspiration risk, intake of 75% does not meet criteria for enteral feeding, and better intake on a modified texture means the dysphagia is being managed, not that it has resolved.

items.stem: Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A resident with moderate dementia becomes agitated and strikes out during morning showers. The nurse should {{1}} and consider offering {{2}} to maintain hygiene while reducing distress.

options: stop and reapproach later, using a calm voice and explaining each step
tell the resident that showers are required by facility policy
skip hygiene for the rest of the week
continue the shower quickly with two staff holding the resident's arms
a cold shower to shorten the time needed
a full bath only when family members are present
a towel bath or bed bath at the time of day the resident is calmest
a sedative before each shower

items.rationale: Resistance to bathing in dementia is usually a response to fear, cold, pain or loss of control, so the nurse stops, reapproaches when the resident is calmer, and explains each step in a soothing voice. A towel bath or bed bath at the time of day the resident is most settled maintains hygiene with far less distress. Restraining the resident, forcing the shower, skipping hygiene or sedating the resident are unsafe or undignified alternatives.

items.stem: Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A 4-year-old with cerebral palsy and a history of aspiration pneumonia is being fed by mouth on the pediatric unit. The nurse positions the child {{1}}, offers {{2}}, and keeps the child upright for {{3}} after the meal.

options: on the caregiver's lap with the head tipped back
upright at 90 degrees with the head in midline and the chin slightly tucked
side-lying on the left side
reclined at 30 degrees with the head extended
small bites and sips, waiting for each swallow before offering more
liquids through a straw between bites
food only when the child is drowsy and calm
large bites to shorten the meal
the rest of the day
5 minutes
at least 30 minutes
2 hours

items.rationale: An upright 90-degree position with the head in midline and a slight chin tuck narrows the airway entrance and helps the child with poor oral-motor control swallow safely; reclining or extending the neck opens the airway to food. Small bites and sips with a pause for each swallow prevent pooling, whereas straws deliver liquid too quickly and a drowsy child has a weaker swallow. Remaining upright for at least 30 minutes after eating limits reflux and aspiration.

items.stem: Click to highlight the observations in the rehabilitation note that indicate the client needs further teaching on walker use.

highlightSegments.text: Rehab nursing note: 77-year-old client, postoperative day 4 after right total knee arthroplasty, using a standard walker.
Walker height adjusted so the handgrips are at wrist level with the elbows slightly bent.
Client lifts the walker and moves it forward about 15 cm, then steps the right leg forward, then the left.
When turning, the client carries the walker and pivots on the right knee.
Wearing nonskid shoes.
When rising from the chair, the client pulls up on the walker handgrips.
Walks with the walker held about 30 cm in front of the feet, leaning forward at the waist.
Reports knee pain 4/10 with walking.
Sits down by backing up until the chair touches the back of the legs, then reaches back for the armrests.
Stops to rest halfway down the hall and says, 'I feel steadier today.'

items.rationale: Carrying the walker while pivoting on the operative knee, pulling up on the walker to stand, and walking with the walker far ahead while leaning forward are unsafe: the walker can tip, and the client's center of gravity falls outside the base of support. The client should take small steps around a turn, push up from the chair armrests before grasping the walker, and stay inside the walker frame. Correct height, sequence, footwear, sitting technique and mild pain are appropriate.

items.stem: A nurse reviews the sleep log of a long-term care resident 1 week after starting a plan that limits naps to 30 minutes, adds daily outdoor light exposure, sets a later consistent bedtime, and stops caffeine after noon. Which conclusion should the nurse draw?
options: The plan is effective and should be maintained
Naps should be eliminated completely to improve sleep further
The resident is now sleeping too little and bedtime should return to 2000
The resident should be given a hypnotic because sleep onset is still delayed
items.rationale: Sleep onset has shortened from 75 to 20 minutes, awakenings have dropped from 4 to 1, and total sleep has risen to 7 hours while daytime napping decreased, so the sleep hygiene plan is working and continues. Total sleep increased even though time in bed decreased, which shows better sleep efficiency rather than deprivation. A 20-minute sleep onset is normal and does not warrant a hypnotic, and a brief early-afternoon nap is acceptable for an older adult.

items.stem: A nurse is checking meal trays on a surgical unit. For each food item, click to specify whether it is allowed on a clear liquid diet, allowed only on a full liquid diet, or not allowed on either diet.
matrixRows: Apple juice without pulp
Thinned cream of wheat cereal
Gelatin dessert
Vanilla ice cream
Scrambled eggs
Clear broth
Mashed potatoes
items.rationale: A clear liquid diet contains only fluids that are transparent and leave little residue, such as pulp-free juice, gelatin and clear broth. A full liquid diet adds milk-based and opaque liquids that are fluid at room temperature, such as thinned cooked cereal and ice cream. Scrambled eggs and mashed potatoes are solid foods that belong on a soft or regular diet, so they are not allowed on either liquid diet.

items.stem: Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A 78-year-old resident with urge incontinence is starting a bladder training program. The nurse teaches the resident to void {{1}} and, when a strong urge occurs before the scheduled time, to {{2}}.

options: once each morning and once at bedtime
every 30 minutes around the clock
only when the urge is felt
on a fixed schedule, such as every 2 hours, gradually lengthening the interval
stop, take slow deep breaths, and contract the pelvic floor muscles until the urge passes
rush to the toilet as quickly as possible
restrict all fluids for the rest of the day
use an absorbent brief instead of toileting

items.rationale: Bladder training uses scheduled voiding, typically every 2 hours, with the interval lengthened gradually so the bladder learns to hold more urine. When urgency strikes early, the resident stands still, breathes slowly and performs pelvic floor contractions, which suppress the detrusor contraction until the urge fades. Rushing to the toilet increases leakage and fall risk, fluid restriction concentrates urine and irritates the bladder, and briefs alone do not retrain the bladder.

items.stem: Click to highlight the findings in the admission nursing assessment that indicate the client is at nutritional risk.

highlightSegments.text: Admission assessment: 69-year-old client admitted for an elective colon resection scheduled tomorrow.
Height 175 cm, weight 61 kg; client reports a usual weight of 70 kg 'about 3 months ago.'
States appetite has been poor and 'nothing tastes right.'
Upper denture is loose; client avoids meat and raw vegetables.
Skin warm and dry, no lesions.
Lives alone and drives to the grocery store weekly.
Drinks 2 to 3 cups of tea daily, no alcohol.
Blood pressure 118/70, pulse 76.
Walks 1.5 km most mornings.
Prealbumin 12 mg/dL on preadmission labs.
Ate 100% of the evening clear liquid tray.

items.rationale: Unintentional loss of 9 kg, about 13% of body weight in 3 months, poor appetite with altered taste, a loose denture that limits protein and fiber intake, and a prealbumin of 12 mg/dL (normal about 15 to 36) together indicate malnutrition risk that should trigger a dietitian referral before surgery. Intact skin, independent shopping, moderate tea intake, normal vital signs, daily walking and finishing a clear liquid tray do not indicate nutritional risk.

items.stem: A nurse is changing the one-piece pouching system for a client with a new ileostomy. Place the steps in the correct order.
options: Measure the stoma and cut the barrier opening 1.5 to 3 mm larger than the stoma
Remove the old pouch by pushing the skin away from the barrier while supporting the skin
Hold a warm hand over the barrier for 30 to 60 seconds to seal the adhesive
Center the new barrier over the stoma and press it into place from the stoma outward
Clean the peristomal skin with warm water and pat it dry
items.rationale: The old pouch is removed gently by pushing the skin away from the barrier to avoid stripping the skin, then the peristomal skin is cleaned with water and patted dry so the new adhesive will stick. The stoma is measured at every change because its size shrinks for several weeks after surgery, and the opening is cut only slightly larger. The barrier is centered and pressed from the stoma outward to remove wrinkles, and warmth from the hand activates the adhesive for a lasting seal.

items.stem: A rehabilitation nurse reviews the voiding record of a client with urge incontinence 1 week after starting timed voiding with increased daytime fluids. Which conclusion should the nurse draw?
options: The voiding interval should be shortened back to 2 hours
The program is working: continence is improving as intake normalizes and the voiding interval lengthens
The post-void residuals indicate the client needs intermittent catheterization
Fluid intake should be cut back to 1,200 mL because episodes only fell after intake rose
items.rationale: Incontinence episodes fell from 6 to 1 per day while the voiding interval was extended to 3 hours and fluid intake rose to a normal 1,800 mL, so timed voiding is succeeding and the interval can keep lengthening as tolerated. Restricting fluids concentrates urine and worsens urgency, so it is not the reason episodes improved. Post-void residuals of 30 to 40 mL are well below the 100 mL threshold of concern and do not call for catheterization or a shorter interval.

items.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A nurse assesses a sacral wound on an immobile client: a shallow open area with a red-pink wound bed, no slough, measuring 3 cm by 2 cm. The nurse documents this as a {{1}} pressure injury and selects a {{2}} dressing to maintain a moist wound environment. The nurse also plans to reposition the client so that pressure is {{3}}.

options: stage 2
stage 1
deep tissue
stage 3
hydrocolloid or foam
povidone-iodine soaked gauze
dry gauze changed every shift
wet-to-dry gauze
distributed by keeping the client supine with the head of bed at 45 degrees
kept off the sacrum, using a 30-degree side-lying position
reduced by sitting in a chair for most of the day
relieved with a ring cushion under the sacrum

items.rationale: Partial-thickness skin loss with a viable pink-red bed and no slough defines a stage 2 pressure injury; stage 1 has intact skin, stage 3 shows full-thickness loss with visible fat, and deep tissue injury is intact purple or maroon skin. A hydrocolloid or foam dressing keeps the bed moist and protected; dry, wet-to-dry and iodine dressings dry or damage healing tissue. A 30-degree side-lying position unloads the sacrum, while supine at 45 degrees, ring cushions and prolonged sitting load it.

items.stem: Click to highlight the findings in the home health note that require the nurse to intervene.

highlightSegments.text: Home visit 1030: 70-year-old client with type 2 diabetes, peripheral neuropathy and chronic low back pain.
Client uses an electric heating pad on the low back for 20 minutes twice daily.
States the pad is set on high and 'I fall asleep with it on most nights.'
Reports lying on top of the heating pad while resting in bed.
Skin on the low back shows a reddish-brown mottled pattern.
Feet inspected: skin intact, no calluses; sensation reduced to the monofilament at 3 sites on each foot.
Client soaks the feet in hot water each evening 'to help them feel warmer.'
Fasting glucose log 110 to 160 mg/dL this week.
Ambulates independently with a cane inside the home.
Client asks whether a warm shower is safe in the morning.

items.rationale: Sleeping on a heating pad set to high, lying on top of the pad, and a reddish-brown mottled pattern (a sign of prolonged heat exposure) show the client is already being injured by heat, and hot foot soaks with neuropathy risk a burn the client cannot feel. The nurse teaches 20-minute applications on low, never lying on or sleeping with the pad, and checking water temperature with a thermometer. The 20-minute use, intact feet, glucose readings, cane use and shower question need no intervention.

items.stem: A nurse is recording oral intake for a client on strict intake and output. Which items should the nurse include in the oral intake total? Select all that apply.
options: Two slices of toast with butter
100 mL for a 200 mL cup of ice chips that the client finished
120 mL of gelatin dessert
120 mL of milk that the client drank from a 240 mL carton
Half of a grilled chicken breast
30 mL of mouthwash used to rinse and spit
180 mL of cream of mushroom soup
items.rationale: Oral intake includes everything that is liquid at room temperature, such as gelatin, soup and milk, and only the amount actually consumed is recorded, so half a carton of milk counts as 120 mL. Ice chips are recorded at about half their volume because they melt to roughly that amount of water. Solid foods such as chicken and toast are not counted as fluid, and mouthwash that is spit out is never swallowed, so it is not intake.

items.stem: A 6-year-old is about to have a peripheral IV inserted on the pediatric unit. Which non-pharmacologic comfort measure is most appropriate for the nurse to use?
options: Let the child blow bubbles or play a handheld game during the insertion
Ask the parent to leave the room so the child is less anxious
Explain the procedure in detail 2 days before admission
Tell the child the needle will not hurt at all
items.rationale: Distraction such as blowing bubbles, a game or a video is an effective, developmentally appropriate comfort measure for a school-age child during a brief painful procedure. Young children cope best with explanations given shortly before the event, not days ahead, because anticipation increases fear. Parental presence usually reduces distress, and promising that a needle will not hurt destroys trust when it does; honest, simple language is used instead.

items.stem: Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A home health nurse learns that an 82-year-old client with a history of falls drinks very little during the day 'so I do not have to get up at night.' The nurse suggests that the client {{1}} and explains that because thirst is blunted in older adults, fluids should be taken {{2}}.

options: drink most fluids before 1800 and keep a bedside commode and night light for safety
drink only when feeling thirsty
stop drinking after lunch
double the fluid intake at bedtime
on a schedule throughout the day rather than in response to thirst
only with meals
mainly as coffee and tea
in one large amount each morning

items.rationale: Shifting most fluid intake to earlier in the day keeps the client hydrated while reducing nighttime voiding, and a bedside commode with a night light makes any nighttime trip safer, addressing the fall fear directly. Older adults have a diminished thirst sensation, so waiting for thirst leads to dehydration; fluids are scheduled through the day. Stopping fluids after lunch causes dehydration, evening loading worsens nocturia, and caffeinated drinks increase urine output.

items.stem: Click to highlight the statements by the parent that indicate a need for further teaching about skin care.

highlightSegments.text: Well-child clinic: 9-month-old infant with a red rash in the diaper area for 5 days.
Parent states, 'I change the diaper about every 2 hours during the day and once during the night.'
'I use scented baby wipes and rub the area well to get it really clean.'
'I sprinkle on talcum powder to keep the skin dry.'
'I let the baby go without a diaper for a while after each change.'
'I put a thick layer of zinc oxide cream on at every change.'
'I fasten the diaper as tightly as I can so nothing leaks.'
'I wash the area with plain warm water when there is stool.'
Rash is bright red with satellite lesions in the skin folds.
'We switched to disposable diapers last week.'

items.rationale: Scented wipes and vigorous rubbing irritate and break down inflamed skin, talcum powder can be inhaled and cakes in skin folds where it traps moisture, and a tightly fastened diaper prevents air circulation and increases friction, so each of these statements needs correction. Frequent changes, air exposure, a thick barrier of zinc oxide and gentle water cleansing are correct care. The rash description is an assessment finding, not a parent statement about care.

items.stem: A nurse evaluates the comfort log for a nonverbal long-term care resident with advanced dementia. Which conclusion should the nurse draw?
options: The behaviors reflect dementia rather than pain and require no action
The resident is not in pain because the score improves slightly after each measure
Non-pharmacologic measures alone are not relieving the pain, so the provider should be contacted about analgesia
Comfort measures should be repeated more often until the score reaches 0
items.rationale: PAINAD scores of 6 to 7 with moaning, rigidity, clenched fists and refusing food indicate moderate to severe pain, and three rounds of non-drug measures produced at most a 1-point change, so the plan needs analgesia and the provider is contacted. A 1-point improvement does not rule out pain, repeating ineffective measures delays relief, and behavioral pain indicators in a person with dementia must be treated as pain until proven otherwise.

items.stem: Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A client in the final days of life has noisy, rattling respirations and is no longer swallowing. The family asks whether the client is choking. The nurse explains that the sound comes from {{1}} and then should {{2}}.

options: a blocked airway that must be suctioned deeply right away
the client trying to speak
fluid filling the lungs, which means the client is drowning
secretions pooling in the throat that the client can no longer clear, which usually does not distress the client
perform deep oropharyngeal suctioning every hour
begin chest physiotherapy
turn the client to the side, raise the head of the bed, and offer gentle mouth care
start oral fluids to thin the secretions

items.rationale: Terminal secretions collect in the pharynx when a dying client loses the swallow and cough reflex; the sound is usually more upsetting to the family than to the client. Side-lying with the head elevated lets secretions drain, and gentle mouth care keeps the mouth comfortable. Deep suctioning is distressing and stimulates more secretions, oral fluids cannot be swallowed and add volume, and chest physiotherapy is uncomfortable and inappropriate at this stage.

items.stem: A nurse is positioning clients on a medical-surgical unit. For each client, click to specify the position that is indicated.
matrixRows: Client with dyspnea during a heart failure exacerbation
Unconscious client with copious oral secretions
Client receiving continuous enteral feeding
Client 2 hours after a lumbar puncture with an order to lie flat
Client with a sacral pressure injury who needs pressure kept off the wound
items.rationale: High Fowler lowers the diaphragm and eases the work of breathing in heart failure. Side-lying lets secretions drain from the mouth of an unconscious client and also keeps the sacrum free of pressure when a wound is present. Semi-Fowler at 30 degrees or more reduces reflux and aspiration during continuous enteral feeding, and lying supine after a lumbar puncture, when ordered, reduces cerebrospinal fluid leakage and post-puncture headache.

items.stem: Click to highlight the findings in the nurses' note that indicate complications of immobility are developing.

highlightSegments.text: Day 6 note: 64-year-old client on bed rest after a pelvic fracture, log-rolled every 2 hours.
Breath sounds diminished in both bases with a moist cough producing thick yellow sputum.
Uses the incentive spirometer 10 times each hour while awake.
Both feet held in plantar flexion with limited dorsiflexion; client says the feet 'want to point down.'
Skin over both heels intact and pink.
No bowel movement in 4 days; client reports feeling bloated.
Urine clear yellow, 1,600 mL over 24 hours.
Blood pressure 132/78 lying; 104/62 sitting on the edge of the bed with dizziness.
Pelvic pain 3/10 with scheduled analgesia.
Family visits each evening and the client watches television.

items.rationale: Diminished basilar breath sounds with thick sputum point to atelectasis or hypostatic pneumonia, feet fixed in plantar flexion indicate developing footdrop, 4 days without stool with bloating indicates constipation from decreased peristalsis, and a 28 mm Hg drop in systolic pressure with dizziness on sitting is orthostatic hypotension from loss of vascular tone. Spirometer use, intact heels, adequate urine output, controlled pain and social activity are appropriate findings.

items.stem: Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A nurse in a memory care unit finds diffuse, blotchy redness with a few superficial erosions spread across the buttocks and perineum of a resident who is incontinent of urine and stool. The nurse identifies this as {{1}} and plans to {{2}}.

options: a deep tissue pressure injury
incontinence-associated dermatitis
a stage 1 pressure injury
a stage 2 pressure injury over both ischial tuberosities
cleanse gently with a pH-balanced no-rinse cleanser after each episode and apply a moisture barrier
scrub the area with soap and water and dry it with a hair dryer
keep the resident in an absorbent brief and check every 6 hours
apply a hydrocolloid dressing over the entire area

items.rationale: Diffuse, poorly defined redness with superficial erosions spread over skin folds and areas exposed to urine and stool is incontinence-associated dermatitis, a moisture injury, whereas pressure injuries are localized over bony prominences with defined edges. Care focuses on gentle pH-balanced cleansing after each episode, a barrier product and prompt changes. Soap and scrubbing strip the skin, a hydrocolloid traps moisture over a wet area, and 6-hour checks leave irritants on the skin too long.

items.stem: A nurse evaluates the intake record of a client with heart failure who is on a 1,500 mL daily fluid restriction. Which conclusion should the nurse draw?
options: Ice chips should be stopped because they add to the fluid intake
The comfort measures are helping the client stay within the restriction and should continue
The thirst rating shows the client is becoming dehydrated
The client is not drinking enough and the restriction should be liberalized
trendRows: Ice chips counted as intake, sugar-free gum
Ice chips, gum, frequent mouth care, fluids spread through the day
items.rationale: Intake has fallen from 2,100 mL to within the 1,500 mL limit while the thirst rating dropped from 8 to 3, so the mouth care, ice chips, gum and spacing of fluids are relieving thirst and supporting adherence. Intake of 1,450 mL is within the prescribed limit, not inadequate. Ice chips are counted at half volume and are an accepted thirst measure within the allowance, and a falling thirst score with intake at the limit does not indicate dehydration.

items.stem: A nurse is teaching a client receiving chemotherapy who has developed oral mucositis. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: Apply a water-based moisturizer to the lips
Brush with a soft toothbrush after each meal and at bedtime
Leave dentures out except for meals if the gums are sore
Suck on lemon-flavored hard candies to stimulate saliva
Rinse the mouth with a bland salt and baking soda solution every 2 to 4 hours while awake
Choose soft, cool or room-temperature foods and avoid citrus and spicy items
Use a commercial mouthwash that contains alcohol for a fresh feeling
items.rationale: Frequent bland rinses and gentle brushing with a soft brush keep the mouth clean and reduce infection without injuring inflamed mucosa, soft non-acidic foods at cool temperatures limit pain, removing dentures between meals prevents rubbing on sore gums, and a water-based lip moisturizer prevents cracking. Alcohol-containing mouthwash burns and dries the mucosa, and acidic lemon candies irritate open lesions; sugar-free, non-acidic lozenges are used for dry mouth instead.

items.stem: An older adult in a rehabilitation facility asks for a sleeping pill because 'I just cannot fall asleep in this place.' Which nursing action is most appropriate first?
options: Ask about the client's usual bedtime routine at home and replicate it as closely as possible
Offer a large glass of warm water at bedtime
Contact the provider for a hypnotic order
Encourage a 2-hour nap each afternoon so the client is less tired at night
items.rationale: Sleep problems in a new setting are usually related to loss of familiar routine, so the nurse first assesses the client's home habits (bedtime, lighting, reading, warm drink, prayer) and recreates them, which is effective and avoids medication risks. Hypnotics increase fall and confusion risk in older adults and are reserved for when non-drug measures fail. A long afternoon nap reduces nighttime sleep drive, and a large drink at bedtime causes nocturia.

items.stem: A home health nurse interviews a client 3 weeks after discharge for a stroke. Click to highlight the statements that indicate the client is at risk for constipation.

highlightSegments.text: 'I sit in my recliner most of the day; walking to the kitchen tires me out.'
'My daughter cooks for me and I eat oatmeal with fruit most mornings.'
'I try not to drink much because getting to the bathroom is such a chore.'
'I take my blood pressure pill and the stool softener every morning.'
'When I feel the urge to go, I usually wait until my daughter is home to help me.'
'I use the raised toilet seat and grab bar the therapist ordered.'
'I had a bowel movement yesterday and it was soft.'
'I take an aluminum antacid for heartburn several times a day.'
'My weight has stayed about the same since I came home.'
'Physical therapy comes twice a week.'

items.rationale: Prolonged sitting slows peristalsis, deliberately limiting fluids hardens stool, repeatedly ignoring the urge to defecate blunts the defecation reflex, and aluminum-containing antacids are constipating, so each statement is a risk factor the nurse addresses through activity, fluids, prompt toileting and a review of the antacid with the provider. A high-fiber breakfast, a daily stool softener, adaptive toilet equipment, a recent soft stool and stable weight are protective or neutral findings.

items.stem: Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A client receiving continuous positive airway pressure through a full-face mask in the ICU has redness across the bridge of the nose that does not blanch when pressed. The nurse recognizes a {{1}} and should {{2}}.

options: medical device-related pressure injury
normal mask imprint that will fade
contact dermatitis from the mask material
stage 3 pressure injury
stop the therapy until the redness resolves
massage the nose to restore circulation
tighten the straps to stop movement and air leak
apply a protective foam dressing under the mask edge and check the skin at least every 2 hours

items.rationale: Nonblanchable redness under a device is a medical device-related pressure injury at stage 1; a mask imprint blanches and fades, dermatitis is itchy and diffuse, and stage 3 requires full-thickness skin loss. The nurse pads the bridge of the nose with thin foam, loosens the straps to the minimum that prevents leak, and inspects the skin with each check. Tightening straps increases pressure, massage damages injured tissue, and stopping ordered respiratory support is not a nursing decision.

items.stem: Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A nurse finds that a client's nasogastric feeding tube will not flush and the pump is alarming for occlusion. The nurse should first {{1}}; if the tube remains blocked, the nurse should {{2}}.

options: check the tubing for kinks and try a gentle push-pull flush with warm water in a 30 to 60 mL syringe
instill a carbonated beverage and clamp the tube for an hour
reinsert the stylet to clear the blockage
force the flush through with a 3 mL syringe
remove the tube and reinsert it without an order
notify the provider about a declogging protocol or tube replacement
leave the tube in place and hold feedings for 24 hours
thread a guidewire through the tube

items.rationale: Kinks and clamped tubing are the most common causes of an occlusion alarm, and warm water with gentle push-pull pressure in a large syringe dissolves most formula plugs. Small syringes generate high pressure that can rupture the tube, stylets and guidewires can perforate the tube or the gut, and carbonated drinks are acidic and curdle formula. A tube that stays blocked needs a provider order for an enzyme declogging protocol or replacement, not unsupervised removal or a prolonged feeding hold.

items.stem: Click to highlight the findings in the nurses' note that require follow-up after removal of the indwelling urinary catheter.

highlightSegments.text: 1500 note: 71-year-old client, postoperative day 3 after bowel resection; indwelling catheter removed at 0700.
Oral intake since 0700: 1,100 mL.
Client has voided twice, 40 mL and 60 mL, and reports a constant urge to void.
Bladder scan at 1445 shows 520 mL.
Lower abdomen firm and tender above the pubic bone.
Ambulated to the bathroom with standby assistance.
Temperature 37.3 C (99.1 F), pulse 88.
Incision pain 3/10.
Client states, 'I keep trying but only a dribble comes out.'
Dressing dry and intact; bowel sounds present in all quadrants.

items.rationale: Small frequent voids with a constant urge, a scanned volume of 520 mL, a firm tender suprapubic area and dribbling indicate urinary retention with overflow 8 hours after catheter removal; the nurse promotes voiding with privacy, running water and an upright position and notifies the provider, because a scanned volume above about 300 to 400 mL usually requires straight catheterization. Adequate intake, ambulation, normal vital signs, mild pain and an intact dressing are expected.

items.stem: A nurse in a long-term care facility reviews the nutrition trend for a resident 3 months after the team started assisted feeding at meals, favorite foods, and twice-daily oral supplements. Which conclusion should the nurse draw?
options: The albumin value shows the resident is still malnourished and the plan is failing
The resident needs a feeding tube because meal intake is still below 100%
The supplements should be stopped now that weight has returned to baseline
The interventions are reversing the weight loss and should be continued
items.rationale: Meal intake has climbed from 40% to 70%, the resident now takes both supplements, albumin has risen to a normal 3.4 g/dL and weight has recovered above baseline, so the nutrition plan is working and continues. Eating 70% of meals with supplements is adequate oral nutrition and does not justify a feeding tube. Stopping supplements as soon as weight recovers risks a return to loss, and an albumin of 3.4 g/dL is within the normal range.

items.stem: Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A client returns from lumbar spinal fusion with an order to logroll for turning. To turn the client, the nurse obtains {{1}}, places a pillow {{2}}, and moves the client's shoulders and hips {{3}}.

options: a trapeze for the client to pull on
the client's agreement to twist at the waist
at least two other staff members and a draw sheet
a mechanical lift
under the lumbar spine
under the client's head only
between the client's knees
across the client's chest
using only the bed's tilt feature
as one unit on the count of three, keeping the spine aligned
with the client's help by twisting the trunk
one at a time, shoulders first

items.rationale: Logrolling keeps the spine in straight alignment after spinal surgery, which requires a draw sheet and enough staff, usually three, so the head, trunk and legs move together on a coordinated count. A pillow between the knees keeps the hips aligned and prevents the upper leg from pulling the spine into rotation. Turning the shoulders before the hips, letting the client twist, or pulling on a trapeze twists the surgical site; a mechanical lift is for lifting, not turning in bed.

items.stem: A nurse assesses clients with new ostomies on a surgical unit. For each finding, click to specify whether it is expected or requires intervention.
matrixRows: Stoma is moist and beefy red
Stoma appears dusky purple
Mild swelling of the stoma 2 days after surgery
Peristomal skin is red and weeping in a pattern that matches pouch leakage
Ileostomy output is liquid, about 800 mL in 24 hours
No output from a colostomy for 2 days with abdominal cramping
Small amount of bleeding when the stoma is wiped during cleaning
items.rationale: A moist beefy-red stoma, mild early postoperative edema, liquid ileostomy output of 500 to 1,200 mL a day and slight bleeding from the vascular mucosa when wiped are all normal. A dusky or purple stoma signals compromised blood flow and must be reported immediately. Peristomal skin breakdown that follows the pattern of leakage means the pouch fit must be corrected, and absent colostomy output with cramping suggests obstruction that needs provider evaluation.

items.stem: Click to highlight the findings in the rehabilitation admission note that place the client at risk for aspiration.

highlightSegments.text: Rehab admission: 68-year-old client with Parkinson disease admitted after a fall at home.
Speech is soft; speech-language pathology evaluation is scheduled for tomorrow.
Client drools and reports that food 'sticks' in the throat.
Lunch was eaten in bed reclined at about 30 degrees because the client was tired.
Takes 20 to 30 seconds to swallow each bite and coughs after drinking coffee.
Blood pressure 122/70 sitting and 106/64 standing, without dizziness.
Ambulates with a front-wheeled walker and standby assistance.
Takes levodopa-carbidopa on schedule 30 minutes before meals.
Skin intact, no edema.
Family brought a favorite thin soup from home for dinner.

items.rationale: Drooling and food sticking show poor oral control and delayed pharyngeal clearance, eating semi-reclined lets food fall toward the airway, a prolonged swallow with coughing after thin coffee signals thin-liquid aspiration, and thin soup from home before the swallow evaluation repeats that risk. The nurse sits the client fully upright for meals and holds thin liquids until speech-language pathology assesses. Soft speech, blood pressure, walker use, medication timing and skin are not cues.

items.stem: A telehealth nurse speaks with the parent of a 5-year-old 3 days after tonsillectomy. Click to highlight the statements that indicate the child needs to be evaluated in person today.

highlightSegments.text: Parent reports on day 3 after the child's tonsillectomy:
'She drank about a cup of fluid all day yesterday and refuses everything today.'
'She has had one wet pull-up since this morning and it was dark yellow.'
'Her pain medicine is given on schedule but she says the pain is 8 out of 10.'
'She had a low fever, 38.0 C (100.4 F), that came down with the fever medicine.'
'She cries without tears and her lips look cracked.'
'She is sleeping more than usual but wakes easily.'
'Her breath smells bad.'
'She has not had a bowel movement since the surgery.'
'She spat out some saliva with dark brown streaks this morning.'

items.rationale: Refusing all fluids after taking only a cup the day before, a single dark void, crying without tears and cracked lips are signs of dehydration in a young child, and pain rated 8 of 10 despite scheduled analgesia is the barrier to drinking, so the child needs same-day evaluation for hydration and pain management. A low-grade fever that responds to antipyretics, extra sleep with easy arousal, bad breath, a delayed bowel movement and dark brown (old blood) streaks are expected after tonsillectomy.

items.stem: Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A client with a perineal laceration after childbirth is prescribed sitz baths for comfort. The nurse teaches the client to use water that is {{1}} for {{2}} and afterward to {{3}}.

options: as hot as can be tolerated
room temperature
warm, about 38 to 40 C (100 to 104 F)
cold with ice added
15 to 20 minutes, 2 to 4 times a day
1 hour after every void
45 minutes at bedtime
5 minutes once daily
rub the area dry with a towel
apply an ice pack immediately
add antiseptic soap to the water next time
pat the area dry from front to back

items.rationale: Warm water at about 38 to 40 C increases perineal circulation, relaxes the muscles and soothes pain without burning; very hot water risks a burn, and cold sitz baths are used only in the first 24 hours for swelling. Sessions of 15 to 20 minutes two to four times daily give relief without excessive vasodilation. Patting dry from front to back prevents trauma and keeps rectal organisms away from the wound; rubbing irritates, ice after warm therapy is contradictory, and soap irritates the tissue.

items.stem: A hospice nurse is caring for a client in the last days of life whose family asks how to keep the client comfortable. Which measures should the nurse teach the family? Select all that apply.
options: Insist that the client eat three meals a day to keep up strength
Use a light blanket and a small fan for air movement if breathing is labored
Moisten the lips and mouth with swabs every 1 to 2 hours
Keep the room brightly lit with the television on to provide stimulation
Speak to the client as if the client can hear, even when unresponsive
Wake the client every hour to ask about pain
Turn and reposition gently every 2 hours, using pillows for support
items.rationale: Frequent mouth moistening prevents the discomfort of a dry mouth, gentle repositioning with pillows prevents pressure and stiffness, hearing is thought to persist so the family is encouraged to talk to the client, and a light cover with moving air eases breathlessness. Forcing food causes nausea and aspiration when the body is shutting down, bright light and noise disturb rest, and waking the client hourly prevents comfort; pain is assessed through behavior while the client rests.

items.stem: Click to highlight the findings in the wound care note that the nurse should report to the provider.

highlightSegments.text: Wound care note 0900: stage 3 pressure injury over the left ischial tuberosity, foam dressing changed every 3 days.
Wound measures 3.5 cm x 3.0 cm x 1.0 cm, unchanged from last week.
Periwound skin is red, warm and firm, extending 4 cm beyond the wound edge.
Drainage has increased to a large amount, thick and green with a foul odor.
Wound bed 70% red, 30% yellow slough.
Client reports new throbbing pain in the wound rated 6/10, previously 2/10.
Temperature 38.3 C (100.9 F) this morning.
Repositioned every 2 hours per schedule; heels floated.
Ate 60% of breakfast with a supplement.
Pressure-redistribution mattress in place.

items.rationale: Spreading periwound erythema with warmth and induration, a change to large, thick, green, foul-smelling drainage, new increasing pain and a fever of 38.3 C are the classic signs of wound infection, which requires provider notification for culture and treatment. Unchanged measurements over a week, a partly sloughy bed, the turning schedule, heel floating, meal intake and the support surface are routine findings documented in the plan and do not need reporting.

items.stem: A nurse is transferring a client with left-sided weakness from the bed to a wheelchair using a gait belt. Place the steps in the correct order.
options: Help the client stand on the count of three, blocking the weaker knee with the nurse's knee
Lock the bed and wheelchair brakes with the chair positioned on the client's stronger side
Apply the gait belt snugly around the client's waist
Assist the client to sit on the edge of the bed and dangle, checking for dizziness
Lower the client into the chair while bending at the knees
Pivot the client until the chair touches the back of the legs
items.rationale: Preparation comes first: the chair is placed on the stronger side and both sets of brakes are locked so nothing rolls. The client then sits on the edge of the bed and dangles, which reveals orthostatic dizziness before standing. The gait belt is applied while the client is seated, the client stands on a coordinated count with the weak knee blocked, pivots toward the strong side until the chair is felt against the legs, and is lowered while the nurse bends at the knees to protect the back.

items.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A 15-year-old athlete comes to the school clinic with a knee injury that occurred 30 minutes ago. The school nurse applies an ice pack {{1}} for {{2}} and elevates the leg. The nurse removes the ice pack early if the skin becomes {{3}}.

options: directly on the skin for the fastest effect
wrapped in a thin towel, never directly on the skin
under an elastic bandage pulled tight
only after the swelling has gone down
5 minutes only
no more than 20 minutes at a time, repeated after an hour off
1 hour continuously
the rest of the school day
dry
warm to the touch
pale, mottled or numb
cool and slightly pink

items.rationale: Cold applied in the first 24 to 48 hours after an acute injury limits swelling, bleeding and pain, but ice is always wrapped in a cloth barrier because direct contact causes frostbite. Applications last no more than 20 minutes because longer exposure triggers reflex vasodilation and tissue injury, and the pack is removed early if the skin turns pale, mottled or numb, which signals impaired circulation. Cool, slightly pink skin is the expected response; waiting for swelling to resolve defeats the purpose.

items.stem: A nurse reviews the mobility progression of an older adult who was on bed rest for 5 days with pneumonia. Which conclusion should the nurse draw?
options: The dizziness on day 1 indicates a cardiac problem requiring immediate evaluation
The client is ready to walk independently without a device or supervision
The client should remain on bed rest until standing pressure equals sitting pressure
Orthostatic tolerance is improving and progressive ambulation should continue
items.rationale: The drop in blood pressure on standing has narrowed from 24 to 8 mm Hg systolic, dizziness has resolved, and walking distance has doubled each day with less help, showing that vascular tone lost during bed rest is recovering; the plan of dangling, standing and longer walks continues. Waiting for identical sitting and standing pressures prolongs immobility, standby help with a walker is still needed on day 4, and the day 1 orthostatic drop is an expected effect of bed rest, not a cardiac emergency.

items.stem: Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A nurse applies an external (condom) urinary catheter to a male resident with urinary incontinence. The nurse leaves {{1}} between the tip of the penis and the end of the sheath, secures it with {{2}}, and checks the skin {{3}}.

options: 2.5 to 5 cm (1 to 2 inches)
the width of three fingers
10 cm (4 inches)
no space, so the sheath fits snugly against the tip
an elastic bandage
the manufacturer's adhesive strip or self-adhesive sheath applied without wrinkles
a rubber band at the base
regular adhesive tape wrapped tightly around the shaft
at least every 4 hours for swelling or color change
every 24 hours when the device is changed
once a week when the device is changed
only if the resident reports pain

items.rationale: A gap of 2.5 to 5 cm between the glans and the end of the sheath keeps urine from pooling against the skin and prevents the tip from kinking; a snug fit or a large gap causes leakage or twisting. Only the manufacturer's adhesive is used, applied spirally without wrinkles, because tape, rubber bands or elastic wraps constrict blood flow. The device is changed daily, but the skin under it is inspected at least every 4 hours for swelling, color change or leakage so ischemia is caught early.

items.stem: Click to highlight the findings in the oral assessment that require nursing intervention.

highlightSegments.text: Oral assessment: 90-year-old long-term care resident, dependent for hygiene, wears full dentures.
Dentures found in a dry cup on the nightstand with dried food debris on the surface.
Tongue coated with a thick white film; resident reports a burning sensation when eating.
Lips pink, moist and intact.
Resident reports the lower denture 'rocks' and has caused a sore on the gum.
Mouth care documented once in the past 3 days.
Gums pink without bleeding.
Resident drinks about 1,500 mL of fluid daily.
Resident is able to hold a toothbrush when supplies are set up.
No swelling or lesions under the tongue.

items.rationale: Dirty dentures stored dry harbor organisms and warp, a thick white coating with burning suggests oral candidiasis that needs assessment and treatment, a rocking denture that has caused a gum sore needs a dental referral and should be left out until fitted, and mouth care once in 3 days falls far short of the twice-daily standard for a dependent resident. Moist lips, healthy gums, adequate fluids, the ability to brush with setup and a normal sublingual area are appropriate findings.

items.stem: Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A client receiving hemodialysis is on a renal diet with sodium and potassium restrictions. When reviewing the client's food diary, the nurse is most concerned about the daily {{1}} and suggests replacing it with {{2}}.

options: cup of cooked green beans
slice of white bread with unsalted butter
baked potato with the skin and a glass of orange juice
serving of plain white rice
white rice and applesauce
potatoes seasoned with a salt substitute
tomato juice
a banana and a glass of milk

items.rationale: Potatoes with skin and orange juice are among the highest-potassium foods, so they are the greatest concern for a client whose kidneys cannot excrete potassium. White rice and applesauce are low in potassium and sodium. Salt substitutes are made of potassium chloride, bananas and milk are high in potassium and milk also adds phosphorus, and tomato juice is high in both potassium and sodium. White bread, plain rice and green beans are acceptable renal diet choices.

items.stem: A rehabilitation nurse reviews client statements about using assistive devices. For each statement, click to specify whether the statement is correct or needs correction.
matrixRows: 'I hold my cane on the same side as my weak leg.'
'I move my walker forward first, then step into it with my weaker leg.'
'I lead with my strong leg going up the stairs and my weak leg going down.'
'I keep my crutch tips dry and replace them when they wear down.'
'I carry my walker up the stairs so I do not have to leave it behind.'
'I look down at my feet while walking with the cane so I do not trip.'
items.rationale: A cane is held on the strong side so it shares the load with the weak leg, and looking down at the feet shifts the center of gravity forward and increases fall risk; the client looks ahead. Standard walkers are not used on stairs, so carrying one up the steps is unsafe and a handrail or crutches are used instead. Advancing the walker and then stepping in with the weaker leg, leading with the strong leg up and the weak leg down, and maintaining crutch tips are all correct techniques.

items.stem: Click to highlight the parts of the nurses' note that describe appropriate alternatives to restraint.

highlightSegments.text: 2200 note: 79-year-old client, postoperative day 1, disoriented to place and time, attempting to remove the oxygen cannula.
Reoriented the client in a calm voice and turned on a low light so the room is visible.
Placed the client's glasses and hearing aid.
Told the client that restraints would be applied if the cannula came off again.
Assessed pain at 5/10, gave the scheduled analgesic, and assisted the client to the bedside commode.
Raised all four side rails and turned off the lights to encourage sleep.
Asked the client's spouse to stay at the bedside and bring the client's own blanket.
Bed alarm activated; client moved to the room across from the nurses' station.
Oxygen saturation 95% on 2 L by nasal cannula.
Will recheck the client every 15 minutes.

items.rationale: Calm reorientation with a low light, restoring glasses and hearing aids, meeting pain and toileting needs, family presence with familiar objects, and a bed alarm with a room near the station are evidence-based ways to reduce agitation and avoid restraint. Threatening restraints is coercive and frightening, and raising all four side rails is itself a restraint that increases injury if the client climbs over them. The saturation reading and recheck plan are documentation, not alternatives.

items.stem: A nurse reviews the tolerance record for a client whose continuous enteral feeding is being advanced toward a goal rate of 80 mL/hr. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Slow the feeding to the last tolerated rate per protocol and notify the provider
Advance to the goal rate to complete the titration
Stop the feeding and remove the tube
Give an antidiarrheal medication and continue at 70 mL/hr
items.rationale: Tolerance was good at 30 and 50 mL/hr, but at 70 mL/hr the client developed cramping, liquid stools, a 7 cm rise in abdominal girth and nausea, which are signs of intolerance, so the nurse returns to the last tolerated rate per the feeding protocol and reports the findings. Advancing further worsens the symptoms, removing the tube ends nutrition unnecessarily, and masking diarrhea with medication while continuing the same rate ignores the cause and leaves distention untreated.

items.stem: Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A resident who requires mildly thick liquids drinks less than 800 mL a day. To improve hydration without increasing aspiration risk, the nurse should offer {{1}} and {{2}}.

options: thickened fluids in small amounts every 1 to 2 hours while awake, in flavors the resident prefers
all fluids through a straw
thin water between meals because water is harmless if aspirated
large volumes at each meal only
ice chips freely throughout the day
gelatin and ice cream as extra fluid sources
moist foods such as pureed fruit and thickened soups, avoiding gelatin and ice cream that melt to thin liquid
carbonated drinks to encourage drinking

items.rationale: Residents on thickened liquids often drink less because the texture is unappealing, so hydration improves with frequent small offerings of preferred flavors rather than large volumes at meals. Water-rich foods add fluid, but gelatin, ice cream and ice chips melt to thin liquid in the mouth and carry the same aspiration risk as thin water, which is not harmless when aspirated. Straws propel liquid quickly to the pharynx and carbonated drinks are thin and unpredictable.

items.stem: Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A 3-year-old hospitalized with pneumonia cries at bedtime and refuses to settle. The nurse should {{1}} and {{2}}.

options: keep the child awake until the child is exhausted
leave the child alone in a dark room until the child falls asleep
ask the parent about the child's bedtime routine at home and follow it as closely as possible
tell the child that big children do not cry
perform vital signs every hour through the night
cluster nighttime care and allow a comfort object such as a favorite blanket
remove all toys from the crib
keep the hallway lights and television on for reassurance

items.rationale: Toddlers depend on ritual, so repeating the home bedtime routine (a story, a song, the same order of steps) and keeping a security object give a sense of control and safety in the strange hospital environment. Clustering care reduces awakenings. Shaming the child, isolating the child in the dark or exhausting the child increase fear and separation anxiety, hourly vital signs fragment sleep, and lights and television are stimulating rather than soothing.

items.stem: A nurse is administering a large-volume cleansing enema to an adult client with constipation. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.
options: Insert the lubricated tip 7.5 to 10 cm (3 to 4 inches) toward the umbilicus
Position the client in the left side-lying (Sims) position
Hang the solution container 90 cm (36 inches) above the rectum
Have the client hold the breath while the tip is inserted
Warm the solution to about body temperature
Instruct the client to expel the solution immediately after it is instilled
Clamp the tubing briefly if the client reports cramping
