items.rationale: Left Sims position follows the sigmoid colon so the solution flows in by gravity, solution near body temperature avoids cramping and mucosal injury, and a 7.5 to 10 cm insertion passes the anal sphincters without perforating the rectum. Pausing the flow relieves cramping. The container hangs only 30 to 45 cm above the rectum because greater height forces solution in too fast, the client retains the solution 5 to 10 minutes, and slow deep breathing rather than breath-holding relaxes the sphincter.

items.stem: A nurse inspects the heels of a client who has been immobile for a week. Which finding indicates a deep tissue pressure injury?
options: Full-thickness tissue loss with visible bone
Persistent purple discoloration of intact skin that does not blanch
Intact skin with redness that blanches with pressure
A shallow open ulcer with a pink wound bed
items.rationale: Deep tissue pressure injury is intact or non-intact skin with a localized area of persistent non-blanchable deep red, maroon or purple discoloration, or a blood-filled blister, caused by damage to underlying soft tissue from pressure and shear. A shallow open ulcer with a pink bed is a stage 2 injury, full-thickness loss with exposed bone is stage 4, and blanchable redness on intact skin is reactive hyperemia that has not yet become a pressure injury.

items.stem: A rehabilitation nurse reviews the record of a client with paraplegia after changing the sitting schedule and wheelchair cushion. Which conclusion should the nurse draw?
options: The day 1 finding was a stage 1 pressure injury that has healed
Sitting time can be extended back to 3 hours now that the redness has resolved
The shorter sitting sessions, cushion and weight shifts are protecting the sacral skin and should continue
The client no longer needs weight shifts because a cushion is in place
items.rationale: Redness that persisted for 40 minutes after sitting showed the tissue was near its tolerance limit; with shorter sessions, a pressure-redistribution cushion and weight shifts every 15 minutes the skin now shows no redness, so the plan is working and sitting time is increased only gradually while the skin is watched. Returning at once to 3 hours or dropping weight shifts removes the protection that produced the result, and blanchable redness is reactive hyperemia, not a stage 1 injury.

items.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A client at 10 weeks of gestation with an uncomplicated pregnancy asks how often prenatal visits will occur. The nurse explains that visits are scheduled every {{1}} until 28 weeks, then every 2 weeks until 36 weeks, and then {{2}} until birth.

options: 8 weeks
6 weeks
2 weeks
4 weeks
weekly
only when symptoms occur
every 2 weeks
every 3 days

items.rationale: The standard low-risk schedule is every 4 weeks through 28 weeks, every 2 weeks from 28 to 36 weeks, and weekly from 36 weeks until birth so that blood pressure, fetal growth and fetal position can be followed closely in the third trimester. Intervals of 6 to 8 weeks would miss the window for routine screening such as the 24 to 28 week glucose test, and visits limited to symptoms would not detect silent problems such as rising blood pressure.

items.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A client at 33 weeks of gestation calls the clinic reporting a persistent headache unrelieved by acetaminophen, spots in the vision, and sudden swelling of the face and hands. The nurse recognizes these as warning signs of {{1}} and instructs the client to {{2}}.

options: preeclampsia
gestational diabetes
migraine unrelated to pregnancy
normal third-trimester fluid retention
take a second dose of acetaminophen and lie on the left side
reduce salt intake and increase water
come in for evaluation today for blood pressure and urine protein assessment
rest with the feet elevated and call back tomorrow

items.rationale: A persistent headache, visual disturbances and sudden facial or hand edema after 20 weeks are classic warning signs of preeclampsia, which can progress rapidly to seizures or placental abruption. The client needs same-day evaluation of blood pressure, urine protein and laboratory values. Third-trimester dependent ankle edema is common, but facial and hand swelling with neurologic symptoms is not, and delaying evaluation or treating the symptoms at home is unsafe.

items.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: At a routine prenatal visit the nurse explains that screening for gestational diabetes is performed between {{1}} of gestation using a {{2}}; a result of 140 mg/dL or higher requires a diagnostic 3-hour oral glucose tolerance test.

options: 16 and 20 weeks
36 and 38 weeks
8 and 12 weeks
24 and 28 weeks
fasting plasma glucose after 12 hours without food
finger-stick glucose 2 hours after a regular meal
hemoglobin A1c drawn with the routine prenatal labs
50 g glucose load with a plasma glucose drawn 1 hour later, no fasting required

items.rationale: Placental hormones cause insulin resistance that peaks in the late second trimester, so universal screening is done at 24 to 28 weeks with a nonfasting 50 g glucose challenge and a 1-hour plasma glucose. A value of 140 mg/dL or higher is followed by the fasting 100 g, 3-hour oral glucose tolerance test for diagnosis. Early first-trimester testing is reserved for clients with risk factors, and hemoglobin A1c and random finger-stick values are not the accepted screening tools in pregnancy.

items.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A client whose blood type is O negative has a negative antibody screen at the first prenatal visit. The nurse teaches that Rh immunoglobulin is given at {{1}} and again within {{2}} after birth if the newborn is Rh positive, and that it is also indicated after {{3}}.

options: the onset of labor
28 weeks of gestation
12 weeks of gestation
20 weeks of gestation
72 hours
7 days
2 weeks
24 hours
a normal ultrasound
amniocentesis or any bleeding episode during pregnancy
each prenatal visit
a negative glucose screen

items.rationale: An unsensitized Rh-negative client receives Rh immunoglobulin prophylactically at 28 weeks and again within 72 hours of birth if the newborn is Rh positive, which prevents the maternal immune system from forming antibodies against fetal red cells. Any event that could mix fetal and maternal blood, such as amniocentesis, abdominal trauma, miscarriage or vaginal bleeding, is an additional indication. Routine visits and normal imaging do not cause fetomaternal hemorrhage and do not require a dose.

items.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A client at 30 weeks of gestation is taught to count fetal movements at the same time each day. The nurse instructs the client to lie on the side after a meal and expect at least {{1}}; if that count is not reached, the client should {{2}}.

options: 5 movements within 12 hours
3 movements within 4 hours
10 movements within 2 hours
20 movements within 30 minutes
drink cold water and count again in 24 hours
record the result and mention it at the next visit
wait and repeat the count the next morning
contact the provider or labor unit the same day for fetal evaluation

items.rationale: A commonly taught method is to count fetal movements after a meal while lying on the side and expect at least 10 movements within 2 hours. Fewer movements than expected can be an early sign of fetal compromise, so the client should call the same day for a nonstress test or other evaluation rather than waiting. Repeating the count the next day or deferring the concern to a scheduled visit could delay recognition of a fetus in distress.

items.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A client in labor is 6 cm dilated with contractions every 3 minutes lasting 60 seconds. The nurse documents that the client has entered the {{1}} of the first stage of labor; the second stage begins when {{2}} and ends with {{3}}.

options: transition phase
fourth stage
active phase
latent phase
the membranes rupture
the fetal head is visible at the perineum
the cervix is completely dilated at 10 cm
contractions occur every 2 minutes
the birth of the infant
complete cervical effacement
the first 2 hours of recovery
the delivery of the placenta

items.rationale: Current labor definitions place the start of the active phase at 6 cm of dilation, when cervical change is expected to speed up. The second stage begins with complete dilation at 10 cm and ends with the birth of the infant; the third stage is delivery of the placenta and the fourth stage is the first 1 to 2 hours of recovery. Rupture of membranes and crowning are events within labor but do not define the stage boundaries.

items.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: During oxytocin augmentation, the nurse observes fetal heart rate decelerations that begin after the peak of each contraction and return to baseline after the contraction ends. The nurse identifies these as {{1}} decelerations caused by {{2}} and should first {{3}}.

options: variable
prolonged
late
early
umbilical cord compression
uteroplacental insufficiency
maternal fever
fetal head compression
encourage the client to push with each contraction
prepare for immediate amniotomy
stop the oxytocin infusion and reposition the client to the side
increase the oxytocin rate to shorten labor

items.rationale: A gradual deceleration that starts after the contraction peak and recovers after the contraction ends is a late deceleration, which reflects uteroplacental insufficiency. Because oxytocin increases uterine activity and further reduces placental perfusion, it is stopped and the client is turned to the side, followed by IV fluid bolus and oxygen as ordered. Early decelerations mirror the contraction and are benign, and variable decelerations are abrupt and caused by cord compression.

items.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: Two hours after a vaginal birth the nurse finds the fundus boggy, 2 cm above the umbilicus, and deviated to the right of midline. The nurse interprets this as {{1}} and should first {{2}}.

options: retained placental fragments
a distended bladder displacing the uterus
normal involution for the first day
uterine inversion
apply an ice pack to the perineum
notify the provider for a bedside ultrasound
administer the ordered methylergonovine immediately
assist the client to void, then massage the fundus and reassess

items.rationale: A fundus above the umbilicus and deviated to one side is the classic sign of a full bladder pushing the uterus out of position, which prevents it from contracting and increases bleeding. The nurse has the client empty the bladder, then massages the fundus and reassesses; a uterotonic is reserved for atony that persists after these measures. Normal involution leaves the fundus firm and midline at or below the umbilicus, and uterine inversion presents with the fundus absent from the abdomen.

items.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A client who is breastfeeding a 2-day-old newborn asks how to know the newborn is getting enough milk. The nurse explains that the newborn should feed at least {{1}}, and by day 5 to 6 should have at least {{2}} wet diapers in 24 hours and stools that have turned {{3}}.

options: only when crying
4 to 5 times in 24 hours
every 4 hours on a fixed schedule
8 to 12 times in 24 hours
black and tarry
yellow and seedy
white and pasty
green and watery

items.rationale: Frequent feeding of 8 to 12 times a day on cue establishes supply and ensures adequate intake. Once milk volume increases, at least 6 wet diapers a day and transition from meconium to yellow, seedy stools by day 5 or 6 indicate the newborn is transferring enough milk. Scheduled or infrequent feeding reduces supply, crying is a late hunger cue, and black tarry stools after the first days or pale stools would signal a problem.

items.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: At a 3-week postpartum telehealth check, a client reports crying most days, not sleeping even when the baby sleeps, and feeling unable to care for the newborn. Because these symptoms have lasted beyond {{1}}, the nurse suspects {{2}} rather than postpartum blues and should {{3}}.

options: 2 days
6 months
2 weeks
1 week
normal adjustment to parenting
sleep deprivation only
postpartum depression
postpartum psychosis
administer a validated screening tool such as the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale and arrange provider follow-up
reassure the client that the feelings will pass with more rest
schedule a routine 6-week visit as planned
recommend stopping breastfeeding so others can help

items.rationale: Postpartum blues are mild, self-limited mood changes that peak around day 5 and resolve within 2 weeks. Tearfulness, insomnia even when able to sleep, and feeling unable to function beyond 2 weeks are consistent with postpartum depression and require a validated screen plus prompt provider follow-up with a safety assessment. Postpartum psychosis involves hallucinations or delusions and is an emergency, and reassurance or waiting for the 6-week visit leaves the client untreated.

items.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A term newborn is noted to have yellow skin on the face and chest at 18 hours of age. The nurse recognizes that jaundice appearing before {{1}} is considered {{2}} and should {{3}}.

options: 1 week of age
72 hours of age
5 days of age
24 hours of age
harmless if the newborn is feeding
physiologic and expected
a sign of breastfeeding jaundice that resolves with formula
pathologic and requires prompt bilirubin measurement
place the newborn in indirect sunlight by a window
document and reassess at 48 hours
offer glucose water between feedings
obtain a transcutaneous or serum bilirubin level and notify the provider

items.rationale: Physiologic jaundice appears after 24 hours of age as the newborn's liver adapts. Jaundice in the first 24 hours is always considered pathologic, most often from hemolysis such as ABO or Rh incompatibility, and bilirubin can rise quickly enough to threaten the brain, so a bilirubin level is measured promptly and the provider is notified. Window sunlight is not effective or safe therapy, waiting a day risks severe hyperbilirubinemia, and glucose water does not promote bilirubin excretion.

items.stem: Click to highlight the findings in the prenatal clinic note that the nurse should report to the provider before the client leaves.

highlightSegments.text: Prenatal visit, 32 weeks of gestation, first pregnancy.
Blood pressure 146/94 mm Hg, repeated after 15 minutes of rest 144/92 mm Hg.
Weight gain 2.5 kg since the visit 2 weeks ago.
Fundal height 32 cm; fetal heart rate 144/min.
Urine dipstick shows 2+ protein.
Client reports occasional heartburn after meals.
States the baby moves 'all the time, especially at night.'
Reports mild ankle swelling at the end of the day.
Has not yet completed the childbirth education class.
Reports a headache 'that comes and goes' over the past 2 days.

items.rationale: Two blood pressure readings of 140/90 mm Hg or higher after 20 weeks, proteinuria, a rapid weight gain that suggests fluid retention, and a new headache together point to preeclampsia and must be reported before the client leaves so labs and management can begin. A fundal height matching gestational age, a reassuring fetal heart rate, active fetal movement, heartburn and dependent ankle edema are expected findings in the third trimester.

items.stem: Click to highlight the findings in the labor nurse's note that require immediate intervention.

highlightSegments.text: 1400: Client at 39 weeks, 5 cm dilated, 90% effaced, station 0.
Oxytocin infusing at 8 mU/min.
Contractions every 90 seconds, lasting 90 seconds, with no return to resting tone between them.
Fetal heart rate baseline 150/min with moderate variability.
Recurrent decelerations beginning after the peak of the contraction and resolving after it ends.
Client using breathing techniques with partner at bedside.
Epidural placed at 1330; blood pressure 92/50 mm Hg, down from 118/72 mm Hg before placement.
IV lactated Ringer's infusing at 125 mL/hr.
Client reports pressure with contractions and asks about pushing.
Voided 250 mL clear urine at 1345.

items.rationale: Contractions every 90 seconds without return to resting tone are uterine tachysystole from oxytocin, recurrent late decelerations show the fetus is not tolerating it, and post-epidural hypotension further reduces placental perfusion; the nurse stops the oxytocin, repositions the client, gives a fluid bolus and notifies the provider. A baseline of 150/min with moderate variability is reassuring, and the labor progress, coping, IV rate and voiding are expected findings.

items.stem: Click to highlight the client statements during postpartum discharge teaching that indicate a need for further teaching.

highlightSegments.text: "I know I should call if I soak more than one pad in an hour."
"A small gush of blood when I first stand up is expected in the early days."
"If my bleeding turns bright red again after it has turned pink, I'll just rest more."
"I'll take my temperature if I feel chilled, and call for 38 C (100.4 F) or higher."
"My pain pills will handle a bad headache with spots in my vision."
"I'll keep taking my iron and stool softener."
"After my cesarean, I can drive as soon as I get home."
"I'll call if one calf becomes painful or swollen."
"I can have sex once the bleeding stops, and breastfeeding means I don't need birth control."
"Feeling weepy for a few days is common, but I'll call if it lasts over 2 weeks."

items.rationale: Lochia that returns to bright red after turning pink suggests subinvolution or retained fragments and must be reported, not rested away. A severe headache with visual changes is a preeclampsia warning sign that needs evaluation, not analgesics. Driving waits after cesarean birth until the client is off opioids and can brake without pain, and breastfeeding is not reliable contraception. The other statements show correct understanding of bleeding, fever, clot and mood warning signs.

items.stem: Click to highlight the findings in the newborn assessment note that require follow-up by the nurse.

highlightSegments.text: Term newborn, 6 hours of age, born by vaginal birth; Apgar 8 and 9.
Axillary temperature 36.1 C (97 F) in an open crib.
Heart rate 138/min; respirations 52/min, unlabored.
Soft, diffuse swelling over the top of the scalp that crosses the suture line.
Small white papules across the nose.
Bluish hands and feet with pink trunk.
Respiratory rate rises to 70/min with nasal flaring and grunting during the exam.
Has not voided since birth; passed meconium at 3 hours.
Blood glucose 32 mg/dL, obtained because the newborn weighs 4,300 g.
Attempted breastfeeding twice with brief latch.

items.rationale: An axillary temperature below 36.5 C (97.7 F) indicates cold stress, which increases oxygen and glucose consumption; tachypnea with flaring and grunting signals respiratory distress; and a glucose of 32 mg/dL in a macrosomic newborn is hypoglycemia that needs feeding and rechecking per protocol. Caput succedaneum, milia and acrocyanosis are normal newborn findings, voiding within the first 24 hours is expected, and brief early latches are common in the first hours.

items.stem: Click to highlight the parts of the first prenatal visit history that identify the client as at increased risk and require follow-up planning.

highlightSegments.text: Client, 36 years old, presents at 9 weeks of gestation by last menstrual period.
Gravida 3, para 2; both previous births were vaginal at term.
Reports that the second child was born weighing 4,400 g.
Height 165 cm; pre-pregnancy weight 62 kg.
Blood pressure 116/70 mm Hg.
Takes a daily prenatal vitamin started 3 months before conception.
Smokes 'about 5 cigarettes a day' and is 'trying to cut down.'
Works from home as an accountant.
Rubella immune; blood type A positive.
Reports nausea most mornings that improves with crackers.

items.rationale: Age 35 or older increases the risk of chromosomal abnormalities, hypertension and gestational diabetes and prompts discussion of genetic screening. A previous infant over 4,000 g is a risk factor for gestational diabetes and warrants early glucose screening. Smoking raises the risk of placental problems, growth restriction and preterm birth, so cessation support is planned. Prior term births, normal weight and blood pressure, rubella immunity, an Rh-positive type and morning nausea add no risk.

items.stem: Click to highlight the findings in the postpartum assessment note that suggest a developing infection and should be reported to the provider.

highlightSegments.text: Postpartum day 2 after a cesarean birth for arrest of labor; membranes were ruptured for 26 hours before surgery.
Temperature 38.6 C (101.5 F), heart rate 108/min, blood pressure 112/68 mm Hg.
Fundus firm at the umbilicus, tender to light palpation beyond the incision.
Lochia rubra, moderate, with a foul odor.
Incision edges approximated, dressing dry, no redness or drainage.
Breasts filling, slightly firm, nipples intact.
Ambulating in the hall with assistance; tolerating a regular diet.
Reports incision pain 4/10 controlled with oral analgesics.
Voided 400 mL after catheter removal this morning.
Newborn rooming in and breastfeeding every 2 to 3 hours.

items.rationale: Fever with tachycardia, uterine tenderness that extends beyond the incision, and foul-smelling lochia are the hallmark findings of endometritis, which is more likely after prolonged rupture of membranes and cesarean birth; the provider is notified for cultures and antibiotics. The clean incision, breast filling on day 2, ambulation, controlled pain, adequate voiding and frequent breastfeeding are expected recovery findings and are not signs of infection.

items.stem: Click to highlight the statements by a client on postpartum day 4 that indicate breastfeeding is going well.

highlightSegments.text: "The baby feeds about 9 or 10 times a day and I can hear swallowing."
"My breasts feel full before a feeding and softer afterward."
"The baby's lips are tucked in and it pinches the whole time."
"I have been giving a bottle of formula at night so the baby will sleep longer."
"Yesterday there were 6 wet diapers and 4 yellow, seedy stools."
"My nipples are cracked and bleeding on the right side."
"The baby seems content and falls asleep after most feedings."
"I usually take the baby off after 5 minutes on each side so I don't get sore."
"I am drinking water each time I sit down to feed."
"My partner burps the baby between sides."

items.rationale: Frequent feedings with audible swallowing, breasts that soften after a feed, 6 or more wet diapers with yellow seedy stools by day 4, and a satisfied newborn are the key indicators of effective milk transfer. Tucked-in lips with continuous pinching pain and cracked nipples indicate a shallow latch, supplemental formula and time-limited feedings reduce supply, and drinking water or having a partner burp the baby are neutral practices that do not measure effectiveness.

items.stem: Click to highlight the statements by the parent of a 3-week-old that describe a safety risk requiring teaching before leaving the clinic.

highlightSegments.text: "The baby sleeps in a bassinet next to our bed."
"We put a soft bumper pad and a small pillow in the crib so the baby is comfortable."
"I lay the baby on the back for every sleep."
"When the baby falls asleep on the couch with me, I just let us both nap there."
"We keep the room at a comfortable temperature and use a sleep sack."
"The baby has a pacifier at naps and bedtime."
"We wash our hands before picking up the baby."
"I warm the bottle in the microwave for 30 seconds and then shake it."
"The car seat is rear-facing in the back seat, installed by a certified technician."
"We set the water heater to 49 C (120 F) before the baby came home."

items.rationale: Bumper pads and pillows in the crib and sleeping with an adult on a couch are leading risk factors for suffocation and sudden unexpected infant death, and microwaving formula creates hot spots that can burn the mouth even after shaking, so all three need teaching. Room-sharing without bed-sharing, back sleeping, a sleep sack, a pacifier, hand hygiene, a properly installed rear-facing car seat and a water heater at 49 C (120 F) are recommended practices.

items.stem: Click to highlight the client statements during a 1-week postpartum telehealth call that require same-day evaluation.

highlightSegments.text: "I had my baby 7 days ago by vaginal birth and we came home on day 2."
"My bleeding is light pink now and I use about 2 pads a day."
"The headache I've had since yesterday isn't going away with acetaminophen and I see spots sometimes."
"My breasts are full and a little tender before feedings."
"My right leg has been aching behind the knee and it looks puffier than the left."
"I get short of breath just walking from the bedroom to the kitchen."
"I'm tired, but I sleep when the baby sleeps."
"My stitches sting a little when I urinate, but the water bottle rinse helps."
"I cried a couple of times this week over nothing."
"My mother is staying with us for another 2 weeks."

items.rationale: A persistent headache with visual changes can be postpartum preeclampsia, which may occur up to 6 weeks after birth; unilateral calf or popliteal pain with swelling suggests deep vein thrombosis; and new exertional dyspnea may indicate pulmonary embolism or peripartum cardiomyopathy. Each requires same-day evaluation. Light pink lochia at 1 week, breast fullness, fatigue, mild perineal stinging relieved by a peri bottle, brief tearfulness and available family support are expected.

items.stem: The nurse reviews the trended prenatal data for a client with a singleton pregnancy. Which conclusion should the nurse draw?
options: The client is developing gestational hypertension based on the blood pressure trend
Fetal heart rate variation between visits indicates fetal distress
Fundal height is lagging more than 3 cm behind gestational age with minimal weight gain, so an ultrasound for fetal growth is warranted
Growth is appropriate because the fundal height continues to increase at each visit
items.rationale: Between 20 and 36 weeks the fundal height in centimeters should be within about 2 to 3 cm of the gestational age in weeks. A measurement 5 cm behind at 32 weeks, with almost no maternal weight gain over 8 weeks, is a screening cue for fetal growth restriction or oligohydramnios and calls for ultrasound. A fundal height that falls further behind each visit is not reassuring, the blood pressure stays well below 140/90 mm Hg, and a fetal heart rate of 110 to 160/min is normal.

items.stem: A client receiving IV oxytocin for labor induction has the following electronic fetal monitoring data recorded over the past hour. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Discontinue the oxytocin infusion, turn the client to the side, and notify the provider
Prepare for amniotomy to speed the active phase
Continue to monitor because the fetal heart rate remains within the normal range
Increase the oxytocin by 2 mU/min because labor is progressing
items.rationale: Contractions every 90 seconds exceed five in 10 minutes, which is tachysystole, and recurrent late decelerations with a rising baseline and minimal variability show the fetus is not tolerating the reduced placental perfusion. The nurse stops the oxytocin, turns the client to the side, gives a fluid bolus and oxygen per protocol, and notifies the provider. Increasing the dose or performing amniotomy would worsen uterine activity, and a baseline within range does not make this tracing reassuring.

items.stem: The nurse reviews the trended assessments of a client during the first 2 hours after a vaginal birth. Which conclusion should the nurse draw?
options: The rising heart rate reflects expected pain and excitement after birth
The client is developing postpartum hemorrhage from uterine atony and needs fundal massage, bladder emptying, and uterotonic medication now
The lochia amount is typical for the first 2 hours after birth
The blood pressure is trending toward the client's pre-pregnancy baseline
trendRows: boggy after massage, 2 cm above umbilicus
items.rationale: A fundus that becomes boggy and rises above the umbilicus while lochia turns heavy with clots indicates uterine atony, and the rising heart rate with falling blood pressure shows significant blood loss; tachycardia is the earliest sign of hemorrhage and precedes hypotension. The nurse massages the fundus, empties the bladder, gives the ordered uterotonic and calls for help. Pain does not explain a progressive rise to 118/min, and a pad saturated in 30 minutes is never typical.

items.stem: The nurse reviews the trended data for a breastfed term newborn with a birth weight of 3,400 g. Which conclusion should the nurse draw?
options: The newborn should be switched to formula permanently because breast milk is causing the jaundice
The findings indicate hemolytic disease and an exchange transfusion is needed
Bilirubin is rising rapidly with weight loss above 10% and poor intake, so the provider should be notified for phototherapy evaluation and a feeding plan
The weight loss is expected for a breastfed newborn and the bilirubin is physiologic
items.rationale: A loss of 380 g is 11% of birth weight, above the 10% threshold, and the falling feeding and diaper counts show inadequate intake. Poor intake reduces stooling and increases enterohepatic recirculation of bilirubin, producing a rise of more than 5 mg/dL a day toward the phototherapy range, so the provider is notified and a feeding plan is started. This is suboptimal-intake jaundice, not a reason to stop breastfeeding, and exchange transfusion is for far higher levels.

items.stem: A client with gestational diabetes managed with diet and exercise brings the following glucose log to the 32-week visit. Which conclusion should the nurse draw?
options: All values are within target and the current plan should continue
Fasting and post-dinner values are consistently above target, so the provider should be notified to consider adding insulin or other medication
Only the breakfast values are elevated, so the client should skip breakfast
The client should stop exercising because activity is raising the values
items.rationale: Targets in gestational diabetes are a fasting glucose below 95 mg/dL and a 1-hour postprandial value below 140 mg/dL. Every fasting and post-dinner value in this log exceeds target and the trend is rising, so diet and exercise alone are no longer adequate and pharmacologic therapy is usually added to protect the fetus from macrosomia and neonatal hypoglycemia. The breakfast and lunch values are at goal, skipping meals worsens control, and exercise lowers rather than raises glucose.

items.stem: The nurse reviews the trended blood pressure and urine results across the prenatal visits of a client with no history of hypertension. Which action should the nurse take at the 34-week visit?
options: Advise the client to limit sodium and return at the routine 36-week visit
Recheck the blood pressure after rest, obtain a urine protein-to-creatinine ratio and preeclampsia labs, and notify the provider before the client leaves
Reassure the client that a gradual rise in blood pressure is normal near term
Instruct the client to go directly to the emergency department for magnesium sulfate
items.rationale: Blood pressure normally dips in the second trimester and returns to baseline but should not reach 140/90 mm Hg; a new reading at that level after 20 weeks with proteinuria, facial edema and a 4 kg gain in 4 weeks meets the screening threshold for preeclampsia. The nurse confirms the pressure, obtains quantitative urine protein and labs, and involves the provider before discharge. Sodium restriction does not treat preeclampsia, waiting 2 weeks is unsafe, and magnesium is a provider decision.

items.stem: The nurse reviews the trended labor assessments of a nulliparous client. Which findings indicate that labor is progressing as expected? Select all that apply.
options: Cervical dilation has advanced at about 1 cm per hour since the active phase began
The client should be prepared for cesarean birth because dilation has not reached 10 cm in 6 hours
Effacement reaching 100% by 1200 indicates the second stage has started
Contractions have become more frequent, longer, and stronger
Contractions every 2 to 3 minutes lasting 70 seconds indicate tachysystole
The presenting part has descended from -2 to +1 station
items.rationale: Steady dilation of about 1 cm per hour in the active phase, progressive descent of the presenting part, and contractions that grow more frequent, longer and stronger are the three markers of normal labor progress. The second stage begins with complete dilation at 10 cm, not complete effacement. Six hours to progress from 4 to 9 cm is normal for a first labor, and tachysystole means more than five contractions in 10 minutes, which every 2 to 3 minutes does not meet.

items.stem: The nurse evaluates teaching provided to a client at the first prenatal visit. For each client statement, click to specify whether the statement indicates the teaching was Effective or Ineffective.
matrixRows: "I'll take my prenatal vitamin with folic acid every day."
"I can keep drinking a glass of wine with dinner as long as it's only one."
"I'll avoid cleaning the cat's litter box."
"Deli meats and soft cheeses are fine as long as they're cold."
"I should get the flu shot and the Tdap during this pregnancy."
"I can keep using the hot tub at the gym to relax my back."
"I'll limit fish that is high in mercury, like swordfish."
items.rationale: Daily folic acid, avoiding cat litter to prevent toxoplasmosis, receiving inactivated influenza and Tdap vaccines, and limiting high-mercury fish are all correct prenatal practices. No amount of alcohol is considered safe in pregnancy. Cold deli meats and soft unpasteurized cheeses carry Listeria, which crosses the placenta, so deli meats should be heated until steaming and only pasteurized cheeses eaten. Hot tubs raise core temperature and are linked to neural tube defects in early pregnancy.

items.stem: The nurse assesses a 12-hour-old term newborn. For each finding, click to specify whether the finding is Expected or Requires follow-up.
matrixRows: Respiratory rate 44/min with brief pauses of 5 seconds
Heart rate 82/min while awake
Hands and feet bluish, trunk and lips pink
Bluish discoloration around the lips and tongue
Small pink patches on the eyelids and nape of the neck
Yellow tint to the sclera and face
Umbilical cord with two arteries and one vein
Has not passed meconium and abdomen is distended
items.rationale: Periodic breathing with pauses under 20 seconds, acrocyanosis, nevus simplex patches and a three-vessel cord are normal newborn findings. A heart rate below 100/min in an awake newborn is bradycardia, central cyanosis of the lips and tongue indicates hypoxemia, jaundice within the first 24 hours is pathologic, and abdominal distention without meconium raises concern for obstruction such as Hirschsprung disease or meconium ileus; each requires prompt provider notification.

items.stem: A client calls the postpartum clinic 10 days after a vaginal birth. For each client report, click to specify whether it is an Expected finding or a Warning sign to report to the provider.
matrixRows: Lochia is now pinkish brown and lighter
Temperature 38.5 C (101.3 F) with chills
One breast has a hard, red, painful wedge-shaped area
Perineal sutures feel tight but are not painful
Bright red bleeding returned today with clots the size of a golf ball
Night sweats for the past several nights
Thoughts of harming self or the baby
items.rationale: Lochia serosa at 10 days, mild tightness of healing sutures and postpartum diaphoresis as the body sheds pregnancy fluid are normal. Fever with chills suggests endometritis or another infection, a hard red wedge in one breast is mastitis, a return of bright red bleeding with large clots after lochia has lightened suggests subinvolution or retained fragments, and any thought of harming self or the infant is a psychiatric emergency; each must be reported immediately.

items.stem: A nurse teaches a client at 20 weeks of gestation about symptoms that must be reported to the provider immediately. Which symptoms should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: Mild backache after standing for a long time
Absence of fetal movement after it has been felt regularly
Regular contractions before 37 weeks
Vaginal bleeding
Gush of fluid from the vagina
Painful urination with fever
Nasal stuffiness and occasional nosebleeds
Darkening of the skin on the face
items.rationale: Leaking fluid may indicate rupture of membranes, bleeding may signal placental problems or preterm labor, dysuria with fever suggests pyelonephritis that can trigger preterm labor, loss of previously regular fetal movement may indicate fetal compromise, and regular contractions before 37 weeks are preterm labor; all require immediate reporting. Mild postural backache, nasal congestion with minor nosebleeds from increased blood volume, and melasma are common expected changes of pregnancy.

items.stem: The nurse provides safe sleep teaching to the parents of a newborn before discharge. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: Avoid overheating and do not cover the newborn's head indoors
Let the newborn finish naps in the car seat after a trip
Place a rolled blanket on each side of the newborn to prevent rolling
Offer a pacifier at sleep time once breastfeeding is established
Use a firm, flat mattress with only a fitted sheet
Keep the crib or bassinet in the parents' room for at least the first 6 months
Place the newborn on the back for every sleep, including naps
items.rationale: Supine positioning, a firm flat sleep surface without soft items, room-sharing without bed-sharing for at least 6 months, avoiding overheating, and offering a pacifier are the evidence-based practices that reduce sudden infant death. Positioning devices and rolled blankets are soft objects that create a suffocation risk, and car seats, swings and other sitting devices allow the head to slump forward and obstruct the airway, so the infant should be moved to a flat surface for sleep.

items.stem: A nurse reviews car seat safety with the parents of a newborn being discharged. Which statements by the parents indicate correct understanding? Select all that apply.
options: "We can use the car seat our neighbor gave us that was in a minor crash."
"The car seat goes in the back seat, never in front of an active airbag."
"The chest clip goes at armpit level."
"The seat stays rear-facing until our baby reaches the seat's rear-facing height or weight limit."
"Once the baby is 1 year old we can turn the seat forward-facing."
"The harness straps should be at or just below the shoulders when rear-facing."
"We'll put a thick winter coat on the baby before buckling the harness."
items.rationale: Children ride rear-facing as long as possible until they reach the seat's limits, harness straps sit at or below the shoulders in rear-facing seats, the chest clip is positioned at armpit level, and the seat is installed in the back seat away from airbags. Bulky coats compress in a crash and leave the harness loose, a seat that has been in a crash may have hidden damage and should be replaced, and turning forward-facing at age 1 is outdated advice that removes protection for the head and spine.

items.stem: The parent of a healthy term newborn born 20 hours ago asks why the nurse wants to wait to collect the newborn screening blood spot. Which explanation should the nurse give?
options: "The heel stick is painful, so it is postponed until the newborn is ready for discharge."
"The newborn must receive the hepatitis B vaccine before the screen can be drawn."
"The screen is only drawn if jaundice develops."
"The test is most accurate after the newborn has had at least 24 hours of feeding so that metabolic byproducts can be detected."
items.rationale: The newborn metabolic screen detects disorders such as phenylketonuria by measuring substances that accumulate only after the newborn has been fed protein, so a sample drawn before 24 hours of age may miss these conditions and would need to be repeated. Pain is managed with sucrose or breastfeeding rather than by delaying the test, the screen is not linked to vaccine administration, and it is a universal screen performed on every newborn regardless of symptoms.

items.stem: A nurse teaches the parent of a 1-day-old newborn to recognize early feeding cues. Which behavior should the nurse identify as an early cue to begin a feeding?
options: Crying loudly with a flushed face
Sleeping quietly for 4 hours
Rooting and bringing the hands to the mouth
Sucking on a pacifier calmly after a feeding
items.rationale: Rooting, lip smacking, stirring and hand-to-mouth movements are early hunger cues that signal the best time to offer a feeding, when the newborn will latch most easily. Crying is a late cue; a crying newborn often needs to be calmed before it can latch. A newborn who sleeps 4 hours should be woken to feed in the first days, and calm non-nutritive sucking after a feeding is a sign of satiety rather than hunger.

items.stem: The nurse is helping a client latch a newborn to the breast for the first time. Place the steps in the correct order.
options: Stroke the newborn's lower lip with the nipple to elicit rooting
Position the newborn tummy-to-tummy at breast level with the nose opposite the nipple
Wait for the newborn to open the mouth wide with the tongue down
Bring the newborn quickly onto the breast so the chin touches first and the nipple aims toward the roof of the mouth
Check that the lips are flanged outward and more areola shows above the upper lip than below
items.rationale: An effective latch starts with positioning the newborn facing the breast so the head does not have to turn, then stimulating the lower lip to trigger rooting, waiting for a wide gape, bringing the newborn onto the breast chin-first with the nipple aimed upward so the tongue draws in a large amount of areola, and finally checking the latch. Latching before the mouth is wide open produces a shallow, painful latch, and checking comes last because it evaluates the other steps.

items.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: During a 6-month well-child visit the nurse expects the infant to {{1}} and to {{2}}. A 6-month-old who cannot {{3}} should be referred for developmental evaluation.

options: say 2 or 3 words with meaning
walk holding onto furniture
roll from back to abdomen and sit with support
stack 2 blocks
babble with consonant sounds and turn toward voices
wave bye-bye and play pat-a-cake
use a pincer grasp to pick up cereal
point to pictures in a book
pull to a standing position
crawl on hands and knees
sit without support
hold the head steady when held upright

items.rationale: By 6 months an infant rolls in both directions, sits with support, babbles consonant sounds and turns toward a voice. Steady head control is expected by 4 months, so its absence at 6 months is a red flag for motor delay. Cruising, waving, pincer grasp and single words emerge between 9 and 12 months, and independent sitting, crawling and pulling to stand are not expected until 7 to 9 months, so their absence at 6 months is not yet a concern.

items.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: At the 12-month well-child visit, the nurse expects the child to {{1}}, to use a {{2}} to pick up small pieces of food, and to {{3}}.

options: walk up stairs with alternating feet
run without falling
ride a tricycle
pull to stand and cruise along furniture
neat pincer grasp with thumb and index finger
spoon held in a fist
raking grasp with the whole hand
palmar grasp
say 1 or 2 words such as 'mama' with meaning and respond to own name
speak in 2-word phrases
name 3 colors
follow 2-step commands

items.rationale: A 12-month-old pulls to stand, cruises along furniture and may take first steps, uses a refined pincer grasp for finger foods, says one or two meaningful words and responds to the name. Running, two-word phrases and two-step commands are 2-year skills, alternating stairs and tricycle riding are 3-year skills, and a raking or palmar grasp at 12 months would indicate a fine motor delay.

items.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A parent asks whether a 24-month-old is 'on track.' The nurse explains that a 2-year-old typically {{1}}, has a vocabulary of about {{2}}, and engages in {{3}} play alongside other children.

options: combines 2 words into short phrases and follows 2-step directions
says single words only
tells a story with a beginning and end
speaks in full sentences with correct grammar
5 to 10 words
50 or more words that are half understandable to strangers
1,000 words
200 words with all sounds pronounced clearly
cooperative
solitary only
associative
parallel

items.rationale: By 2 years a child combines two words, follows two-step directions, has at least 50 words and is about 50% intelligible to strangers, and plays beside rather than with peers, which is parallel play. Single words only at 24 months is a language delay, full grammatical sentences and storytelling are preschool skills, and cooperative play with shared goals appears around 4 to 5 years.

items.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: At a 9-month well-child visit, an infant's weight has fallen from the 50th percentile at 4 months to the 10th percentile, while length remains at the 50th percentile. The nurse recognizes this pattern as {{1}} and should first {{2}}.

options: a sign of constitutional short stature
a concerning deceleration in weight gain that crosses two major percentile lines
normal for an infant who is breastfed
an expected shift as infants become more active
recommend adding cereal to every bottle
obtain a detailed feeding history including how formula is mixed and how often the infant feeds
refer to a pediatric endocrinologist
reassure the parent and recheck at 12 months

items.rationale: Weight that drops across two major percentile lines while length is preserved is the pattern of inadequate caloric intake, the most common cause of faltering growth in infancy, and is not explained by activity level or feeding method. The first nursing step is a thorough feeding history covering formula preparation, frequency, volume and feeding difficulties. Waiting 3 months delays intervention, cereal in bottles is not recommended, and endocrine referral applies when length is affected.

items.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: At the 2-month well-child visit the nurse prepares the routine immunizations, which include {{1}}. The nurse teaches the parent that {{2}} is an expected reaction and that the parent should call if {{3}}.

options: DTaP, IPV, Hib, pneumococcal conjugate, rotavirus, and hepatitis B
influenza and HPV
MMR, varicella, and hepatitis A
meningococcal conjugate and Tdap
a seizure within 24 hours
fussiness with mild fever and soreness at the injection site for 1 to 2 days
inconsolable crying for more than 3 hours
a fever of 40.5 C (104.9 F) that lasts 3 days
the infant sleeps more than usual on the day of the vaccines
the injection site is slightly red the next morning
the infant has a seizure, cries inconsolably for more than 3 hours, or has a fever of 40.5 C (104.9 F) or higher
the infant refuses one feeding

items.rationale: The 2-month schedule includes DTaP, IPV, Hib, pneumococcal conjugate, oral rotavirus and the second hepatitis B dose. Mild fever, fussiness and local soreness for a day or two are expected. Prolonged inconsolable crying, very high fever and seizures are rare events that must be reported because they may influence future pertussis dosing. MMR, varicella and hepatitis A begin at 12 months, and influenza, HPV, meningococcal and Tdap vaccines are given later in childhood or adolescence.

items.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A parent of a 12-month-old asks about the vaccines due today. The nurse explains that the first doses of {{1}} are given between 12 and 15 months, that a child's {{2}} is not a reason to delay them, and that {{3}} would require postponing the live vaccines.

options: MMR and varicella
DTaP and IPV
rotavirus and hepatitis B
HPV and meningococcal
fever of 39.5 C (103.1 F) with lethargy
mild cold with a temperature of 37.8 C (100 F)
recent high-dose corticosteroid course
current chemotherapy
attending daycare
receiving intravenous immune globulin last month
a family history of egg allergy
having a sibling with a cold

items.rationale: MMR and varicella are live vaccines first given at 12 to 15 months. A mild illness with low-grade fever is not a contraindication, so vaccination should not be delayed for a cold. Recent immune globulin or blood products interfere with the response to live vaccines, so MMR and varicella are deferred for several months depending on the dose. Moderate or severe illness, high-dose steroids and chemotherapy are reasons to defer, whereas a sibling's cold, daycare and egg allergy are not.

items.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: At the 4-month well-child visit the nurse provides anticipatory guidance for the coming months. Because the infant will soon roll and reach, the nurse tells the parent to {{1}}, keep the water heater set no higher than {{2}}, and {{3}}.

options: never leave the infant unattended on a bed or changing table
introduce a pillow in the crib for head support
move the infant to a forward-facing car seat
begin using a walker with wheels to build leg strength
keep small objects, cords, and plastic bags out of reach
install a trampoline net
allow the infant to hold the bottle in the crib
offer honey on the pacifier to soothe teething

items.rationale: Falls from elevated surfaces become likely once an infant rolls, so the infant is never left unattended on a bed or table. A water heater at 49 C (120 F) prevents scald burns, and small objects, cords and bags are choking and strangulation hazards once reaching begins. Wheeled walkers cause falls, pillows in the crib risk suffocation, forward-facing seats are for older toddlers, honey before 12 months risks botulism, and propped bottles cause choking and ear infections.

items.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A parent asks when a 4-month-old can start solid foods. The nurse explains that complementary foods are introduced at about {{1}} when the infant can sit with support and has lost the tongue-thrust reflex, that {{2}} should not be given before 12 months, and that {{3}}.

options: 2 months
12 months
6 months
9 months
iron-fortified cereal
honey and cow's milk as the main drink
pureed vegetables
peanut-containing foods
fruit juice should replace one breast milk or formula feeding daily
allergenic foods such as eggs should be delayed until 3 years
cereal should be added to the bottle to help the infant sleep
single-ingredient foods are introduced one at a time, a few days apart, to identify reactions

items.rationale: Solids are started around 6 months when the infant shows readiness, and iron-fortified cereal, pureed vegetables and even peanut-containing foods are appropriate early foods. Honey carries a risk of infant botulism and cow's milk lacks adequate iron and stresses the kidneys, so both wait until after the first birthday. Introducing single foods several days apart identifies allergies, whereas juice before 12 months, cereal in bottles and delaying allergenic foods are all discouraged.

items.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: The parent of an 18-month-old asks whether it is time to begin toilet training. The nurse explains that most children show readiness between {{1}}, that signs of readiness include {{2}}, and that if the child resists the parent should {{3}}.

options: 18 and 30 months
6 and 12 months
4 and 5 years
12 and 15 months
staying dry for 2 hours, walking to the potty, and showing interest in the toilet
weighing more than 12 kg
sleeping through the night without a diaper
being able to say the alphabet
use a diaper only at night starting immediately
keep the child on the potty until success
stop for a few weeks and try again without pressure or punishment
withhold fluids in the afternoon

items.rationale: Readiness for toilet training depends on physical and cognitive maturation that usually occurs between 18 and 30 months: staying dry for a couple of hours, walking to the potty, following simple directions and showing interest. Nighttime dryness comes months to years after daytime control and is not a readiness sign. Resistance means the child is not ready, so a break of a few weeks without pressure works best, whereas restricting fluids or forcing sitting creates fear and withholding.

items.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A 16-year-old arrives for a sports physical with a parent. To assess risk behaviors, the nurse should {{1}}, screen using {{2}}, and explain that the conversation is confidential except when {{3}}.

options: give the adolescent a written questionnaire to take home
skip the psychosocial screen because the visit is for sports clearance
interview the adolescent only with the parent present so answers can be verified
ask the parent to step out for part of the visit and interview the adolescent alone
the Denver Developmental Screening Test
the HEEADSSS interview covering home, education, activities, drugs, sexuality, suicide, and safety
the Ages and Stages Questionnaire
the Modified Checklist for Autism in Toddlers
the adolescent reports being sexually active
the adolescent discloses danger to self or others or abuse
the adolescent admits to drinking alcohol at a party
the parent asks for the information

items.rationale: Adolescents disclose risk behaviors far more honestly when interviewed privately, so part of every adolescent visit is conducted without the parent using a structured screen such as HEEADSSS. Confidentiality is promised with clear limits: the nurse must act when there is risk of serious harm to self or others or abuse. A parent's request alone does not override confidentiality, and sexual activity or alcohol use are the behaviors confidentiality is meant to elicit so counseling can occur.

items.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A 45-year-old client with no family history of cancer asks which screenings are recommended. The nurse explains that colorectal cancer screening begins at age {{1}} for average-risk adults, that {{2}} is one accepted screening option, and that screening mammography for average-risk women is recommended starting at age {{3}}.

options: a carcinoembryonic antigen blood test every 5 years
an abdominal ultrasound every 3 years
a digital rectal exam every year
a colonoscopy every 10 years or an annual fecal immunochemical test

items.rationale: Current guidelines lowered the starting age for average-risk colorectal cancer screening to 45 because of rising incidence in younger adults; colonoscopy every 10 years or an annual fecal immunochemical test are both acceptable. Digital rectal exam, carcinoembryonic antigen and ultrasound are not screening tests for colorectal cancer. Screening mammography for average-risk women is now recommended every 2 years beginning at age 40, with earlier imaging reserved for higher-risk clients.

items.stem: Click to highlight the findings in the 9-month well-child visit note that indicate a possible developmental delay requiring further evaluation.

highlightSegments.text: 9-month well-child visit; weight and length tracking along the 40th percentile.
Parent reports the infant sits only when propped and slumps forward when the support is removed.
Transfers a rattle from one hand to the other.
Does not babble; parent reports 'mostly just squeals.'
Reaches for toys and puts them in the mouth.
Does not turn toward the parent's voice when called from behind.
Eats pureed foods and some soft table foods with fingers.
Smiles at the parent and enjoys peek-a-boo.
Sleeps 11 hours at night with one nap.
Immunizations current through 6 months.

items.rationale: By 9 months an infant should sit without support, babble consonant strings such as 'bababa' and turn toward a voice, so the inability to sit independently, absence of babbling and failure to orient to sound are red flags that warrant a standardized developmental screen and a hearing evaluation. Transferring objects, mouthing toys, finger feeding, social smiling, enjoying peek-a-boo and a consolidated sleep pattern are all expected at this age.

items.stem: Click to highlight the findings in the 18-month well-child visit note that the nurse should identify as cues for autism spectrum disorder screening follow-up.

highlightSegments.text: 18-month visit; growth parameters at the 60th percentile.
Walks independently and climbs onto furniture.
Says about 5 words; does not point to show the parent things of interest.
Does not respond to name most of the time, though hearing screen passed at birth.
Stacks 3 blocks and scribbles with a crayon.
Parent notes the child lines up cars for long periods and becomes upset if they are moved.
Rarely makes eye contact during the exam.
Eats a variety of table foods with a spoon and cup.
Tantrums 'a few times a day' when told no.
M-CHAT-R completed by parent in the waiting room.

items.rationale: Absence of pointing to share interest, not responding to the name, repetitive lining up of objects with distress when disrupted, and poor eye contact are core social-communication and restricted-behavior cues for autism spectrum disorder and require M-CHAT-R scoring with follow-up interview and referral. Walking, climbing, stacking blocks, scribbling, self-feeding and tantrums are age-appropriate, and a passed newborn hearing screen does not rule out later hearing loss.

items.stem: Click to highlight the statements by the parent of a 2-year-old that indicate a safety risk the nurse must address with anticipatory guidance.

highlightSegments.text: "We have gates at the top and bottom of the stairs."
"I keep the cleaning supplies under the sink where they're easy to reach when I'm cooking."
"The car seat is still rear-facing in the back seat."
"She likes to eat whole grapes and popcorn as snacks."
"I sit right beside her in the bath, and I never leave the room."
"Our pool has a fence with a self-latching gate."
"We turn the pot handles toward the back of the stove."
"She sleeps in a regular bed now, and we anchored the dresser to the wall."
"My father's heart pills are in a weekly organizer on his nightstand when he visits."
"We keep the poison control number on the refrigerator."

items.rationale: Toddlers explore by climbing and mouthing, so cleaning products within reach under a sink, whole grapes and popcorn that can occlude a small airway, and a visiting grandparent's cardiac medications in a non-childproof organizer are each a leading cause of poisoning or choking at this age and need immediate guidance. Stair gates, a rear-facing seat, constant bath supervision, a fenced pool, turned pot handles, anchored furniture and a posted poison control number are correct practices.

items.stem: Click to highlight the parts of the 15-year-old's psychosocial interview that require follow-up by the nurse.

highlightSegments.text: Lives with mother and younger brother; describes home as 'fine, mostly quiet.'
Grades dropped from mostly A's to C's this semester.
Plays soccer and works part-time at a grocery store.
Reports vaping nicotine 'most days' and drinking at parties 'a couple times a month.'
Has a close group of friends and a supportive coach.
Sexually active with one partner; uses condoms 'most of the time.'
Sleeps about 8 hours on school nights.
States 'sometimes I feel like everyone would be better off without me.'
Denies ever riding with a driver who has been drinking.
Wears a helmet when biking and a seat belt in the car.

items.rationale: A sudden drop in grades is a marker of depression, substance use or other stressors; daily nicotine vaping and periodic alcohol use need brief intervention; inconsistent condom use calls for contraception and sexually transmitted infection counseling and testing; and saying others would be better off without the adolescent is passive suicidal ideation requiring a safety assessment before the visit ends. Sports, work, friendships, sleep, avoiding impaired drivers and helmet use are protective.

items.stem: Click to highlight the findings in the school nurse's screening note that require referral for further evaluation.

highlightSegments.text: First-grade screening, 6-year-old student, cooperative during testing.
Visual acuity 20/20 right eye, 20/50 left eye with the standard chart.
Student squints and tilts the head when reading the board, per teacher.
Cover-uncover test shows no eye movement.
Pure-tone hearing screen: no response at 4,000 Hz in the right ear on two attempts.
Height and weight at the 55th percentile; BMI at the 50th percentile.
Blood pressure 96/60 mm Hg.
Two visible cavities on the lower molars; last dental visit 'over a year ago.'
Immunization record complete for school entry.
Student reports eating breakfast most mornings.

items.rationale: A two-line difference between the eyes with 20/50 in one eye at age 6 suggests amblyopia or refractive error, and the squinting and head tilt reinforce that concern; a failed pure-tone screen at any frequency after a repeat attempt requires audiology referral; and visible caries without recent dental care need a dental referral. A normal cover-uncover test, growth at the 50th percentile, a normal blood pressure, complete immunizations and regular breakfast are expected findings.

items.stem: Click to highlight the statements by the parent of a 2-month-old that indicate a need for feeding teaching.

highlightSegments.text: "I mix the powdered formula with one scoop for every 60 mL of water, just like the can says."
"I add a little extra water so the can lasts longer."
"I prop the bottle with a rolled towel so I can get dinner started."
"The baby takes about 120 mL every 3 to 4 hours."
"I put rice cereal in the evening bottle so the baby sleeps through the night."
"I throw away any formula left in the bottle after an hour."
"We burp the baby halfway through each feeding."
"The baby has about 6 wet diapers a day and soft yellow stools."
"I sterilize the bottles and nipples in the dishwasher."
"I give a little water between feedings on hot days so the baby stays hydrated."

items.rationale: Diluting formula reduces calories and can cause hyponatremia and poor growth; propping bottles risks choking, aspiration and otitis media; cereal in a bottle adds calories without benefit and increases choking risk; and plain water before 6 months displaces nutrition and can cause water intoxication. Mixing per label directions, about 120 mL every 3 to 4 hours, discarding leftover formula within an hour, mid-feed burping, 6 wet diapers and dishwasher cleaning are all appropriate.

items.stem: Click to highlight the findings in the 4-year-old's well-child visit note that require follow-up.

highlightSegments.text: 4-year-old at annual well-child visit with parent; no acute concerns.
Weight at the 97th percentile; BMI above the 95th percentile, up from the 85th last year.
Blood pressure 96/58 mm Hg on the right arm with an appropriately sized cuff.
Speaks in sentences understandable to strangers; counts to 10.
Hops on one foot; draws a circle and a cross.
Drinks about 950 mL of juice daily; 'snacks on and off all day.'
Visual acuity 20/30 both eyes with picture chart.
Brushes teeth 'when he remembers'; no dental visit yet.
Screen time about 4 hours a day, with a television in the bedroom.
Immunizations: due for DTaP, IPV, MMR, and varicella boosters today.

items.rationale: A BMI that has crossed from overweight into the obesity range, excessive juice with constant grazing, unsupervised brushing without a dental home, and 4 hours of daily screen time with a bedroom television are modifiable risks requiring counseling on nutrition, limiting juice to 120 to 180 mL a day, supervised brushing with a first dental visit, and a screen plan of 1 hour or less. The blood pressure, language, motor skills and 20/30 acuity are normal at age 4, and the boosters are due now.

items.stem: Click to highlight the parts of the 68-year-old client's annual visit note that identify preventive care the nurse should address today.

highlightSegments.text: 68-year-old client for annual wellness visit; retired teacher, lives with spouse.
Last colonoscopy 12 years ago with no polyps.
Received influenza vaccine last month; COVID-19 vaccine current.
Has never received a pneumococcal vaccine.
Reports two falls in the past 6 months, one while getting up at night.
Blood pressure 128/78 mm Hg; walks 30 minutes daily.
Shingles vaccine series completed 2 years ago.
Last lipid panel and diabetes screen 1 year ago, within normal limits.
Smokes 1 pack per day for 40 years and has never had a lung cancer screening scan.
Tdap booster given 4 years ago.

items.rationale: A normal colonoscopy is repeated every 10 years, so this client is 2 years overdue; pneumococcal vaccination is recommended for all adults 65 and older; two falls in 6 months triggers a multifactorial fall-risk assessment; and a current smoker with a 40 pack-year history aged 50 to 80 qualifies for annual low-dose CT lung screening plus cessation counseling. Current influenza, COVID-19, zoster and Tdap vaccines, controlled blood pressure, and recent normal labs need no action.

items.stem: Click to highlight the statements by the parent of a 2-month-old that reflect a misconception the nurse should correct before today's immunizations.

highlightSegments.text: "I read the vaccine information sheets you gave us at the last visit."
"I'd like to space the shots out over several visits so we don't overload the immune system."
"The baby had a slight runny nose yesterday, so I figured the shots would have to wait."
"I know a low fever tonight can happen."
"My cousin's child got autism from the MMR, so we'll skip that one when the time comes."
"I'll give the acetaminophen dose the pharmacist calculated if the baby seems uncomfortable."
"I can breastfeed during the injections to help with the pain."
"We'll keep the immunization record in the diaper bag."
"Since I'm breastfeeding, the baby gets my immunity and doesn't really need the hepatitis B shot."

items.rationale: An infant's immune system handles many antigens daily and spacing vaccines only prolongs vulnerability; a mild upper respiratory infection is not a contraindication; large studies have found no link between MMR and autism; and breast milk provides only partial, temporary passive antibodies that do not replace active immunization against hepatitis B. Reading the information sheets, expecting a low fever, a weight-based acetaminophen dose and breastfeeding during injections are appropriate.

items.stem: The nurse reviews the growth measurements recorded at the well-child visits of a formula-fed infant. Which conclusion should the nurse draw?
options: Weight has crossed two major percentile lines downward while length and head growth are preserved, which suggests inadequate caloric intake and requires a feeding assessment
Length lagging behind weight suggests an endocrine problem
The pattern indicates a genetic short-stature syndrome
The infant is growing normally because head circumference is stable
items.rationale: In faltering growth from insufficient calories, weight falls first, length slows later and head circumference is spared longest, which is exactly this pattern. Crossing two major percentile lines downward is the accepted threshold for concern and prompts a detailed feeding history, observation of a feeding and evaluation for medical causes. A stable head circumference does not make the weight loss normal, genetic short stature affects length early, and endocrine causes slow length before weight.

items.stem: The nurse reviews the blood pressure readings of a 15-year-old recorded at three visits over 6 months, each taken with an appropriately sized cuff after 5 minutes of rest. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Recheck in 1 year at the next sports physical
Reassure the adolescent that readings under 140/90 mm Hg are normal at any age
Advise the adolescent to stop playing sports until the pressure is lower
Report the readings to the provider because three elevated readings on separate visits meet the criteria for hypertension in an adolescent and need evaluation
items.rationale: For adolescents 13 years and older, blood pressure of 130/80 mm Hg or higher is stage 1 hypertension, confirmed when present on three separate occasions. This adolescent also has an overweight BMI trend and a new headache, so the provider needs to evaluate for causes and begin lifestyle management. Adult thresholds do not apply, waiting a year delays treatment, and physical activity is part of the treatment rather than something to restrict.

items.stem: The nurse reviews the growth trend of an 8-year-old at annual well-child visits. Which action should the nurse take at this visit?
options: Place the child on a 1,000-calorie restricted diet
Discuss family-based nutrition and activity changes and review screen time, sugary drinks, and sleep, because the BMI has crossed into the obesity range
Reassure the parent that the child will 'grow into' the weight during puberty
Obtain a thyroid panel because rapid weight gain always indicates hypothyroidism
items.rationale: A BMI at or above the 95th percentile defines obesity in children, and the steady climb across percentile lines over 3 years shows an ongoing energy imbalance best addressed early with family-centered changes to diet, activity, screen time and sleep. Severe caloric restriction is inappropriate in a growing child and can impair growth. Waiting for puberty allows the trend to continue, and endocrine causes are unlikely when height is growing normally, so thyroid testing is not indicated.

items.stem: The nurse plots the head circumference of an infant at each well-child visit. Which conclusion should the nurse draw?
options: Head growth is expected because the brain grows fastest in the first year
The fontanel change indicates the infant is dehydrated
The infant's large head is familial and needs no follow-up
Head growth is accelerating across percentile lines out of proportion to body growth, which with a full fontanel suggests increased intracranial pressure and requires prompt provider evaluation
items.rationale: Head circumference should track along a consistent percentile; a rise from the 50th to the 95th percentile in 4 months while weight stays at the 50th, with a fontanel that is full when the infant is calm, is the pattern of hydrocephalus or another cause of raised intracranial pressure and needs same-day evaluation with imaging. Rapid brain growth follows the curve rather than crossing it, familial macrocephaly is present from birth with a soft fontanel, and dehydration sinks the fontanel.

items.stem: The nurse reviews the developmental screening results documented at a child's well-child visits. Which conclusion should the nurse draw?
options: Global developmental delay is present, so a full neurologic workup is needed
Development is on track and the parent should be reassured
Expressive language is delayed while social and motor skills are on track, so a hearing evaluation and speech-language referral are indicated
The pattern suggests autism spectrum disorder because the child has few words
items.rationale: By 24 months a child should use at least 50 words and combine two words; 8 single words with no phrases is an expressive language delay. Because receptive language, joint attention and motor skills are intact, this is an isolated expressive delay, and the first steps are a formal hearing test to rule out hearing loss and referral to early intervention for speech-language therapy. Preserved pointing and command-following argue against autism, and normal other domains rule out global delay.

items.stem: The nurse reviews the annual screening results of a 52-year-old client at a primary care clinic. Which conclusion should the nurse draw?
options: All values remain within normal limits for a 52-year-old
Only the cholesterol is abnormal and a statin will address the whole trend
The client has type 2 diabetes and should start insulin
The client is developing metabolic risk factors that meet the threshold for prediabetes and elevated blood pressure, so lifestyle counseling and provider follow-up are needed now
items.rationale: A fasting glucose of 100 to 125 mg/dL is prediabetes, a blood pressure of 130 to 139/80 to 89 mm Hg is stage 1 hypertension, total cholesterol above 200 mg/dL is borderline high, and a growing waist circumference reflects central adiposity; together they form a metabolic trend that responds best to early diet, activity and weight counseling with provider follow-up. Diabetes requires a fasting glucose of 126 mg/dL or higher twice and is not treated first with insulin; a statin fixes one factor.

items.stem: The nurse reviews screening results and diet history recorded at a toddler's well-child visits. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Reassure the parent that the hemoglobin is normal for a toddler
Advise the parent to stop all milk until the hemoglobin normalizes
Recommend switching from whole milk to skim milk to correct the anemia
Notify the provider of the falling hemoglobin and counsel the parent to limit milk to about 480 to 720 mL per day and offer iron-rich foods
items.rationale: A hemoglobin below 11 g/dL in a toddler is anemia, and the steady fall alongside rising milk intake and declining iron-rich foods points to iron deficiency: excess cow's milk is low in iron, displaces solid foods and can cause occult intestinal blood loss. The nurse reports the result so iron therapy can be ordered and teaches the parent to limit milk to 480 to 720 mL daily while offering meats, fortified cereals and vitamin C foods. Milk fat is not the issue, and stopping milk removes calcium.

items.stem: The nurse assesses a 12-month-old during a well-child visit. For each finding, click to specify whether the finding is Expected for age or a Concern requiring follow-up.
matrixRows: Pulls to stand and cruises along the couch
Uses a raking grasp only and cannot pick up a small piece of cereal
Says 'dada' and 'baba' with meaning
Does not sit without support
Anterior fontanel still open and soft
Persistent Moro reflex when startled
Has 4 to 6 teeth
items.rationale: Cruising, meaningful first words, an anterior fontanel that remains open until 12 to 18 months, and 4 to 6 teeth are expected at 12 months. A pincer grasp should be present by 9 to 10 months, so a raking grasp only is a fine motor concern; independent sitting is expected by 7 to 8 months, so its absence is a gross motor concern; and the Moro reflex should disappear by 4 to 6 months, so its persistence suggests a neurologic problem and requires evaluation.

items.stem: A nurse screens children before administering routine vaccines. For each situation, click to specify whether the vaccine should be Given or Withheld today.
matrixRows: A 4-month-old with a runny nose and temperature of 37.6 C (99.7 F)
A 12-month-old who had anaphylaxis to a previous dose of the same vaccine
A 6-month-old currently taking amoxicillin for otitis media and feeling well
A 15-month-old receiving chemotherapy for leukemia, due for MMR
A 2-month-old whose parent is pregnant, due for rotavirus vaccine
A 4-year-old with a temperature of 39.6 C (103.3 F) and vomiting
A 6-year-old with a family history of seizures
items.rationale: Mild illness with low-grade fever, current antibiotic therapy, a pregnant household contact and a family history of seizures are not contraindications, so those children are vaccinated on schedule. Anaphylaxis to a prior dose is a permanent contraindication to that vaccine, live vaccines such as MMR are contraindicated during chemotherapy because of immunosuppression, and moderate or severe acute illness with high fever is deferred until recovery so reactions are not confused with the illness.

items.stem: A nurse teaches a 50-year-old client about recommended health screenings and vaccines. For each client statement, click to specify whether it indicates Correct understanding or a Need for further teaching.
matrixRows: "I'll have my blood pressure checked at least once a year."
"Since my colonoscopy was normal, I don't need another for 10 years."
"I only need a cholesterol check if I start having chest pain."
"I should get the shingles vaccine now that I'm 50."
"A skin check is only necessary if I had a lot of sunburns as a child."
"My diabetes screening can wait until I'm 65 because I feel fine."
"I'll get a flu shot every fall."
items.rationale: Annual blood pressure screening, a 10-year interval after a normal colonoscopy, the recombinant zoster vaccine from age 50 and yearly influenza vaccination reflect current recommendations. Lipid screening is done every 4 to 6 years in adults regardless of symptoms because dyslipidemia is silent, any adult should have skin changes evaluated and use sun protection regardless of sunburn history, and diabetes screening is recommended from age 35 with periodic repeat, not deferred until 65.

items.stem: A school nurse presents an injury prevention session to parents of 8-year-old children. Which recommendations should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: Require a properly fitted helmet for bicycles, scooters, and skateboards
Teach the child to swim and supervise all water activities
Use a booster seat until the vehicle seat belt fits properly, usually at about 145 cm (4 feet 9 inches) tall
Let the child operate a lawn mower to build responsibility
Skip the helmet for short rides in the neighborhood
Allow the child to ride in the front seat at age 8
Store firearms unloaded and locked, with ammunition locked separately
items.rationale: Motor vehicle crashes, bicycle injuries, firearm injuries and drowning are leading causes of death and injury in school-age children, so booster seats until the belt fits, consistent helmet use, locked and separated firearm storage, and swimming skills with supervision are core recommendations.
