Children ride in the back seat until age 13, most bicycle injuries happen close to home so helmets are always required, and children should not run push mowers before 12 or riding mowers before 16.

items.stem: The nurse provides dental health teaching to the parent of an 18-month-old. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: Brush the teeth twice a day with a smear of fluoride toothpaste the size of a grain of rice
Avoid sharing utensils or cleaning the pacifier with the parent's mouth
Let the child brush independently so the child learns the routine
Schedule the first dental visit now if it has not already occurred by the first birthday
Offer only water in a bottle or cup at bedtime
Give fruit juice in a sippy cup throughout the day instead of candy
Wait until all the primary teeth have erupted before using toothpaste
items.rationale: Fluoride toothpaste in a rice-grain smear twice daily from the first tooth, a dental home by 12 months, only water at bedtime to prevent early childhood caries, and avoiding saliva sharing that transmits cavity-causing bacteria are the key preventive measures. Toothpaste starts with the first tooth rather than after all teeth erupt, parents must brush for the child until about age 7 or 8 because toddlers lack the dexterity, and sipping juice all day bathes the teeth in sugar and causes caries.

items.stem: A 66-year-old client at an annual wellness visit asks which vaccines are recommended at this age. Which vaccines should the nurse identify as routinely recommended for adults 65 and older? Select all that apply.
options: Meningococcal conjugate vaccine
Human papillomavirus vaccine series
Recombinant zoster vaccine, 2-dose series
Pneumococcal conjugate vaccine if not previously received
Annual influenza vaccine
Rotavirus vaccine
Updated COVID-19 vaccine
Tetanus, diphtheria, and pertussis booster every 10 years
items.rationale: Adults 65 and older are routinely offered a yearly influenza vaccine, preferably a high-dose or adjuvanted formulation, a pneumococcal conjugate vaccine if not previously immunized, the 2-dose recombinant zoster series, a Td or Tdap booster every 10 years, and the current COVID-19 vaccine. HPV vaccination is not recommended after age 45, rotavirus is an infant vaccine, and meningococcal vaccine is given to older adults only for specific risk conditions such as asplenia or travel.

items.stem: The parent of a 3-year-old asks why the clinic wants to check the child's vision when the child 'sees fine.' Which response by the nurse is best?
options: "Screening at this age can detect amblyopia and refractive errors early, while treatment is most effective."
"We only screen children whose parents wear glasses."
"Vision screening is required only before starting kindergarten."
"Children cannot be screened reliably until they can read letters."
items.rationale: Amblyopia, strabismus and significant refractive errors are usually silent to parents because a young child does not know what normal vision looks like, and treatment works best before the visual pathways mature around age 7, so routine screening begins by age 3 with picture charts or instrument-based screening. Screening is recommended at every well visit from age 3, not only at school entry, is not limited to children with a family history, and does not require letter recognition.

items.stem: The parent of an 11-year-old asks why the human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine is recommended now rather than 'when they're older.' Which explanation should the nurse give?
options: "It is required for school entry in most states, so it must be given now."
"Children this age are less likely to have side effects than teenagers."
"The vaccine only works if it is given before age 12."
"Starting at age 11 to 12 produces a stronger immune response, only 2 doses are needed, and protection is in place before any exposure."
items.rationale: HPV vaccine is routinely started at 11 to 12 years because preteens mount a stronger antibody response, a 2-dose series is sufficient when started before age 15, and immunity is established well before the age of likely exposure. The vaccine remains effective when given later, although 3 doses are needed from age 15, side effects are similar across ages, and it is not a school-entry requirement in most states, so those explanations are inaccurate.

items.stem: The nurse prepares to examine a fearful 2-year-old during a well-child visit. Place the steps in the correct order.
options: Palpate the abdomen while the child is distracted with a toy
Observe the child's activity, gait, and interaction with the parent from across the room
Inspect the ears with the otoscope and examine the throat
Auscultate the heart and lungs while the child sits quietly on the parent's lap
Offer the child a chance to handle the stethoscope before touching the chest
items.rationale: A toddler examination proceeds from least to most intrusive: observation from a distance yields developmental and respiratory information before the child becomes upset, letting the child handle equipment builds trust, auscultation is done early while the child is calm so heart and breath sounds are not obscured by crying, the abdomen is palpated with distraction, and the ears and throat are left for last because they are the most distressing and often provoke crying.

items.stem: Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: At the start of the shift the nurse receives report on four clients: a client 1 day after laparoscopic cholecystectomy asking for discharge instructions, a client with pneumonia whose oxygen saturation has dropped from 95% to 88% on 2 L/min by nasal cannula, a client with cellulitis due for IV antibiotics in 30 minutes, and a client with diabetes reporting a fasting glucose of 160 mg/dL. The nurse should assess {{1}} first because the finding reflects {{2}}.

options: the client with diabetes
the client with cellulitis
the client after cholecystectomy
the client with pneumonia
a mildly elevated glucose
an elective teaching need
a scheduled medication that is not yet late
a problem with oxygenation that can deteriorate rapidly

items.rationale: A saturation that falls to 88% despite supplemental oxygen is a breathing problem and the most immediate threat to life under the ABC framework, so that client is assessed first. Discharge teaching, an antibiotic due in 30 minutes and a modestly elevated fasting glucose are real needs, but each client is stable and can safely wait a few minutes.

items.stem: Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A registered nurse on a medical unit is caring for a client admitted 2 hours ago with community-acquired pneumonia who is receiving oxygen at 3 L/min by nasal cannula. The nurse may delegate {{1}} to the unlicensed assistive personnel (UAP) but must personally perform {{2}}.

options: measuring and recording vital signs every 4 hours
evaluating the client's response to oxygen therapy
teaching the client to use the incentive spirometer
assessing breath sounds after the first antibiotic dose
the initial admission assessment
the bath and linen change
recording of intake and output
ambulation to the bathroom

items.rationale: Routine vital signs on a stable client are a repetitive, predictable task within UAP scope when the nurse specifies which values to report. Assessment, evaluation and teaching require nursing judgment and cannot be delegated, and the admission assessment in particular must be completed by the RN. Hygiene, ambulating a stable client and recording intake and output are appropriate UAP tasks, so they are not the ones the RN must do personally.

items.stem: Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A nurse calls the provider about a client 6 hours after open reduction of a femur fracture whose heart rate has risen from 84 to 118 beats/min while the blood pressure has fallen to 92/56 mm Hg and the dressing shows a 10 cm area of new bright-red drainage. Using SBAR, the nurse reports the vital signs and dressing findings in the {{1}} component and says 'I would like you to come evaluate the client and consider ordering a complete blood count' in the {{2}} component.

options: Recommendation
Situation
Background
Assessment
Situation
Recommendation
Background
Assessment

items.rationale: In SBAR the Situation names the client and the reason for the call, Background gives pertinent history such as the surgery and its time, Assessment presents the current objective data and the nurse's interpretation (tachycardia, hypotension and fresh bleeding suggesting hemorrhage), and Recommendation states clearly what the nurse wants the provider to do. Placing the vital signs under Situation or the request under Assessment blurs the structure that makes the report quick and safe.

items.stem: Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A client scheduled for a colonoscopy tells the nurse who arrives with the consent form, 'The doctor mentioned a scope, but I'm not sure what could go wrong.' The client received IV midazolam 10 minutes ago. The nurse should {{1}} because the responsibility to explain the risks, benefits and alternatives of the procedure belongs to {{2}}.

options: withhold the form and notify the provider that the client has unanswered questions and has been sedated
ask a family member in the waiting room to sign for the client
have the client sign now and answer the questions afterward
explain the risks of colonoscopy and then witness the signature
the provider performing the procedure
the client's next of kin
the endoscopy charge nurse
the nurse witnessing the signature

items.rationale: Valid consent requires that the client understand the procedure and its risks and be capable of deciding; a client who voices confusion and has just received a benzodiazepine meets neither condition, so the nurse stops and contacts the provider. The nurse's role is to witness the signature and confirm identity, apparent understanding and voluntariness, not to give the explanation. A family member cannot sign for a competent adult simply because sedation was given.

items.stem: Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: An alert and oriented client with end-stage heart failure has a living will declining mechanical ventilation and has named an adult child as durable power of attorney for health care. The client now tells the nurse, 'If it comes to that, I do want the breathing machine.' The nurse recognizes that {{1}} and should {{2}}.

options: the nurse must follow the living will until a court rules
the durable power of attorney must approve any change
the client's current verbal wishes take precedence because the client retains decision-making capacity
the living will cannot be changed once it is signed and witnessed
request an ethics consultation before doing anything else
disregard the statement because the living will is a legal document
tell the client the decision now belongs to the adult child
document the statement, notify the provider and help the client update the advance directive

items.rationale: An advance directive speaks only when the client cannot; a client with intact capacity may change or revoke it at any time, verbally or in writing. The durable power of attorney has authority only after the client loses capacity, so the agent's approval is not needed. The nurse documents the stated wishes, informs the provider and helps the client formally update the directive so the record matches current wishes; an ethics consult is reserved for unresolved conflict.

items.stem: Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A caller who identifies as the sibling of a hospitalized client asks the nurse for the client's diagnosis and test results. The nurse should first {{1}} because protected health information may be released only {{2}}.

options: transfer the call to the provider
provide a brief summary because siblings are immediate family
check whether the client has authorized information to be shared with this person
ask the caller for the client's date of birth and then answer
with the client's permission or as the law otherwise permits
after the client has been discharged
to any relative who can confirm the client's date of birth
to callers who state they are family

items.rationale: Being a relative does not create a right to a client's health information; the client decides who may receive it, and many facilities use a client-chosen passcode for callers. The nurse verifies authorization before saying anything, because a date of birth is easy to obtain and does not prove consent. Transferring the call simply moves the disclosure decision to someone else without resolving whether it is permitted.

items.stem: Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A nurse finds a client sitting on the floor beside the bed; the client says, 'I slipped trying to get to the bathroom.' After assessing the client and notifying the provider, the nurse documents {{1}} in the medical record and {{2}}.

options: that the UAP left the call light out of reach
that an incident report was completed and filed
the objective findings, the client's statement in quotation marks and the actions taken
the nurse's opinion that the bed alarm had failed
completes a report only if the client was injured
waits until the end of the shift to decide whether a report is needed
completes a separate incident report through the facility's reporting system
attaches a copy of the incident report to the chart

items.rationale: The medical record holds factual, objective documentation of what was found, what the client said and what was done. The incident report is a separate risk-management tool completed for every unplanned event, injured or not, and it is never referenced in or attached to the chart because doing so can make it discoverable and defeats its quality-improvement purpose. Opinions about causes or blame belong in neither document.

items.stem: Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A client with newly diagnosed lymphoma declines the recommended chemotherapy after the oncologist explains that the disease is likely curable. The nurse confirms the client understands the consequences of refusal and then supports the decision. In supporting the client's choice the nurse upholds the principle of {{1}}, while the nurse's discomfort about the likely outcome reflects the competing principle of {{2}}.

options: fidelity
autonomy
justice
beneficence
autonomy
beneficence
justice
veracity

items.rationale: Autonomy is the client's right to make an informed decision about their own care, including refusing treatment that clinicians believe would help. Beneficence, the duty to act for the client's good, pulls the nurse toward the treatment and creates the ethical tension. Justice concerns fair distribution of care and resources, veracity is truth-telling and fidelity is keeping commitments; none of these describes the conflict in this scenario.

items.stem: Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A 79-year-old client who lives alone is admitted for a bowel resection with creation of a colostomy. Discharge planning should begin {{1}}, and the referral most needed to support a safe transition home is {{2}}.

options: on postoperative day 3 when the stoma begins to function
on the day of admission
after the client demonstrates an independent pouch change
when the provider writes the discharge order
hospice services
placement in a long-term care facility
home health nursing with wound, ostomy and continence nurse support
outpatient physical therapy

items.rationale: Effective discharge planning starts at admission so that equipment, teaching and follow-up needs are identified early rather than on the day the order is written. An older adult living alone with a new stoma needs skilled reinforcement of ostomy care at home, which a home health referral with WOC nurse support provides. Long-term care and hospice are not indicated for a treatable surgical condition, and physical therapy does not address ostomy self-care.

items.stem: Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A medical-surgical nurse is floated for the shift to the orthopedic unit and is assigned a client using a continuous passive motion machine, a device the nurse has never operated. The nurse's most appropriate action is to {{1}}; refusing the entire assignment and leaving the unit could be considered {{2}}.

options: care for the client but avoid touching the machine
accept the assignment, tell the charge nurse about the knowledge gap and request a brief orientation to the device
refuse the assignment until a formal orthopedic competency has been completed
ask the UAP to manage the device because it is a routine task
client abandonment
a reportable incident
appropriate advocacy
malpractice

items.rationale: A floated nurse is expected to provide care within their general competence, communicate any specific skill gap to the charge nurse and receive orientation or a modified assignment for that task. Walking away after accepting responsibility for clients meets the definition of abandonment. Handing an unfamiliar device to the UAP or ignoring it leaves the client unsafe, and demanding a full competency before giving any care is not realistic advocacy.

items.stem: Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A charge nurse is making assignments with one registered nurse and one licensed practical nurse (LPN/LVN). The most appropriate client to assign to the LPN is {{1}}, and for that client the RN must still retain responsibility for {{2}}.

options: a client 3 days after hip replacement with stable vital signs who needs wound care and oral medications
a client with a new tracheostomy whose oxygen requirement is rising
a client receiving a first-time blood transfusion
a client admitted an hour ago with chest pain awaiting troponin results
the daily dressing change
the LPN's own medication administration
the comprehensive assessment and plan of care
the client's hygiene needs

items.rationale: LPN/LVN practice fits stable clients with predictable outcomes who need routine wound care and oral medications. New admissions, unstable clients and clients receiving a first transfusion require RN assessment and judgment because their condition can change quickly. Even when a client is appropriately assigned, the RN retains the comprehensive assessment, care planning and evaluation, while medications the LPN gives remain the LPN's own accountability.

items.stem: Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: After a client receives another client's insulin dose, the unit conducts a root cause analysis. The primary purpose of the analysis is to {{1}}, and the team then trials a change on one shift for two weeks before spreading it, which is the {{2}} phase of the Plan-Do-Study-Act cycle.

options: identify the system and process failures that allowed the error to occur
calculate the cost of the error to the facility
determine which nurse should be disciplined
satisfy the requirement to disclose the error to the client
Do
Act
Plan
Study

items.rationale: Root cause analysis takes a systems view, asking why the process permitted the error rather than who made it, because most errors stem from latent conditions such as look-alike storage or interrupted workflows. Disclosure to the client is a separate ethical duty, not the purpose of the analysis. In PDSA, Plan designs the change, Do implements it on a small scale, Study examines the resulting data and Act decides whether to adopt, adapt or abandon the change.

items.stem: Click to highlight the parts of the handoff report that require the oncoming nurse to act immediately.

highlightSegments.text: 1900 report: 62-year-old client, postoperative day 0 after open bowel resection completed at 1300.
Alert and oriented; pain 4/10 on hydromorphone PCA.
Urine output was 30 mL/hr at 1500 but has been 10 mL/hr for each of the last 2 hours.
Blood pressure has trended down from 128/76 to 96/58 mm Hg with a heart rate of 112.
Abdominal dressing has a 4 cm area of dried serosanguineous drainage, outlined and dated.
Nasogastric tube to low intermittent suction has drained 200 mL of green fluid.
Maintenance IV infusing at 100 mL/hr.
The 1800 dose of IV cefazolin was not given because pharmacy has not delivered it.
Family at the bedside; client asks when clear liquids may begin.
Sequential compression devices in place and functioning.

items.rationale: Urine output below 30 mL/hr for 2 consecutive hours together with falling blood pressure and rising heart rate indicates hypovolemia or early shock after abdominal surgery and must be escalated before anything else. A missed postoperative antibiotic dose needs immediate follow-up with pharmacy and the provider. Controlled PCA pain, an outlined area of old drainage, expected nasogastric output, maintenance fluids and diet questions are routine handoff details.

items.stem: Click to highlight the tasks in the charge nurse's plan that are inappropriately delegated to unlicensed assistive personnel (UAP).

highlightSegments.text: Day-shift plan, 24-bed medical unit, two UAP on duty.
The UAP for rooms 1-12 will obtain vital signs every 4 hours on stable clients and report any systolic pressure below 90 mm Hg.
That UAP will also complete the admission assessment on the client arriving from the emergency department at 1000
and assist the client in room 4 with a bed bath and linen change.
The UAP for rooms 13-24 will ambulate the client in room 15 in the hallway twice,
reposition the client in room 18 every 2 hours,
and teach the client in room 20 how to use the incentive spirometer before discharge.
Both UAP will record intake and output on all clients,
empty urinary drainage bags and document the amounts,
and check the fingerstick glucose in room 22, then select the insulin dose from the sliding scale.
Refusals of care are reported to the assigned nurse.

items.rationale: Admission assessment, client teaching and any decision about a medication dose require nursing judgment and stay with the licensed nurse; a UAP may obtain a fingerstick glucose but cannot select or adjust insulin. Vital signs with clear reporting parameters, hygiene, ambulation of a stable client, repositioning, intake and output, and emptying drainage bags are standardized tasks with predictable outcomes that are appropriately delegated.

items.stem: Click to highlight the findings in the preoperative note that indicate the surgical consent is not valid and the nurse must notify the surgeon.

highlightSegments.text: 0630 preoperative note: 54-year-old client scheduled for laparoscopic inguinal hernia repair at 0800.
Client identified using two identifiers; allergy band in place.
Consent form signed by the client and witnessed by the night nurse at 0500.
Client states, 'I thought they were only doing an x-ray of my stomach today.'
Client received lorazepam 2 mg IV at 0430 for anxiety and is drowsy.
Nothing by mouth since midnight; IV infusing at 75 mL/hr.
Surgical site marked by the surgeon at 0615.
The consent form lists 'repair of left inguinal hernia,' but the site marking is on the right groin.
Spouse at the bedside.
Preoperative antibiotic is due on call to the operating room.

items.rationale: A client who misunderstands the planned procedure has not given informed consent, a client sedated with a benzodiazepine shortly before signing may have lacked capacity, and a mismatch between the consented side and the marked site is a wrong-site surgery risk; each requires the surgeon to be contacted before the client leaves the unit. Identification bands, NPO status, site marking by the surgeon and the timed antibiotic are expected elements of preoperative preparation.

items.stem: Click to highlight the findings in the home health note that the nurse should report to the provider and case manager today.

highlightSegments.text: Home visit, 1030: 72-year-old client discharged 4 days ago after treatment for a heart failure exacerbation.
Client reports sleeping in a recliner for the past two nights because of shortness of breath when lying flat.
Weight 84.2 kg today; documented discharge weight was 81.9 kg.
Ankle edema 1+, unchanged from the discharge assessment.
Client has not filled the furosemide prescription because the pharmacy asked for a $60 copayment.
Blood pressure 138/84 mm Hg, heart rate 88, oxygen saturation 95% on room air.
Client is following a low-sodium diet with the help of a daughter who cooks.
Client weighs self each morning on a bathroom scale and records the number.
Follow-up appointment with the cardiology clinic is scheduled for next week.
Client denies chest pain.

items.rationale: A weight gain of more than 2 kg in 4 days, new orthopnea and a diuretic that was never started together signal early recurrence of fluid overload plus a medication-access problem; the provider needs the clinical data and the case manager can arrange copay assistance or an alternative prescription. Stable vital signs, unchanged 1+ edema, dietary adherence, daily weights, a scheduled follow-up and absence of chest pain are reassuring and do not require same-day reporting.

items.stem: Click to highlight the statements in the draft nurses' note about a client fall that should be removed before the note is entered into the medical record.

highlightSegments.text: 2215: Heard a call for help and found the client lying on the left side on the floor between the bed and the bathroom.
Client stated, 'I got dizzy when I stood up.'
The night shift was short-staffed again, which is why no one answered the call light.
Client alert and oriented; 3 cm abrasion to the left elbow without bleeding; denies striking head.
Blood pressure 104/62 mm Hg lying, heart rate 92; full range of motion in all extremities.
This never would have happened if the UAP had turned the bed alarm on like I asked.
Assisted back to bed by two staff; bed alarm activated; bed placed in low position.
Provider notified at 2225; orders received for orthostatic vital signs and neurologic checks every 4 hours.
Incident report number 4471 completed and filed.
Client's spouse notified at 2240.

items.rationale: The medical record contains objective observations, the client's own words, assessment findings, interventions and notifications. Statements that assign blame, speculate about causes such as staffing, or mention that an incident report was filed do not belong in the chart; they are opinions rather than findings, and referencing the incident report can make a confidential quality document discoverable. The objective descriptions, vital signs, provider orders and family notification are appropriate entries.

items.stem: Click to highlight the actions described in the shift summary that violate client confidentiality.

highlightSegments.text: Day shift, oncology unit, six assigned clients.
At 0900 the nurse gave a bedside handoff to the float nurse while the roommate was out of the room.
At 1030 the nurse discussed a client's biopsy results with a colleague in the cafeteria line.
At 1200 the nurse left the medication room computer logged in with a chart open while answering a call light.
At 1300 the nurse faxed discharge orders to the receiving skilled nursing facility using its verified number.
At 1415 the nurse confirmed a client's name and date of birth aloud before starting a transfusion.
At 1500 the nurse posted on social media, 'Rough day, lost a favorite patient to leukemia,' without naming the client.
At 1600 the nurse placed a printed report sheet in the locked shredding bin.
At 1800 the nurse gave a spouse the update the client had authorized, after verifying the passcode.

items.rationale: Discussing identifiable results in a public area, leaving a chart open on an unattended screen, and posting about a client on social media all expose protected information; even a post without a name can identify a client through timing and detail. Handoff within the care team, secure transmission to a receiving facility, verifying identifiers before a transfusion, shredding paper records and giving an update the client authorized are appropriate uses of health information.

items.stem: Click to highlight the client updates that require the nurse to assess the client immediately.

highlightSegments.text: 1400 UAP report on a surgical unit.
Room 2, postoperative day 1 after appendectomy: temperature 37.9 C (100.2 F), asking for a warm blanket.
Room 3, thyroidectomy this morning: speaking in a high-pitched, hoarse voice and says the neck dressing feels tight.
Room 5: heart rate 62, wants to walk in the hallway.
Room 6, blood transfusion started 15 minutes ago: new low back pain and chills.
Room 8: refusing the evening dose of docusate.
Room 9, 3 days after hip replacement: says the operative leg is 'very painful and shorter' after physical therapy, and the foot is turned outward.
Room 10: wants the television repaired.

items.rationale: A tight dressing with voice change after thyroidectomy suggests a hematoma compressing the airway, back pain and chills minutes into a transfusion are classic signs of an acute hemolytic reaction, and a shortened, externally rotated, painful leg after hip arthroplasty indicates prosthetic dislocation; each is a time-critical complication. A low-grade temperature on postoperative day 1, a heart rate of 62 in a client wanting to walk, a refused stool softener and a television problem are not urgent.

items.stem: Click to highlight the parts of the nurses' note that conflict with the client's documented advance directive and require the nurse to intervene.

highlightSegments.text: 0800: 88-year-old client with advanced dementia and metastatic lung cancer admitted from a long-term care facility with pneumonia.
Portable medical order (POLST) on the chart, signed by the client's health care agent and a provider: do not resuscitate, comfort-focused treatment, no artificial nutrition.
Client receiving oxygen 2 L/min for comfort and scheduled morphine for dyspnea.
Admitting resident entered an order for a nasogastric feeding tube to be placed this afternoon.
Admission orders list the code status as full code pending confirmation with the family.
Health care agent at the bedside states, 'We just want her comfortable.'
Blood cultures were drawn in the emergency department.
Night nurse documented telling the agent, 'If her heart stops we have to try to restart it unless a new form is signed here.'
Client resting with eyes closed; respirations 22 and unlabored.

items.rationale: A valid POLST signed by the authorized agent and a provider is a medical order that travels with the client and remains in force across settings; a full code order, a feeding tube order and telling the family that resuscitation is mandatory all contradict it, so the nurse contacts the provider to reconcile the orders and corrects the misinformation. Comfort oxygen, morphine for dyspnea and the agent's statement are consistent with the directive, and cultures already drawn do not conflict with comfort-focused care.

items.stem: Click to highlight the statements from discharge planning rounds that require the nurse to initiate a referral to another member of the interprofessional team before discharge.

highlightSegments.text: Discharge planning rounds, hospital day 3: 66-year-old client admitted with an ischemic stroke, now with residual left-sided weakness.
The client says, 'My bedroom is upstairs and I can't manage the steps yet.'
Swallow screen passed; the client is eating 75% of a regular diet.
The spouse says, 'I don't know how we'll pay for the new blood thinner; we lost our insurance when he stopped working.'
The client can name each discharge medication and the reason for it.
The client asks, 'How am I supposed to button my shirt with one hand?'
Blood pressure has been at goal for 48 hours on the current regimen.
A follow-up appointment with the neurology clinic is scheduled in 2 weeks.
The spouse reports that the client has become tearful and says he is 'useless' since the stroke.

items.rationale: Inability to climb stairs and difficulty with dressing are functional deficits that need physical and occupational therapy input and a home safety evaluation; inability to afford the anticoagulant is a social work and case management issue that could lead to a second stroke if unaddressed; and tearfulness with statements of worthlessness warrants depression screening and a mental health referral. Diet tolerance, medication knowledge, controlled blood pressure and a scheduled follow-up show readiness for discharge.

items.stem: Click to highlight the assignments in the charge nurse's plan that should be changed to keep clients safe.

highlightSegments.text: Night shift, 30-bed telemetry unit: four RNs, including a new graduate in the third week of orientation and a nurse floated from postpartum, plus one LPN and two UAP.
The postpartum float nurse is assigned the client on a titrated diltiazem infusion for atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response.
The new graduate is assigned four clients, including one admitted an hour ago with chest pain and a rising troponin.
The most experienced RN is assigned the client who returned from cardiac catheterization 2 hours ago.
The LPN is assigned scheduled oral medications and wound care for six stable clients under the charge nurse's direction.
The LPN is also assigned to complete the initial assessment on any client admitted after midnight.
The UAP will obtain vital signs every 4 hours and complete hourly rounding.
The charge nurse keeps no client assignment in order to respond to admissions and emergencies.

items.rationale: A nurse floated from postpartum should receive clients whose needs match that nurse's competence, not a titrated antiarrhythmic infusion; a new graduate still on orientation should not carry an unstable, newly admitted chest pain client; and initial admission assessments are outside LPN scope and must be done by an RN. Giving the LPN stable clients for medications and wound care, assigning UAP vital signs and rounding, and keeping the charge nurse free of an assignment are appropriate.

items.stem: A unit-based council implemented a fall prevention bundle in March. The nurse manager reviews the quality data. Which conclusion should the nurse manager draw?
options: The bundle is effective and the unit should sustain the practices while continuing to monitor monthly
Rounding compliance is now high enough that bed alarms can be discontinued
The improvement is explained by a lower census rather than by the bundle
The fall rate is essentially unchanged, so the bundle should be abandoned
trendHeaders: Bed alarm use for high-risk clients (%)
items.rationale: Falls per 1,000 patient days more than halved and injury falls fell to zero as rounding and bed alarm compliance rose, which is the pattern expected when a bundle is adopted; the next step in a PDSA cycle is to standardize the practice and keep measuring so the gains are sustained. A rate per 1,000 patient days already adjusts for census, so a lower census does not explain the drop, and removing one element of a working bundle risks losing the improvement.

items.stem: The nurse reviews the vital signs recorded over the shift for a client admitted with cellulitis of the leg who is receiving IV antibiotics. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Administer the scheduled acetaminophen and reassess in 1 hour
Document the findings and report them at the change-of-shift handoff
Increase the frequency of vital signs to every 2 hours
Activate the rapid response team and prepare to give a 30 mL/kg crystalloid bolus as ordered
items.rationale: Rising temperature, tachycardia, tachypnea, falling blood pressure, dropping urine output and new drowsiness over 8 hours describe progression from infection to septic shock, an emergency that requires immediate escalation, rapid fluid resuscitation, cultures and broadened antibiotics. Treating the fever alone, waiting for handoff or simply monitoring more often delays treatment during the window in which sepsis outcomes are decided.

items.stem: The charge nurse reviews the acuity data for four clients before making assignments. Which client is most appropriate to assign to the licensed practical nurse (LPN/LVN)?
options: Client A
Client B
Client D
Client C
trendRows: Afebrile, oxygen weaned to room air
Hemoglobin fell from 9.8 to 8.1 g/dL, transfusion ordered
Heart rate 130-150, diltiazem infusion being titrated
Insulin infusion with hourly glucose checks
items.rationale: The client with pneumonia who is afebrile and off oxygen is stable with a predictable course, which fits LPN/LVN scope for medication administration and routine care under RN direction. A client with a falling hemoglobin awaiting transfusion, a client on a titrating antiarrhythmic infusion and a client on an insulin infusion with hourly monitoring all require ongoing RN assessment and rapid decision-making.

items.stem: A hospital implemented barcode medication administration and a non-punitive error reporting policy in the first quarter. The quality nurse reviews the medication safety data. Which conclusion is accurate?
options: Increased near-miss reporting reflects a stronger safety culture, and errors reaching clients have decreased
The rise in reported near misses shows that the new system is causing more errors
Reporting should be limited to errors that reach the client to reduce paperwork
Scanning compliance can be relaxed because it has not affected harm
items.rationale: Near-miss reports climbing while errors that reach clients and cause harm fall is the expected signature of a just culture: staff report interceptions they once kept quiet, and the data expose weak points before harm occurs. Near misses are errors caught before administration, not evidence that the system creates errors. Rising scan compliance alongside falling harm supports keeping the practice, and restricting reporting would blind the organization to the causes it needs to fix.

items.stem: A case management department began a transitional care program for clients discharged with heart failure. The nurse manager evaluates the data for the year. Which conclusion should the nurse manager draw?
options: The program is meeting its goal and its components should be maintained and refined
The 48-hour call is unnecessary because the 7-day visit rate is high
The program should be discontinued because 11% of clients are still readmitted
Readmissions fell because fewer clients were discharged
items.rationale: Readmissions fell by more than half as the proportion of clients receiving early calls and prompt clinic visits rose, while the number discharged stayed constant, which supports the program's effectiveness. The early telephone contact catches medication confusion and weight gain before the visit and complements rather than duplicates it. Some readmissions in heart failure are unavoidable, so residual readmissions are a reason to refine the program, not abandon it.

items.stem: The nurse reviews the 0700 and 1100 data for four assigned clients on a medical unit. Which client should the nurse assess first?
options: Client D
Client C
Client B
Client A
trendRows: RR 24, SpO2 94% on 2 L/min, wheezing, speaking in full sentences
RR 30, SpO2 91% on 4 L/min, chest quieter, speaking in short phrases
K+ 5.1 mEq/L after treatment, HR 76 and regular
items.rationale: A rising respiratory rate, a saturation that is falling despite doubled oxygen, and a chest that has become quieter while the client can no longer speak in full sentences point to worsening airflow obstruction and impending respiratory failure; a quiet chest in asthma is an ominous sign, not improvement. The client with cellulitis is defervescing, the potassium is falling with a regular rhythm, and the postoperative client's pain and mobility are improving, so all three are stable.

items.stem: The charge nurse reviews the staffing and workload projections for the next 24 hours on a 28-bed medical unit. Which action should the charge nurse take first?
options: Contact the staffing office now to request an additional RN for the night shift
Ask each day-shift nurse to stay 4 extra hours into the night shift
Close the unit to admissions for the night shift
Give the night charge nurse a full client assignment to cover the gap
trendHeaders: Total acuity points (unit target: 4 per RN)
items.rationale: The night shift projects 29 acuity points plus 3 admissions for 4 RNs, roughly 7 points per nurse against a target of 4, while the day shifts are within target; the earliest and safest fix is to request an additional nurse through the staffing office while there is still time to fill the need. Mandatory overtime produces fatigued nurses, closing to admissions is a last resort requiring administrative approval, and loading the charge nurse removes the resource needed for emergencies.

items.stem: A registered nurse is planning care on a medical-surgical unit with a licensed practical nurse (LPN/LVN) and unlicensed assistive personnel (UAP). For each task, select the most appropriate team member to whom the task may be assigned or delegated.
matrixRows: Administer scheduled oral medications to a stable client
Develop the plan of care for a newly admitted client
Measure and record the daily weight of a client with heart failure
Reinforce previously taught insulin self-injection technique
Assess a client 15 minutes after the start of a first-time blood transfusion
Apply a condom catheter to a client with urinary incontinence
items.rationale: Care planning and assessment of a client during the first minutes of a transfusion require RN judgment because early recognition of a reaction depends on skilled assessment. Administering routine oral medications and reinforcing teaching the RN has already provided are within LPN/LVN scope. Daily weights and applying a condom catheter are standardized tasks with predictable outcomes that UAP may perform, with results reported to the nurse.

items.stem: For each nursing action, select the ethical principle it best demonstrates.
matrixRows: The nurse tells a client the truth about a medication error even though the client was not harmed
The nurse honors a client's decision to leave against medical advice after explaining the risks
The nurse advocates so that an uninsured client receives the same standard of wound care as other clients
The nurse returns at the promised time to help a client walk after saying she would
The nurse double-checks a heparin dose with a colleague before giving it to prevent harm
items.rationale: Veracity is truth-telling, including disclosure of errors. Autonomy respects the client's right to self-determination even when the choice is medically unwise. Justice is fairness in the distribution of care regardless of ability to pay. Fidelity is faithfulness to promises and commitments. Nonmaleficence is the duty to avoid causing harm, illustrated by verification steps before giving a high-alert medication.

items.stem: For each action by a nurse, select whether it is permitted under privacy regulations or is a violation of client confidentiality.
matrixRows: Reviewing the chart of a neighbor who was admitted to another unit out of concern
Sharing the client's care plan with the physical therapist assigned to the client
Giving a client's lab results to a police officer who calls without a court order or client consent
Reporting a positive tuberculosis test to the public health department
Reading a coworker's chart to find out why the coworker was hospitalized
Telling a client's employer that the client is hospitalized when the employer calls to verify
items.rationale: Health information may be used for treatment by those involved in the client's care, and reporting communicable diseases to public health is legally required, so sharing with the assigned therapist and reporting tuberculosis are permitted. Accessing records out of curiosity or concern, whether for a neighbor or a coworker, is a violation regardless of intent, as is releasing information to police or an employer without the client's authorization or a lawful order.

items.stem: For each situation, select the legal concept it best illustrates.
matrixRows: A nurse tells a confused client who tries to get up, 'If you get out of bed again I will tie you down.'
A nurse gives an intramuscular injection to a competent client who has clearly refused it
A nurse fails to raise the side rails after sedating a client, and the client falls and fractures a hip
A nurse locks a competent, non-dangerous client in a room to prevent the client from leaving against medical advice
A nurse tells another nurse in the break room that a client is 'a drug seeker' with no basis in the record, and the comment reaches the client's employer
items.rationale: Assault is a threat that creates fear of harmful contact, while battery is the harmful or offensive contact itself, including treatment given over a competent client's refusal. Negligence is failure to meet the standard of care that results in injury. False imprisonment is unlawfully restricting a competent client's freedom of movement. Defamation is a false statement that damages reputation; when spoken it is slander.

items.stem: A nurse is reviewing events that occurred on the unit during the shift. Which events require the nurse to complete an incident report? Select all that apply.
options: A client's blood pressure was 148/90 mm Hg on the morning assessment
A client received a scheduled dose of metoprolol 2 hours late because of a pharmacy delay
A client's dentures were found to be missing after return from the operating room
A client's IV pump alarmed for a kinked line, and the nurse straightened the tubing
A visitor slipped on a wet floor in the hallway and was not injured
A client refused a scheduled dose of docusate
A client with a documented penicillin allergy received a dose of ampicillin and had no reaction
items.rationale: Incident reports capture any event that is not consistent with routine care or that could have caused harm, whether or not injury occurred: a late medication, a visitor fall, administration of a drug to which the client is allergic, and lost client property all qualify. A pump alarm resolved during normal monitoring, a client's right to refuse a medication and an elevated blood pressure reading are part of ordinary care and are documented in the record, not reported as incidents.

items.stem: A nurse is asked to witness a client's signature on a consent form for central venous catheter insertion. Which actions are the nurse's responsibilities in this process? Select all that apply.
options: Confirm that the client can describe the procedure in their own words
Ensure the client is signing voluntarily without pressure from staff or family
Explain the risks and alternatives of the procedure to the client
Decide whether the procedure is medically necessary
Obtain the signature before any ordered preprocedure sedation is given
Verify the client's identity using two identifiers
Sign as the witness only after the client has signed
items.rationale: The witness confirms identity, that the client appears to understand what was explained, that the signature is voluntary and that it is obtained before sedation clouds judgment, and then signs after the client. Explaining risks, benefits and alternatives is the legal duty of the provider performing the procedure, and a nurse who takes on that role assumes liability for the adequacy of the explanation. Determining medical necessity is a provider decision, not part of witnessing.

items.stem: A nurse is preparing a client with a healing stage 3 sacral pressure injury for transfer to a skilled nursing facility. Which information should the nurse include in the transfer handoff to ensure continuity of care? Select all that apply.
options: The current wound measurements and the dressing type and change frequency
Pending laboratory results and who will follow up on them
The client's code status and the location of the advance directive
The client's turning schedule and the pressure-redistribution surface in use
The names of the nurses who cared for the client during the hospital stay
The times of the last doses of pain medication and antibiotics
The nurse's personal opinion about the client's family dynamics
items.rationale: A safe transfer handoff gives the receiving team what it needs to continue care without gaps: current wound status and treatment plan, timing of last medications so doses are neither missed nor duplicated, code status and advance directive location, the prevention plan already in place, and any results still pending with a clear owner. Personal opinions about the family are subjective and inappropriate, and the names of prior caregivers do not affect the client's ongoing care.

items.stem: A nurse on a medical unit receives the following reports from the UAP at the same time. Which client should the nurse assess first?
options: A client with a tracheostomy placed 2 weeks ago who is coughing effectively and has thick secretions visible at the tube opening
A client with a urinary tract infection whose temperature is 38.6 C (101.5 F) and who is asking for acetaminophen
A client with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease whose oxygen saturation is 89% and who is resting comfortably using pursed-lip breathing
A client 1 hour after cardiac catheterization via the femoral artery whose groin dressing is saturated with bright-red blood
items.rationale: Bright-red saturation of a femoral access site within an hour of catheterization indicates active arterial bleeding, which can progress to hemorrhage or retroperitoneal bleeding within minutes; the nurse applies direct pressure and calls for help immediately. A saturation of 89% is within the usual target for a comfortable client with COPD, visible secretions in a client who is coughing effectively can be suctioned next, and fever with a request for an antipyretic is expected with infection.

items.stem: A nurse observes a UAP preparing to transfer a client with left-sided weakness from the bed to a wheelchair by pulling the client up by the weak arm. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Document the observation in the UAP's performance file
Allow the transfer to finish and then discuss the technique privately
Report the UAP to the nurse manager after the shift
Stop the transfer and demonstrate the correct technique using a gait belt
items.rationale: Pulling on a weak or paralyzed arm can cause shoulder subluxation and a fall, so the nurse intervenes immediately to protect the client and then teaches the correct technique with a gait belt and transfer toward the stronger side. Supervision of delegated tasks includes correcting unsafe practice at the moment it occurs. Reporting or documenting may follow if the problem recurs, but neither protects the client now, and allowing an unsafe transfer to finish exposes the client to injury.

items.stem: A well-known local athlete is admitted to the unit. A nurse from another unit who is not involved in the client's care asks the assigned nurse, 'What happened to him? I saw the ambulance.' Which response by the assigned nurse is appropriate?
options: 'I can't share information about any client with staff who aren't involved in that client's care.'
'You can look it up in the chart if you're that curious.'
'He's stable, that's all I can say.'
'I'll tell you after he's discharged.'
items.rationale: Information is shared only with members of the team who need it to provide care; even confirming that someone is a client or is stable discloses protected information. Inviting a coworker to read the chart encourages unauthorized access, which is a reportable privacy breach that audit trails will reveal. Discharge does not end the duty of confidentiality, so promising to share later is equally inappropriate.

items.stem: A nurse realizes that a client was given another client's oral antihypertensive medication 20 minutes ago. Place the steps in the correct order.
options: Document the medication given, the assessment findings and the notifications in the medical record
Implement any orders received, such as additional monitoring
Assess the client's blood pressure, heart rate and symptoms
Complete the facility incident report
Notify the provider and the charge nurse of the error
items.rationale: Client safety comes first, so the nurse assesses for effects of the wrong drug before anything else, then notifies the provider and charge nurse so that orders such as increased monitoring or treatment can be given and carried out. Factual documentation of what occurred and what was done goes in the medical record, and the incident report is completed last as a separate quality document that is not referenced in the chart.

items.stem: Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A client admitted with a productive cough, night sweats and a chest x-ray suggestive of pulmonary tuberculosis is awaiting sputum results. The nurse places the client in {{1}}, and staff entering the room wear {{2}}.

options: a room near the nurses' station with the door open for observation
a private room with negative-pressure ventilation and the door kept closed
a semi-private room with a client who has bacterial pneumonia
a private room with positive-pressure ventilation
a face shield only
a fit-tested N95 respirator or higher
a standard surgical mask
a gown and gloves only

items.rationale: Suspected pulmonary tuberculosis requires airborne precautions from the moment it is suspected: an airborne infection isolation room with negative pressure and frequent air exchanges, door closed, and a fit-tested N95 or powered air-purifying respirator for anyone entering. Positive-pressure rooms protect immunocompromised clients from hallway air and would push infectious particles out. Surgical masks block droplets but do not filter the small droplet nuclei that carry tuberculosis.

items.stem: Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A client on a medical unit has had three watery stools in 8 hours and tests positive for Clostridioides difficile toxin. The nurse initiates contact precautions, performs hand hygiene with {{1}} after care, and ensures the room is cleaned daily with {{2}}.

options: chlorhexidine hand rub only when hands are visibly soiled
an antiseptic hand wipe
soap and water
alcohol-based hand rub
warm water and detergent only
a sporicidal, bleach-based disinfectant
alcohol wipes
a quaternary ammonium disinfectant

items.rationale: C. difficile forms spores that alcohol does not kill, so hand hygiene after caring for the client must be mechanical washing with soap and water to physically remove spores, and surfaces need a sporicidal agent such as diluted bleach rather than the standard quaternary ammonium cleaner. Contact precautions with gown and gloves and dedicated equipment complete the bundle. Alcohol rubs remain appropriate for other clients but are ineffective here.

items.stem: Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A young adult is admitted with fever, severe headache and a stiff neck, and the provider suspects meningococcal meningitis. The nurse initiates {{1}} precautions, which can be discontinued {{2}}.

options: contact
droplet
airborne
protective environment
after 24 hours of effective antibiotic therapy
when the fever resolves
after the lumbar puncture is completed
when the client is discharged

items.rationale: Neisseria meningitidis spreads through large respiratory droplets, so a private room and a surgical mask for staff within about 1 meter (3 feet) of the client are required, and the client wears a mask during transport. The organism is cleared from respiratory secretions after 24 hours of appropriate antibiotics, at which point droplet precautions end. Airborne precautions are for small-particle pathogens such as tuberculosis and measles, and neither fever resolution nor a completed lumbar puncture indicates loss of infectivity.

items.stem: Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A client who received a hematopoietic stem cell transplant 5 days ago has an absolute neutrophil count of 300/mm3. The nurse places the client in a private room with {{1}} and instructs visitors that {{2}}.

options: negative-pressure ventilation
a portable fan to circulate the air
positive-pressure ventilation and HEPA-filtered air
the door propped open to improve airflow
fresh flowers and potted plants may not be brought into the room
the client may be taken to the garden for fresh air
raw fruits and vegetables are the safest snacks to bring
a mask is needed only if the visitor has a fever

items.rationale: Protective environment precautions for a severely neutropenic transplant recipient use a positive-pressure room with HEPA-filtered air so that unfiltered hallway air cannot enter, and the door stays closed. Flowers, plants and standing water harbor mold and gram-negative organisms and are excluded. Visitors with any symptoms stay away, raw produce may carry organisms and is usually restricted, and outdoor exposure to construction dust and soil molds is avoided while counts are low.

items.stem: Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A nurse sustains a needlestick from a used insulin syringe while placing it in a sharps container. The nurse should first {{1}} and then {{2}}.

options: apply a bleach solution to the wound
squeeze the site to express blood
cover the site with a bandage and finish the medication pass
wash the puncture site with soap and running water
report the exposure immediately to the supervisor and go to employee health for evaluation and possible postexposure prophylaxis
document the injury at the end of the shift
ask the client whether they have any infections and decide based on the answer
wait to see whether symptoms develop before reporting

items.rationale: Immediate washing with soap and water removes contaminants; squeezing, caustic agents and delaying care do not reduce transmission and may worsen tissue damage. Prompt reporting starts the exposure protocol, including source testing with consent and baseline testing of the nurse, and HIV postexposure prophylaxis is most effective when started within hours, so reporting cannot wait for symptoms or the end of the shift.

items.stem: Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A confused older adult keeps pulling at a nasogastric tube despite redirection, a mitt and a sitter, and the provider orders soft wrist restraints. The nurse secures the ties with a quick-release knot to {{1}} and assesses circulation, skin and the client's needs at least {{2}}.

options: the movable part of the bed frame
the side rail
the IV pole
the headboard
once per shift
every 8 hours
every 2 hours, releasing the restraints to reposition the client and offer fluids and toileting
only when the client calls out

items.rationale: Ties fastened to the bed frame move with the bed, whereas a side rail can be lowered and pull on the limb, and a headboard or IV pole can injure the client when the bed is adjusted or the pole tips. Standards require frequent monitoring, commonly every 2 hours or more often per policy, with release for range of motion, skin checks, hydration and toileting. Restraints remain the last resort after less restrictive measures, and the order must be renewed within the time limit set for nonviolent restraint.

items.stem: Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A nurse enters a client's room and finds a small fire in the wastebasket next to the bed. Following the RACE sequence, the nurse first {{1}}; when using the extinguisher, the nurse aims the nozzle at {{2}}.

options: pulls the fire alarm at the nearest station
closes the doors along the unit hallway
tries to smother the fire with a blanket
moves the client out of the room to safety
the base of the fire
the ceiling above the fire
the client's bed
the top of the flames

items.rationale: RACE stands for Rescue, Alarm, Confine, Extinguish: the person in immediate danger is removed first, then the alarm is activated, doors are closed to confine smoke and fire, and only then is a small fire extinguished. The PASS technique (Pull, Aim, Squeeze, Sweep) directs the extinguisher at the base of the fire where the fuel is, because spraying the flames themselves does not stop combustion.

items.stem: Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: At a mass-casualty scene the nurse finds an adult who is not breathing. After the airway is repositioned the client begins breathing at 34 breaths/min. The nurse assigns a {{1}} tag; an adult who is walking around with a bleeding scalp laceration receives a {{2}} tag.

options: yellow (delayed)
red (immediate)
black (expectant)
green (minor)
black (expectant)
yellow (delayed)
green (minor)
red (immediate)

items.rationale: Under START triage, an apneic adult who resumes breathing once the airway is opened is tagged red because the condition is immediately life-threatening but salvageable; black is reserved for clients who remain apneic after repositioning. A respiratory rate above 30 also independently qualifies for red. Anyone who can walk is tagged green regardless of visible bleeding, and yellow is for those who cannot walk but have adequate breathing, perfusion and mental status.

items.stem: Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: During a home visit to an 82-year-old client with osteoporosis who lives alone, the nurse notes throw rugs in the hallway, a dimly lit bathroom and a water heater set at 60 C (140 F). The nurse recommends {{1}} and lowering the water heater setting to no more than {{2}} to prevent scalds.

options: keeping the bathroom door closed at night
taping down the corners of the rugs
removing the throw rugs and installing night lights along the path to the bathroom
wearing socks instead of shoes indoors

items.rationale: Loose rugs are a leading cause of trips and hip fractures in older adults with fragile bones, and taped corners still leave a raised edge; removal plus lighting for the night route to the bathroom addresses two of the most common home fall hazards. Water at 60 C can cause a full-thickness burn within seconds, so 49 C (120 F) is the recommended maximum. Socks without grips increase slipping, and a closed door does not improve visibility.

items.stem: Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A client weighing 130 kg who cannot bear weight must be moved from the bed to a stretcher for a procedure. To protect the client and staff, the nurse uses {{1}} and positions the bed {{2}} before the move.

options: a gait belt with one staff member on each side
a slide board with the client pushing with the arms
a mechanical lift or friction-reducing lateral transfer device with enough staff to operate it
a draw sheet with two staff members lifting on the count of three
at the staff's waist height, locked, with the stretcher aligned at the same level
in high Fowler's position
with the wheels unlocked so it can be pulled closer during the move
in the lowest position with the side rails down

items.rationale: Safe client handling programs replace manual lifting with mechanical lifts and air-assisted or friction-reducing lateral transfer devices for dependent clients, because manually moving more than about 16 kg (35 lb) of client weight exceeds safe limits and causes back injuries. The bed and stretcher are locked and aligned at the caregivers' waist height to avoid bending and reaching. Draw-sheet lifts, gait belts and slide boards depend on staff strength or client participation that is not available here.

items.stem: Click to highlight the findings in the home visit note that represent safety hazards for this client.

highlightSegments.text: Home visit, 1400: 79-year-old client recovering from a left hip fracture, ambulating with a walker.
Client lives in a two-story house and sleeps in a first-floor bedroom set up by the family.
An extension cord runs across the living room floor to a lamp beside the recliner.
Grab bars have been installed in the shower and beside the toilet.
Client uses a step stool to reach medications kept on a high kitchen shelf.
The hallway smoke detector chirps intermittently; client says the battery has been low for a month.
Client wears well-fitting shoes with rubber soles.
Client reports taking a sleeping pill at bedtime and getting up twice each night to void.
The walker is adjusted to the correct height and the client uses it consistently.
Family visits daily and helps with meals.

items.rationale: A cord across a walkway is a trip hazard, climbing a step stool for medications risks a fall in a client recovering from a hip fracture, a non-functioning smoke detector removes early fire warning, and a sedative combined with nighttime toileting is a well-established fall risk that should be raised with the provider. First-floor sleeping, grab bars, appropriate footwear, a correctly fitted walker and daily family support are protective factors.

items.stem: Click to highlight the findings in the nurses' note that require immediate action for a client in bilateral soft wrist restraints.

highlightSegments.text: 1400: Client in bilateral soft wrist restraints for pulling at the endotracheal tube; order renewed by the provider at 0800.
Restraint checks documented every 2 hours through 1200; no check has been documented since.
Right hand warm with capillary refill under 2 seconds.
Left hand cool and dusky, and the client is unable to move the fingers on command.
Left restraint tie is secured to the side rail.
Client is oriented to self only and follows simple commands.
Two fingers fit between the right restraint and the wrist.
Client was turned and offered water at 1200.
The endotracheal tube remains secured at 23 cm at the lip.
A family member asks when the restraints can come off.

items.rationale: A cool, dusky hand with loss of movement means the restraint is compromising circulation or nerve function and must be released immediately with the limb reassessed; a tie on a side rail can tighten or pull the arm when the rail moves and must be moved to the bed frame; and a gap in monitoring beyond the required interval means the nurse assesses now and corrects the process. A warm hand with good refill, a correct two-finger fit, needs met at 1200 and a secure tube are expected findings.

items.stem: Click to highlight the factors in the incident narrative that contributed to the client's fall.

highlightSegments.text: 0310: 84-year-old client admitted with pneumonia; Morse Fall Scale score 65 on admission.
Client received zolpidem at 2200 for sleep.
Found on the floor beside the bed at 0305 after attempting to walk to the bathroom unassisted.
Bed was in the high position and the bed alarm had been switched off after the 0200 linen change.
Client was wearing hospital socks without non-slip soles.
Call light was clipped to the pillow within reach.
Client was oriented to person and place at the 2400 check.
The room's night light was on.
IV pole was positioned on the far side of the bed, away from the path to the bathroom.
Client states, 'I didn't want to bother anyone.'

items.rationale: A sedative-hypnotic impairs balance and judgment at night, a bed left high with the alarm off removes two barriers to an unassisted exit, smooth-soled socks slip on hard floors, and a client's reluctance to ask for help means the call light will not be used even when reachable; each is a modifiable factor the post-fall huddle should address. The admission risk score, a reachable call light, earlier orientation, the night light and IV pole placement did not cause the fall.

items.stem: Click to highlight the actions in the scenario that increase the risk of a medication error.

highlightSegments.text: 0900 medication pass on a cardiac unit.
The provider called with a telephone order for 'Lasix 40 IV now'; the nurse wrote it down and hung up without reading it back.
The nurse confirmed the client's name and date of birth against the wristband.
Because the client's regular insulin was not yet in the drawer, the nurse took a vial from a neighboring client's supply.
The nurse documented the insulin dose as '10 U' on the paper flow sheet.
The nurse held the metoprolol because the heart rate was 52 and notified the provider.
While preparing the heparin infusion the nurse was interrupted twice and did not restart the calculation.
The nurse scanned the barcode on the client's band and on each medication before administration.
The nurse asked a second nurse to verify the heparin rate before starting the pump.

items.rationale: Verbal orders must be written down and read back to catch transcription errors; borrowing another client's medication bypasses pharmacy verification and invites wrong-drug or wrong-dose errors; the abbreviation 'U' can be misread as a zero, so 'units' is written in full; and an interrupted calculation that is not restarted is a recognized source of dosing errors. Two identifiers, holding a beta blocker for bradycardia, barcode scanning and independent double-checks of high-alert infusions are safe practices.

items.stem: Click to highlight the practices described in the charge nurse's rounding note that break transmission-based precautions.

highlightSegments.text: Rounding note, 1100, infectious disease unit.
Room 1: client with active pulmonary tuberculosis; the door is propped open so the client can see the hallway.
The pressure indicator outside room 1 shows air flowing into the room.
Room 2: client with influenza on droplet precautions; the client wore a surgical mask during transport to x-ray.
Room 3: client with C. difficile diarrhea; the UAP was observed using alcohol hand rub after removing gloves.
A disposable stethoscope and a dedicated blood pressure cuff are kept in room 3.
Room 4: client with a MRSA wound on contact precautions; the nurse carried the shared glucometer into the room and back to the medication room without disinfecting it.
Room 5: client with disseminated herpes zoster; the nurse entered wearing an N95 respirator, gown and gloves.
Visitors to room 5 were taught to wear the same protective equipment.

items.rationale: An airborne isolation room only works with the door closed to maintain negative pressure, alcohol rub does not remove C. difficile spores so soap and water is required, and equipment shared between rooms must be disinfected after use in a contact isolation room or dedicated to that client. Inward airflow at the indicator, a masked influenza client during transport, dedicated equipment for the C. difficile room and airborne plus contact precautions for disseminated zoster are all correct.

items.stem: Click to highlight the parent statements during a 15-month well-child visit that indicate a safety risk requiring teaching.

highlightSegments.text: Parent reports the toddler is walking well and climbing onto furniture.
'We turned her car seat to face forward last month because her legs looked cramped.'
'She sleeps in a crib with the mattress at the lowest setting.'
'I keep my blood pressure pills in my purse on the floor by the couch so I remember to take them.'
'We put safety gates at the top and bottom of the stairs.'
'The blinds in her room have the long looped cords, but she can't reach them yet.'
'Our water heater is set at 49 C (120 F).'
'We use a baby walker so she can zip around the kitchen while I cook.'
'We have latches on the cupboards under the sink.'
'I test the smoke alarms every month.'

items.rationale: Children ride rear-facing as long as possible and at least until age 2 or the seat's rear-facing limit; bent legs are not a safety concern, but facing forward raises the risk of neck injury. Medications in a purse on the floor are a leading cause of toddler poisoning, looped blind cords are a strangulation hazard because a toddler's reach changes quickly, and mobile baby walkers cause falls down stairs and give access to hot surfaces. Crib height, stair gates, water temperature, cabinet latches and alarm checks are protective.

items.stem: Click to highlight the actions in the incident narrative that were incorrect responses to the fire.

highlightSegments.text: 2130: Smoke was seen coming from the linen closet at the end of the hallway on a 20-bed unit.
The nurse who discovered the smoke opened the closet door fully to look for the source.
The nurse then activated the pull station and called the emergency number.
A second nurse began moving clients from the two rooms nearest the closet to the far end of the hallway.
The UAP opened the windows in the client rooms to clear the smoke.
The charge nurse closed all client room doors after verifying who was inside.
A nurse shut the oxygen zone valve after placing the clients who needed oxygen on portable cylinders.
A visitor was directed to leave the floor by the elevator.
Staff used a fire extinguisher only after the clients nearest the fire had been moved.

items.rationale: Opening a door to a fire admits oxygen and can cause a flashover, so doors to a fire stay closed. Opening windows likewise feeds the fire and draws smoke through the unit. Elevators can stall or open onto the fire floor, so evacuation uses the stairs. Activating the alarm, rescuing those in immediate danger, closing client doors, shutting the oxygen zone valve after providing portable supply, and extinguishing only after rescue follow the RACE sequence.

items.stem: Click to highlight the findings in the nurses' note that indicate escalating risk for violence and the need for immediate de-escalation and security notification.

highlightSegments.text: 1620, emergency department: 34-year-old client waiting 3 hours for results after a minor motor vehicle collision.
Client has been pacing the room and repeatedly asking why others are being seen first.
Vital signs stable; pain 2/10.
Client's speech has become loud and rapid, and the client is now standing close to the nurse with clenched fists.
Client accepted a cup of water and sat down briefly.
Client states, 'If someone doesn't get in here in five minutes, somebody is going to get hurt.'
A family member at the bedside is calm and apologizes for the client's behavior.
Client denies alcohol or drug use and has no psychiatric history.
Client picks up the tray table and slams it down.

items.rationale: Pacing, invasion of personal space with clenched fists, loud rapid speech, a direct threat and striking objects form the recognized progression toward physical aggression; each is a cue to use calm, non-threatening de-escalation, keep an exit accessible and alert security before the client acts. Stable vital signs, briefly accepting water, a calm family member and the absence of substance use or psychiatric history do not remove the risk but are not escalation cues.

items.stem: An infection prevention nurse reviews the quality data for an intensive care unit after a hand hygiene campaign began in February. Which conclusion should the nurse draw?
options: Improved hand hygiene and bundle compliance are associated with the decline in central line infections
The infection rate fell because fewer central lines were in use
Hand hygiene compliance above 90% means the observation audits can stop
The absence of infections in July proves the unit no longer needs the bundle
items.rationale: Central line days were essentially constant, so the falling infection rate cannot be explained by less line use, and the rate per 1,000 line days already adjusts for exposure. The decline tracks rising hand hygiene and bundle compliance, which is the expected relationship. Hand hygiene performance drifts when observation stops, so audits continue, and a single month without infections shows the bundle working rather than a reason to remove it.

items.stem: The nurse reviews the restraint monitoring flowsheet for a client in bilateral soft wrist restraints on a medical unit. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Document the findings and continue the current plan
Ask the provider to renew the restraint order for another 24 hours
Remove the restraints, assess the left wrist and neurovascular status, and notify the provider
Pad the left restraint and continue monitoring every 2 hours
trendRows: Calm, oriented to person and place
Red area 5 cm with skin abrasion
Calm, asking to have hands free
items.rationale: The flowsheet shows worsening skin injury and deteriorating circulation on the left wrist over 4 hours, care not provided at 1400, and a client who is now calm and oriented and no longer pulling at lines; the behavior that justified restraint has resolved, so the restraints are removed at the earliest possible moment and the injury is assessed and reported. Padding or documenting prolongs a harmful restraint, and renewal is inappropriate when the indication no longer exists.

items.stem: A medical unit introduced bleach-based terminal cleaning and a soap-and-water hand hygiene reminder for Clostridioides difficile rooms in April. The infection control committee reviews the data. Which conclusion should the committee draw?
options: The environmental cleaning and hand hygiene interventions are associated with a sustained decrease in hospital-onset cases
One case in August indicates the interventions have failed
Cases dropped only because antibiotic stewardship reviews improved
The rate fell because the unit had fewer patient days
items.rationale: The rate per 10,000 patient days fell by more than 80% while patient days stayed level and stewardship reviews changed little, so the cleaning and hand hygiene changes introduced in April are the most plausible driver. Stewardship matters for C. difficile, but its modest change cannot explain the drop. A rate already adjusts for patient days, and a single residual case is consistent with success rather than failure because some community-acquired colonization will always be present.

items.stem: The infection prevention nurse reviews surveillance data for a surgical unit. Which action should the nurse take first based on the trend?
options: Wait for another month of data before acting
Place every surgical client on contact precautions
Investigate the decline in shared equipment disinfection and reeducate staff on cleaning between clients
Discontinue preoperative chlorhexidine bathing because infections rose while it was in use
items.rationale: New MRSA infections rose sevenfold in step with a steady fall in disinfection of shared equipment, while contact precaution compliance and preoperative bathing remained high; the data point to contaminated shared equipment as the likely transmission route, so that process is corrected first.
