Blanket contact precautions do not address the equipment problem, chlorhexidine bathing is a proven prevention measure that should continue, and an upward trend of this size is a signal to act, not to wait.

items.stem: The nurse reviews the fall risk assessments for a hospitalized 76-year-old client over 5 days. Which action should the nurse take based on the trend?
options: Continue the universal fall precautions because the client was low risk on admission
Ask the UAP to remind the client to call for help before getting up
Apply a vest restraint at night to keep the client from getting up
Implement high-risk fall interventions, including a bed alarm, hourly rounding with scheduled toileting and a low bed
trendRows: Oxycodone added for back pain, nocturia
items.rationale: The score has tripled into the high-risk range as gait deteriorated, a diuretic and an opioid were added and the client now overestimates ability, so the plan must escalate to a full high-risk bundle: bed alarm, low bed, non-slip footwear, hourly rounding with proactive toileting and a medication review. The admission score no longer describes the client. Restraints increase injury and are not a fall prevention strategy, and a reminder alone will not work for a client who forgets limitations.

items.stem: For each client condition, select the transmission-based precaution the nurse should implement in addition to standard precautions.
matrixRows: Pulmonary tuberculosis with a positive sputum smear
Pertussis in a 3-year-old
Vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus in a urine culture
Measles
Scabies
Pneumonia caused by an antibiotic-susceptible organism
items.rationale: Tuberculosis and measles are carried on tiny droplet nuclei that stay suspended in air, requiring an airborne infection isolation room and N95 respirators. Pertussis spreads by large droplets, so a surgical mask within about 1 meter is sufficient. Vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus and scabies are transmitted through direct contact with the client or the environment, calling for gown and gloves. Ordinary bacterial pneumonia without a multidrug-resistant organism needs standard precautions only.

items.stem: A nurse is planning care for a hospitalized 81-year-old client with a Morse Fall Scale score of 60 who is oriented but unsteady. For each intervention, select whether it is appropriate or not appropriate for this client's fall prevention plan.
matrixRows: Raise all four side rails whenever the client is in bed
Keep the bed in the lowest position with the brakes locked
Place non-slip footwear on the client before ambulation
Have the client walk to the bathroom independently to build strength
Offer toileting every 2 hours while the client is awake
Keep the call light and personal items within reach
items.rationale: A low locked bed, non-slip footwear, proactive toileting and reachable belongings are core elements of a fall bundle for a high-risk client. Raising all four rails is considered a restraint and increases injury because clients climb over them and fall from a greater height. An unsteady client should ambulate with assistance and a gait belt; unassisted trips to the bathroom are when most inpatient falls occur.

items.stem: A nurse is using the START method at the scene of a building collapse. For each adult casualty, select the correct triage tag.
matrixRows: Walking with a bandaged forearm, asking where to go
Not breathing and remains apneic after the airway is repositioned
Breathing 36 breaths/min, radial pulse present, unable to walk
Breathing 20 breaths/min, capillary refill 4 seconds, follows commands
Breathing 18 breaths/min, radial pulse present, cannot walk because of a deformed lower leg, follows commands
Breathing 24 breaths/min, radial pulse present, does not respond to simple commands
items.rationale: START sorts by the ability to walk (green), then breathing (apneic after airway opening is black), respiratory rate over 30 (red), perfusion with capillary refill over 2 seconds or no radial pulse (red), and mental status with failure to follow simple commands (red). A casualty who cannot walk but breathes under 30 times per minute, has a pulse with good perfusion and follows commands is yellow and can wait for treatment.

items.stem: A nurse is reviewing restraint practices with a group of newly hired staff. For each statement, select whether it describes correct or incorrect practice.
matrixRows: A restraint may be applied in an emergency before the order is obtained, with the provider notified immediately
A prescriber may write a restraint order as needed (PRN) so staff can reapply it when necessary
The least restrictive method that keeps the client safe is tried before a restraint is used
A client restrained for violent behavior is evaluated face-to-face by a qualified practitioner within 1 hour
Restraints may be released briefly only while the client is asleep
A family member's request is sufficient reason to keep a client in restraints
items.rationale: Emergency application followed by an immediate order, use of the least restrictive alternative first, and the 1-hour face-to-face evaluation for violent or self-destructive behavior are regulatory requirements. PRN restraint orders are prohibited because each episode needs a fresh clinical justification. Restraints are released at regular intervals for range of motion, skin care and needs regardless of sleep, and family preference is never a clinical indication; only the client's safety need is.

items.stem: A client with confirmed measles is admitted to a medical unit. Which measures should the nurse implement for airborne precautions? Select all that apply.
options: Wear a fit-tested N95 respirator before entering the room
Place a surgical mask on the client when transport out of the room is unavoidable
Keep a supply of gowns and gloves at the door for all client contact
Remove the N95 respirator inside the room before stepping into the hallway
Assign the client to a private room with negative-pressure ventilation and keep the door closed
Limit staff caring for the client to those with documented immunity to measles
Schedule the client's chest x-ray in the radiology department at the end of the day when it is empty
items.rationale: Airborne precautions require a negative-pressure room with the door closed, an N95 or higher respirator for everyone who enters, a mask on the client during essential transport, and assignment of immune staff only because measles is highly contagious. Gowns and gloves follow standard precautions rather than being required for all contact with measles. The respirator is removed after leaving the room, not inside it, and a portable x-ray avoids moving the client through the facility.

items.stem: A nurse is teaching new staff about sharps safety. Which practices reduce the risk of needlestick injury? Select all that apply.
options: Fill sharps containers to the top before replacing them to reduce waste
Use needleless systems for IV medication administration whenever available
Dispose of sharps in a puncture-resistant container at the point of use
Pass an uncapped needle to a colleague by hand so it is not left on the tray
Replace the sharps container when it is three-quarters full
Activate the safety device on the needle immediately after use
Recap needles using two hands before disposal
items.rationale: Engaging safety-engineered devices right after use, disposing of sharps at the point of use, using needleless connectors and replacing containers at the three-quarter mark are the core elements of sharps injury prevention. Two-handed recapping is the classic cause of needlesticks; if recapping is unavoidable, a one-handed scoop technique is used. Overfilled containers cause injuries when sharps are forced in, and passing exposed needles hand to hand is unsafe.

items.stem: A nurse manager is developing a plan to reduce errors with high-alert medications on a medical unit. Which strategies should be included? Select all that apply.
options: Use tall-man lettering on labels for look-alike, sound-alike names such as hydrOXYzine and hydrALAzine
Store concentrated potassium chloride on the unit for rapid access
Require an independent double-check by a second nurse before starting insulin and heparin infusions
Rely on nurses' experience rather than smart pump dose limits to speed up administration
Apply auxiliary warning labels to high-alert medications in the automated dispensing cabinet
Standardize infusion concentrations so only one strength of each high-alert drug is stocked
items.rationale: Independent double-checks, tall-man lettering, warning labels and standardized concentrations are recognized strategies that make errors with high-alert drugs less likely and easier to catch. Concentrated potassium chloride is removed from client care units because inadvertent IV push administration is fatal; premixed dilutions are used instead. Smart pump dose limits are a safety barrier, and bypassing them to save time removes protection at the point of greatest risk.

items.stem: A nurse wearing a gown, gloves, N95 respirator and face shield is preparing to leave the room of a client on airborne and contact precautions. Which item should the nurse remove first?
options: N95 respirator
Gloves
Gown
Face shield
items.rationale: Gloves are the most contaminated item and come off first, followed by the face shield and the gown; the respirator comes off last, after leaving the room, and hand hygiene follows. Removing the face shield or gown while still gloved transfers contamination to the face and hair, and the respirator is never removed inside an airborne isolation room because the air remains infectious.

items.stem: A nurse is preparing to enter the room of a client on droplet and contact precautions. Place the steps for putting on personal protective equipment in the correct order.
options: Put on gloves, pulling the cuffs over the gown sleeves
Put on eye protection
Put on the gown and tie it at the neck and waist
Put on the surgical mask and mold the nosepiece
Perform hand hygiene
items.rationale: Personal protective equipment is donned in the order that keeps the hands clean and each layer sealed: hand hygiene, gown, mask or respirator, eye protection, then gloves last so they overlap the gown cuffs and cover the wrists. Putting gloves on early contaminates the other items, and a mask applied after eye protection would disturb the fit of the shield.

items.stem: Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A client admitted for major depressive disorder says to the nurse, 'There is really no point in any of this anymore.' The nurse should first respond by {{1}} because this statement is a cue for {{2}}.

options: changing the subject to the day's group schedule
asking directly whether the client is having thoughts of ending their life
telling the client that many people feel that way
reassuring the client that things will look better after treatment
suicidal ideation that requires immediate assessment
medication nonadherence
a normal reaction to hospitalization
a side effect of antidepressant therapy

items.rationale: Hopeless statements such as 'no point anymore' are verbal warning signs of suicide, so the nurse asks directly and calmly about suicidal thoughts; asking does not plant the idea and opens the safety assessment. False reassurance, changing the subject and generalizing ('many people feel that way') are communication blocks that minimize the client's feelings and can close the door on disclosure.

items.stem: Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A client with alcohol use disorder whose last drink was 36 hours ago has a coarse tremor, diaphoresis, heart rate 118/min and reports seeing insects on the wall. The nurse scores the CIWA-Ar at 24 and should {{1}}, because the client is at greatest risk for {{2}}.

options: apply wrist restraints to prevent injury
hold all medications until the hallucinations resolve
offer a glass of juice and dim the lights
administer the symptom-triggered lorazepam dose per protocol and reassess in 1 hour
opioid overdose
withdrawal seizures and delirium tremens
hypoglycemia from poor intake
serotonin syndrome

items.rationale: A CIWA-Ar score above 20 with tremor, autonomic hyperactivity and visual hallucinations indicates severe alcohol withdrawal, which is treated with symptom-triggered benzodiazepines to prevent seizures and progression to delirium tremens; reassessment guides further dosing. Juice and dim lights do not treat the withdrawal, restraints are not a first-line response, and withholding medication allows the withdrawal to escalate.

items.stem: Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A client being discharged after a suicide attempt by overdose has completed a written safety plan with the nurse. Before discharge the nurse should confirm that {{1}} and that the plan lists {{2}}.

options: the client has promised in writing never to attempt suicide again
a family member has agreed to lock up or remove medications and firearms from the home
the client has a 90-day supply of the new antidepressant
the client will avoid all contact with friends until the follow-up visit
the reasons the attempt was not serious
a schedule for tapering the antidepressant
the names of staff who cared for the client
the client's personal warning signs, coping steps and crisis line numbers

items.rationale: Means restriction, especially securing medications and firearms, is one of the most effective ways to reduce suicide deaths, and a safety plan is a stepwise list of the client's own warning signs, coping strategies, supportive contacts and crisis resources. No-suicide contracts are not evidence based, isolation removes support, and sending a large supply of medication home after an overdose increases risk.

items.stem: Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: Three weeks after the death of a spouse, a client at a primary care visit reports crying daily, poor sleep and occasionally hearing the spouse's footsteps in the hallway. The nurse recognizes these findings as {{1}} and should {{2}}.

options: complicated grief requiring psychiatric hospitalization
symptoms of major depressive disorder
early signs of a psychotic disorder
expected manifestations of acute grief
acknowledge the loss, explore the client's support system and offer bereavement resources
tell the client that the grief should be over within a month
request an urgent antipsychotic prescription
advise the client to remove all reminders of the spouse from the home

items.rationale: Tearfulness, sleep disturbance and brief sensory experiences of the deceased are common in the first weeks of acute grief and do not indicate psychosis or complicated grief, which is identified only when intense yearning and impairment persist far beyond the expected course. The nurse supports the process by acknowledging the loss, assessing supports and offering bereavement resources; removing reminders or setting a timeline for grief is nontherapeutic.

items.stem: Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A client who was told yesterday that a biopsy showed cancer tells the nurse, 'The lab must have mixed up my results with someone else's.' The client is using the defense mechanism of {{1}}, and the nurse's best initial response is to {{2}}.

options: sublimation
rationalization
denial
projection
stay with the client and allow time to process the diagnosis without forcing acceptance
ask the oncologist to re-explain the results immediately
tell the client that denial will delay treatment
repeat the diagnosis firmly until the client agrees it is correct

items.rationale: Denial is the refusal to accept a painful reality and is a common first response to a serious diagnosis; it can be protective in the short term. The nurse remains present, listens and lets the client absorb the news at their own pace, while watching that denial does not delay needed care. Confronting the client or pressing for immediate acceptance increases anxiety and damages trust; projection attributes one's own feelings to others and rationalization offers excuses.

items.stem: Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: An 8-month-old infant is brought to the emergency department with a spiral fracture of the femur; the caregiver states the infant 'rolled off the couch' two days ago. The nurse should recognize that {{1}} and is legally required to {{2}}.

options: spiral fractures are typical of short falls in infants
a two-day delay is expected because femur fractures are hard to detect
the caregiver's calm demeanor rules out abuse
the injury pattern and delay in seeking care are inconsistent with the explanation
report the suspected abuse to child protective services regardless of proof
confront the caregiver and demand the true story
wait until the provider confirms abuse before documenting
obtain the caregiver's permission before contacting any agency

items.rationale: A spiral femur fracture in a non-ambulatory infant requires a twisting force, and a short fall does not explain it; combined with a two-day delay in seeking care, this raises strong suspicion of abuse. Nurses are mandated reporters and must report reasonable suspicion to child protective services without waiting for proof or caregiver consent. Confronting the caregiver may endanger the child and is not the nurse's role; documentation of objective findings proceeds at once.

items.stem: Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A client with bipolar disorder who takes lithium reports 2 days of vomiting and diarrhea and now has a coarse hand tremor and slurred speech; the serum lithium level is 2.1 mEq/L. The nurse should {{1}} and anticipate {{2}}.

options: administer an antiemetic and reassess in 4 hours
give the scheduled dose with a large glass of water
hold the next lithium dose and notify the provider immediately
encourage the client to restrict sodium until the level falls
an increase in the lithium dose once vomiting stops
discharge with instructions to double fluid intake
a switch to a thiazide diuretic to lower the level
IV fluids and serial lithium levels, with hemodialysis if the level or symptoms worsen

items.rationale: Coarse tremor, slurred speech and GI losses with a level above 1.5 mEq/L indicate lithium toxicity, which can progress to seizures and renal failure; the dose is held and the provider notified at once. Vomiting and diarrhea deplete sodium and water, which raises lithium reabsorption, so treatment is IV normal saline with serial levels, and hemodialysis for severe toxicity. Sodium restriction and thiazides raise lithium levels further, and giving the dose worsens toxicity.

items.stem: Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A client in the clinic waiting room suddenly reports a racing heart, difficulty breathing and a feeling of dying, and is hyperventilating. After an acute medical cause is ruled out, the nurse should {{1}} and speak using {{2}}.

options: stay with the client in a quiet space and model slow breathing
give the client a paper bag to breathe into
leave the client alone to calm down
ask detailed questions about what triggered the attack
open-ended questions about childhood stressors
a firm, loud voice to get the client's attention
short, simple, calm directions
detailed explanations of the physiology of panic

items.rationale: During a panic attack the client cannot process complex information, so the nurse stays present, reduces stimulation, and uses brief, calm statements while modeling slow breathing to interrupt hyperventilation. Leaving the client alone increases fear, detailed questioning or teaching waits until the attack subsides, and paper-bag rebreathing is no longer recommended because it can cause hypoxia if a medical cause is present.

items.stem: Click to highlight the findings in the nurses' note that indicate the client is at increased risk for suicide and require immediate follow-up.

highlightSegments.text: 1900 note: 54-year-old client admitted 5 days ago for major depressive disorder after a job loss.
Attended two groups today and ate 75% of dinner.
This afternoon the client gave a wristwatch and family photographs to a roommate, saying 'I won't be needing these.'
Client describes mood as 'calm, better than in weeks' but still endorses feeling like a burden to the family.
Sleeping 6 hours per night with trazodone.
Asked twice when the 15-minute checks would stop.
Vital signs within normal limits.
Client requested extra time in the shower area alone this evening.
Plan: continue current level of observation.

items.rationale: Giving away valued possessions, a sudden lift in mood while feelings of being a burden persist, questioning when observation ends, and seeking time alone are classic warning signs that a client may have decided on suicide and is looking for an opportunity; the nurse increases observation and completes a suicide risk assessment now. Group attendance, eating, sleep and normal vital signs are not risk cues, and continuing the current observation level is inadequate.

items.stem: Click to highlight the findings in the emergency department note that indicate the client's aggression is escalating and require immediate intervention.

highlightSegments.text: 2210: 29-year-old client brought by police after a bar altercation; breath positive for alcohol.
Sitting on the stretcher answering questions in a normal tone.
2245: Client is now pacing the length of the cubicle
and speaking in a loud voice with clenched fists.
Refused vital signs, stating 'Don't touch me.'
Laceration to the left eyebrow dressed; bleeding controlled.
2300: Client kicked the trash can and told the technician, 'You'll be sorry if you come back in here.'
Sister at bedside states this is the first time the client has been in trouble.
Security notified and remains outside the curtain.
Client is oriented to person, place and time.

items.rationale: Pacing, a rising voice, clenched fists, refusing touch, striking objects and verbal threats form the classic escalation sequence from anxiety to verbal aggression toward physical violence; recognizing these cues allows early de-escalation, removal of other people and preparation of a team response before injury occurs. A normal tone earlier, a controlled laceration, family history and intact orientation do not indicate escalation, and security standing by is an action already taken rather than a cue.

items.stem: Click to highlight the findings in the home health nurse's note that raise concern for elder abuse or neglect and must be reported.

highlightSegments.text: Home visit to an 82-year-old client with heart failure who lives with an adult grandson.
Client is thinner than at the last visit 3 weeks ago, weight down 4 kg, and the refrigerator contains only condiments and a carton of milk.
Grandson answers all questions for the client and stays within arm's reach during the exam.
Client's furosemide bottle, filled 30 days ago, is nearly full.
Bilateral 2+ pitting edema of the lower legs.
Bruises of different colors noted on both upper arms in a fingertip pattern.
Client states, 'He does his best, he's very busy.'
Blood pressure 138/84 mmHg, heart rate 88/min.
Next visit scheduled in 1 week.

items.rationale: Unexplained weight loss with an empty refrigerator, a caregiver who controls the interview and hovers, medications that are not being given, and fingertip-pattern bruises in various stages of healing are cues for neglect and physical abuse of a dependent older adult; the nurse is a mandated reporter and contacts adult protective services. Edema from untreated heart failure is a consequence rather than a cue in itself, and the client's minimizing statement is common in abuse and does not remove the duty to report.

items.stem: Click to highlight the findings in the nurses' note that suggest the client is developing alcohol withdrawal and should be reported to the provider.

highlightSegments.text: Postoperative day 2 after open reduction of an ankle fracture, 46-year-old client.
Admission history lists 'social drinking'; the client's partner reports 6 to 8 beers nightly for years.
0600: Client slept poorly, sheets damp with sweat.
Pain 4/10 at the surgical site, relieved with oxycodone.
0800: Fine tremor of both hands noted when holding a coffee cup; heart rate 112/min, blood pressure 156/94 mmHg.
Surgical dressing clean, dry and intact.
Client is irritable and asked the nurse twice to 'get the cat off the bed'; there is no cat.
Ate half of breakfast.
Ambulated to the bathroom with crutches.

items.rationale: Heavy daily drinking reported by the partner, with diaphoresis, tremor, tachycardia, hypertension, irritability and a visual hallucination emerging about 48 hours after the last drink, is the picture of alcohol withdrawal, which can progress to seizures and delirium tremens; the nurse reports the findings, obtains a CIWA-Ar score and anticipates benzodiazepines. Controlled pain, an intact dressing, intake and ambulation are expected postoperative findings rather than withdrawal cues.

items.stem: Click to highlight the findings in the nurses' note that indicate the client with schizophrenia is responding to treatment.

highlightSegments.text: Day 14 of admission for acute exacerbation of schizophrenia; risperidone started on day 1.
On admission the client was mute, hid under the bed and refused all meals.
Today the client attended community meeting and answered when spoken to.
Showered and dressed independently before breakfast.
States the voices are 'quieter and only come at night now.'
Still believes the food may be poisoned and eats only packaged items.
Slept 7 hours per night for the last 3 nights.
Took oral medication without prompting this morning.
Reports mild restlessness in the legs after the evening dose.
Family visit planned for tomorrow.

items.rationale: Attending groups, responding to others, independent self-care, quieter and less frequent hallucinations, restored sleep and taking medication without prompting all show that positive and negative symptoms are improving with antipsychotic therapy. The persistent poisoning delusion is an unresolved symptom, leg restlessness is a possible akathisia side effect that needs follow-up rather than a sign of improvement, and the admission description and family visit are background information.

items.stem: Click to highlight the statements in the parent's account that indicate the adolescent may be at risk for suicide and needs a same-day assessment.

highlightSegments.text: A parent calls the school nurse about a 16-year-old student and says:
'She has been quieter than usual since school started, but her grades are about the same.'
'Last night she posted online that everyone would be better off without her.'
'She still texts her best friend every day and started a part-time job in August.'
'On Sunday she gave her guitar to her younger brother and said she would not need it anymore.'
'She has been sleeping until noon on weekends, which is normal for her.'
'This morning I found a note in her room listing the pills in our medicine cabinet.'
'Her father died by suicide when she was 9.'
'I am not sure if I am overreacting.'
The parent asks whether the nurse can see the student today.

items.rationale: A statement that others would be better off without her, giving away a treasured possession, a written list of available pills and a family history of suicide are serious warning signs and risk factors; the nurse arranges a same-day suicide risk assessment, advises the parent to secure medications, and ensures the student is not left alone until safety is established. Being quieter, keeping friendships and a job, and weekend sleep are not by themselves indicators of imminent risk.

items.stem: Click to highlight the findings in the adolescent clinic note that support the suspected diagnosis of anorexia nervosa.

highlightSegments.text: 17-year-old client brought by a parent for a sports physical; the parent is worried about the client's eating.
Height 165 cm, weight 42 kg, down 9 kg in 6 months.
Client states, 'I am still fat; I just need to lose a little more before the meet.'
Runs 10 km every morning in addition to two team practices a day.
Reports last menstrual period about 5 months ago.
Denies vomiting or laxative use.
Heart rate 52/min, blood pressure 92/58 mmHg, and fine downy hair on the forearms.
Immunizations are up to date.
Client is a straight-A student and captain of the cross-country team.
No family history of eating disorders reported.

items.rationale: Significant weight loss to a low body weight, an intense fear of gaining weight with distorted body image, compulsive exercise, secondary amenorrhea, bradycardia, hypotension and lanugo are the characteristic findings of anorexia nervosa, restricting type. Denying purging does not exclude the diagnosis, and academic achievement and perfectionism are common traits rather than diagnostic criteria; immunization status and family history are neutral.

items.stem: The nurse reviews the trended data for a client admitted 24 hours ago for alcohol withdrawal on a symptom-triggered lorazepam protocol. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Document the scores and reassess in 4 hours
Continue the protocol because the doses are being given as ordered
Notify the provider that the client is not responding to the protocol and needs a higher level of care
Apply a cooling blanket and recheck the temperature in 30 minutes
items.rationale: Rising CIWA-Ar scores above 20 with escalating tachycardia, hypertension and fever despite increasing benzodiazepine doses indicate impending delirium tremens, a medical emergency with significant mortality; the client needs urgent provider evaluation, IV benzodiazepines and likely ICU-level monitoring. Simply continuing the oral protocol or waiting 4 hours allows further deterioration, and a cooling blanket treats only one sign without addressing the withdrawal driving it.

items.stem: A clinic nurse reviews a client's PHQ-9 depression screening results over 6 weeks of sertraline therapy. Which conclusion should the nurse draw?
options: The improving total score means item 9 can be disregarded
The client has fully recovered and the medication can be tapered
The medication is ineffective and should be changed
The client needs an immediate suicide risk assessment because increasing energy with persistent thoughts of death raises risk
trendHeaders: Item 9: thoughts of being better off dead
items.rationale: Although the total PHQ-9 score is falling, responses to item 9 have increased to more than half the days while energy and sleep improve; early antidepressant response can restore the energy to act on suicidal thoughts before hopelessness lifts, so a positive item 9 always triggers an immediate suicide risk assessment. A score of 9 is still mild depression, not recovery, and the falling total shows the medication is working, so tapering or switching is not indicated.

items.stem: The nurse at a mental health clinic reviews the trended data for a client with bipolar disorder who takes lithium carbonate. Which conclusion should the nurse draw?
options: The findings are expected therapeutic effects of lithium
The rising level reflects reduced renal lithium clearance from NSAID use and sodium restriction, and the client is now toxic
The client is having a manic relapse and needs a higher lithium dose
The level is rising because the client is taking extra lithium doses
trendRows: Ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily for knee pain
items.rationale: NSAIDs reduce renal blood flow and lithium excretion, and a low-sodium diet increases lithium reabsorption in the proximal tubule; together they explain the climb from a therapeutic 0.8 mEq/L to a toxic 1.7 mEq/L with coarse tremor, diarrhea and confusion. Nothing in the data suggests extra dosing, coarse tremor and confusion are toxic rather than therapeutic effects, and increasing the dose would be dangerous; the nurse holds lithium and notifies the provider.

items.stem: The nurse reviews the trended data for a client admitted with acute mania who is receiving a mood stabilizer and an antipsychotic. Which conclusion should the nurse draw?
options: The treatment plan is effective and the client is moving toward remission
The changes are too small to indicate a response
The client is becoming depressed and needs an antidepressant
The client is oversedated and the antipsychotic should be held
trendRows: Pacing, sat for 10 minutes at group
Attended full group, stayed in own room at night
items.rationale: Sleep restored to 6 hours, speech slowing to a normal rate, the ability to remain in one place and completing all meals show that the hyperactivity, pressured speech and insomnia of mania are resolving, which is the expected response to a mood stabilizer and antipsychotic. Six hours of sleep and full participation in group do not indicate oversedation or depression, and the progression across all four parameters is a clear, not marginal, response.

items.stem: A client hospitalized for depression says, 'I have let my whole family down. Nothing I do ever works out.' For each nurse response, click to specify whether it is therapeutic or nontherapeutic.
matrixRows: 'It sounds like you are feeling like a failure right now. Tell me more about that.'
'Don't say that; your family loves you and everything will be fine.'
'Why do you think you have let them down?'
'You feel that nothing you try succeeds.'
'Everyone feels that way sometimes.'
'I would like to sit with you for a while.'
items.rationale: Reflecting feelings, restating, and offering self encourage the client to explore feelings and convey acceptance without judgment. False reassurance dismisses the client's experience, 'why' questions demand justification and increase defensiveness, and generalizing to 'everyone' minimizes the client's individual distress; these are communication blocks that shut down disclosure.

items.stem: The nurse assesses three older adults with cognitive changes. For each finding, click to specify whether it is most characteristic of delirium, dementia, or depression.
matrixRows: Onset over hours to days with a clear precipitating event such as infection
Level of consciousness fluctuates during the day and is worse at night
Gradual decline in memory over months to years with stable alertness
Client answers 'I don't know' quickly and appears uninterested in testing
Attention is markedly impaired and the client cannot follow a conversation
Client confabulates or gives near-miss answers to hide memory gaps
Sleep disturbance with early morning awakening and poor appetite
items.rationale: Delirium is an acute, fluctuating disturbance of attention and consciousness with an identifiable cause; dementia is a gradual, progressive loss of memory and function with intact alertness in which clients often cover deficits; and depression in older adults produces apathy, 'I don't know' responses, early waking and anorexia with preserved attention when engaged. Separating these patterns matters because delirium is a medical emergency and depression is treatable.

items.stem: A client on the psychiatric unit is shouting at staff, pacing and demanding to leave. Which actions by the nurse are appropriate for de-escalating the situation? Select all that apply.
options: Speak in a calm, low voice and use short sentences
Ask other clients to leave the immediate area
Match the client's volume so the client can hear the nurse clearly
Stand in the doorway to block the client's exit
Offer the client choices, such as going to a quiet room or talking with staff
Tell the client that restraints will be applied if the shouting does not stop
Approach the client from the front, keeping at least an arm's length of distance
items.rationale: Effective de-escalation uses a calm, non-threatening stance with personal space, simple language, removal of an audience, and realistic choices that restore the client's sense of control. Threatening restraints, blocking the exit and raising the nurse's voice are perceived as challenges and increase the likelihood of violence; restraints are only a last resort after less restrictive measures fail.

items.stem: A nurse in a primary care clinic assesses a client who presents with a wrist sprain. Which findings should prompt the nurse to screen privately for intimate partner violence? Select all that apply.
options: The partner insists on staying in the room and answers questions directed at the client
The client is wearing a wrist brace from a prior visit
The client reports frequent headaches and difficulty sleeping with no clear cause
The client mentions a recent job promotion
The client has had three visits in 4 months for injuries with vague explanations
The client avoids eye contact and glances at the partner before answering
items.rationale: A controlling partner who will not leave the room, repeated injuries with inconsistent explanations, unexplained somatic complaints such as headaches and insomnia, and fearful, deferential body language are recognized indicators of intimate partner violence; the nurse arranges to interview the client alone before screening. Wearing a prescribed brace and a job promotion are not risk indicators.

items.stem: A nurse meets a newly admitted client for the first time on the psychiatric unit. Which action is the priority during the orientation phase of the nurse-client relationship?
options: Share personal experiences to show the client that the nurse understands
Establish trust by explaining the nurse's role, the purpose of the meetings and the limits of confidentiality
Help the client practice new coping skills learned in group
Review the client's progress and discuss feelings about the upcoming discharge
items.rationale: The orientation phase begins the relationship by introducing the nurse's role, agreeing on goals, and clarifying boundaries and confidentiality so trust can develop. Practicing coping skills belongs to the working phase, reviewing progress and preparing for separation belongs to the termination phase, and self-disclosure of personal experiences blurs professional boundaries and shifts the focus away from the client.

items.stem: Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A client admitted with acute mania has not sat down for a meal in 2 days, weighs 3 kg less than on admission, and talks constantly to anyone nearby. The nurse should provide {{1}} and assign the client to {{2}}.

options: a liquid diet only until the client agrees to sit
high-calorie finger foods and fluids the client can eat while moving
small servings of favorite desserts as rewards for sitting
three large meals in the dining room with other clients
a private room away from the busy dayroom
a shared room with a talkative client to encourage socialization
a room near the nurses' station with the door open
the most active group activities to use up excess energy

items.rationale: During mania the client cannot sit long enough to eat, so portable, high-calorie foods and fluids offered frequently prevent weight loss and dehydration. A quiet, low-stimulus room limits the environmental input that fuels hyperactivity and intrusiveness. Crowded dining rooms, group activities and talkative roommates increase stimulation, a liquid-only diet does not meet caloric needs, and withholding food as a reward is punitive.

items.stem: Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A veteran waiting in the emergency department drops to the floor when a metal tray crashes, covers their head and shouts for others to 'get down.' The nurse recognizes {{1}} and should first {{2}}.

options: a flashback triggered by a sound resembling combat
a seizure with automatisms
a panic attack unrelated to the noise
malingering to be seen sooner
calmly state the client's name, where they are and that they are safe, without touching them from behind
ask the client to describe the combat memory in detail
restrain the client to prevent self-injury
leave the area quietly so the client can recover alone

items.rationale: A sudden loud noise resembling gunfire can trigger a dissociative flashback in a client with PTSD, in which the client re-experiences the trauma as if it were happening now. Grounding, using the client's name, stating the place and safety, and approaching from the front without sudden touch, re-orients the client without adding threat. Restraint or touch from behind can be perceived as an attack, exploring the memory during the flashback deepens distress, and leaving the client alone is unsafe.

items.stem: Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A client with schizophrenia tells the nurse, 'The voice keeps telling me to cut my arms so the evil will drain out.' The nurse should first {{1}} and then {{2}}.

options: ask the client to describe what the voice sounds like
explain that the voice is not real and cannot hurt anyone
reassure the client that everyone hears voices sometimes
ask what the voice is saying and whether the client feels able to resist it
leave the client alone to rest in a darkened room
initiate self-harm precautions and notify the provider
encourage the client to return to the group activity
give the client a pencil and paper to record the voice's messages

items.rationale: Command hallucinations directing self-harm are a psychiatric emergency; the nurse assesses the content and the client's ability to resist, because the risk is highest when the client feels compelled to obey. Safety precautions and provider notification follow immediately. Arguing that the voice is not real, minimizing with 'everyone hears voices', sending the client to group, or leaving the client alone ignore the safety threat.

items.stem: Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A client who uses heroin daily and last used 14 hours ago reports muscle aches and nausea, and the nurse notes yawning, rhinorrhea, dilated pupils and piloerection with a COWS score of 15. The nurse interprets this as {{1}} and anticipates {{2}}.

options: severe alcohol withdrawal
moderate opioid withdrawal
opioid overdose
a panic attack
initiation of buprenorphine now that withdrawal is clearly established
naloxone 0.4 mg IV
a benzodiazepine taper over 5 days
a stat serum lithium level

items.rationale: Yawning, rhinorrhea, mydriasis, piloerection, myalgia and nausea beginning 8 to 24 hours after the last heroin use are hallmark opioid withdrawal findings, and a COWS score of 13 to 24 is moderate withdrawal. Buprenorphine is started only after objective withdrawal is present, usually a COWS of 8 or more, to avoid precipitated withdrawal. Naloxone treats overdose and would worsen withdrawal, benzodiazepine tapers are for alcohol or sedative withdrawal, and lithium is unrelated.

items.stem: Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A client with borderline personality disorder tells the day nurse, 'You are the only one who really cares; the night staff are cruel and useless.' The nurse recognizes this as {{1}} and the team should respond by {{2}}.

options: regression
splitting
identification
transference
allowing the client to choose which staff provide care
confronting the night staff about the client's complaints
assigning the client only to the preferred nurse
maintaining consistent limits and a single treatment plan across all shifts

items.rationale: Splitting is viewing people as all good or all bad, a hallmark of borderline personality disorder that can divide a treatment team. The therapeutic response is a unified plan with consistent expectations and limits from every staff member, so the client cannot play one against another. Assigning a favorite nurse, acting on unverified complaints, or letting the client select staff reinforces the split and undermines the milieu.

items.stem: Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: An 84-year-old client who was alert and oriented on admission becomes agitated on the second night after hip surgery, picks at the sheets and does not recognize family. The nurse should suspect {{1}} and first {{2}}.

options: delirium related to a reversible cause
the normal progression of dementia
an acute psychotic disorder
a personality change from anesthesia that will resolve on its own
assess for pain, urinary retention, hypoxia, infection and medications such as opioids
reassure the family that confusion is expected at this age
request a psychiatric consult for antipsychotic therapy
apply soft wrist restraints and dim the lights

items.rationale: An abrupt change in attention and behavior in a previously oriented older adult after surgery is delirium until proven otherwise, and the priority is to find and treat the precipitating cause such as pain, retention, hypoxia, infection or deliriogenic medications. Dementia does not develop over hours, psychosis is rare at this age, and confusion is never a normal consequence of age. Restraints and antipsychotics worsen delirium and are not first-line.

items.stem: Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: The adult child of a client with terminal pancreatic cancer asks the hospice nurse, 'Should we tell Mom she is dying, or will that take away her hope?' The nurse's best response is to {{1}} and then {{2}}.

options: tell the family it is the physician's job to disclose prognosis
state that clients always have the right to be told everything immediately
advise the family to withhold the prognosis to protect her
explore what the client already understands and wants to know about her illness
schedule a psychiatric evaluation for the client
offer a family meeting with the client, care team and chaplain to talk about her goals
ask the family to sign a form documenting their decision
suggest the family avoid emotional conversations at the bedside

items.rationale: Truth-telling at the end of life is guided by the client's own wishes; many clients already sense they are dying, and hope can be redirected toward comfort, relationships and meaning rather than cure. The nurse assesses the client's understanding and preferences and facilitates a family meeting with spiritual support so goals of care are shared openly. Withholding information without the client's consent, deferring entirely to the physician, or imposing full disclosure ignores the client's autonomy.

items.stem: Click to highlight the statements in the client's account at the 2-week postpartum visit that require immediate follow-up.

highlightSegments.text: A client attending a 2-week postpartum visit with her first baby says:
'I get teary sometimes and I am tired, but everyone says that is normal.'
'I can't sleep even when the baby sleeps because I have to keep checking that she is breathing.'
'Breastfeeding is going well and she is gaining weight.'
'Sometimes I hear a voice at night telling me the baby is not really mine.'
'My partner has been home and helps with night feedings.'
'Yesterday I had a thought that she would be safer if I were not here.'
'My mother had something like this after I was born and was in the hospital for a while.'
'I have an appointment with the lactation consultant next week.'
The client is dressed appropriately and makes eye contact.

items.rationale: Inability to sleep even when the infant sleeps, an auditory hallucination about the baby, a thought that the baby would be safer without the mother, and a maternal history suggesting postpartum psychiatric illness are red flags for postpartum psychosis or severe depression with suicide risk, a psychiatric emergency requiring same-day evaluation and a plan for the infant's safety. Mild tearfulness, successful feeding, partner support and lactation follow-up are reassuring or neutral findings.

items.stem: Click to highlight the statements in the roommate's report to the campus health nurse that suggest the student is experiencing psychosis.

highlightSegments.text: A roommate comes to student health about a 19-year-old classmate and reports:
'He was fine last semester and always went to class.'
'For the past month he stays up all night talking to someone who isn't there.'
'He covered the smoke detector because he says the government put a camera in it to track him.'
'He hasn't showered in about two weeks and the room smells.'
'He drinks a few beers on weekends like everyone else.'
'When I ask what's wrong he says the professors are sending him messages through the lecture slides.'
'He still calls his parents on Sundays.'
'He seems scared more than angry.'
'Is there someone who can check on him?'

items.rationale: Responding to unseen voices, a persecutory delusion about surveillance, ideas of reference in which ordinary lecture slides carry personal messages, and marked deterioration in self-care over a month are cues for a first psychotic episode in a young adult, and the nurse arranges an urgent evaluation. Weekend drinking, ongoing family contact, fear rather than anger, and the roommate's request are context, not evidence of psychosis.

items.stem: Click to highlight the findings in the outpatient nurse's note that indicate the client may be relapsing into mania.

highlightSegments.text: Telehealth follow-up with a 34-year-old client with bipolar I disorder, stable for 18 months on lithium.
Client reports sleeping about 3 hours a night for the past week and 'not needing more.'
Speech is rapid and the client changes topics several times without prompting.
States that lithium was stopped 2 weeks ago because 'I'm cured and it dulls my creativity.'
Works full time as a graphic designer and reports the job is going well.
Has started three new business ventures this week and spent 4,000 dollars on equipment.
Denies any thoughts of harming self or others.
Lives with a partner who joined the call and appears worried.
Last serum lithium level 3 months ago was 0.7 mEq/L.
Appointment with the psychiatric provider is scheduled in 6 weeks.

items.rationale: Decreased need for sleep, pressured and tangential speech, abrupt discontinuation of the mood stabilizer, and grandiose plans with impulsive spending are the early warning signs of a manic relapse; the nurse arranges a same-week provider visit rather than waiting 6 weeks. Steady employment, denial of harmful thoughts, a concerned partner and a previously therapeutic lithium level are baseline or protective information rather than relapse cues.

items.stem: Click to highlight the findings in the pediatric emergency department note that raise suspicion of physical abuse and must be reported.

highlightSegments.text: 4-year-old child brought in by the mother's partner for 'falling down the stairs' 3 hours ago.
Child is quiet, does not cry during the exam and flinches when the nurse raises a hand to adjust the light.
Bruises of yellow, green and purple color on the back and buttocks.
A loop-shaped mark 6 cm long on the left thigh.
Scraped left knee consistent with a fall.
Partner states the child 'is clumsy and bruises easily'; the mother, arriving later, says the fall happened yesterday.
Immunizations are up to date and growth is at the 50th percentile.
Child clings to the nurse and asks to stay 'here where it's safe.'
No prior emergency visits in the record.
Radiographs of the femur ordered.

items.rationale: Bruises in multiple stages of healing on protected areas such as the back and buttocks, a patterned loop mark suggesting a cord or belt, a fearful child who flinches and wants to stay where it is safe, and caregiver stories that conflict about timing and mechanism are hallmark indicators of physical abuse. A scraped knee fits a fall, and normal growth, immunizations and record history neither confirm nor exclude abuse; the nurse documents objectively and makes a mandated report.

items.stem: Click to highlight the findings in the home health note that indicate caregiver role strain requiring the nurse to intervene.

highlightSegments.text: Home visit for a 78-year-old client with moderate Alzheimer disease cared for by a 74-year-old spouse.
Client is clean, dressed and ate breakfast without difficulty.
Spouse begins crying when asked how things are going and says, 'I haven't slept more than 3 hours a night in weeks because he wanders.'
Spouse has lost 5 kg since the last visit 2 months ago and has not filled their own blood pressure prescription.
The couple's daughter visits every Sunday.
Spouse states, 'Sometimes I get so angry I have to leave the room so I don't do something I'd regret.'
Client's medications are set out correctly in a weekly pill organizer.
Spouse declined the adult day program last visit, saying, 'No one else can take care of him.'
Front door has a chime alarm installed.
Next visit in 2 weeks.

items.rationale: Chronic sleep deprivation, tearfulness, unintended weight loss and neglect of the caregiver's own health, anger that the caregiver fears could lead to harm, and refusal of respite are signs of caregiver role strain that place both the client and the caregiver at risk; the nurse addresses respite, support groups and safety. Good client hygiene, correct medications, a weekly visitor and a door alarm show that care is currently adequate rather than indicating strain.

items.stem: Click to highlight the findings in the clinic note that indicate the client's panic disorder is improving after 8 weeks of cognitive behavioral therapy and sertraline.

highlightSegments.text: Follow-up visit, 41-year-old client with panic disorder with agoraphobia.
At intake the client reported four to five panic attacks a week and had not left home alone in 3 months.
Client reports one brief panic attack in the past 2 weeks.
Drove alone to the grocery store twice last week.
States, 'When I feel it starting, I use the breathing and remind myself it will pass.'
Reports occasional nausea after taking sertraline in the morning.
Still avoids crowded places such as the mall.
Sleeping 7 hours a night and back at work part time.
Blood pressure 118/76 mmHg.
Next visit in 4 weeks.

items.rationale: A fall from several attacks a week to one in 2 weeks, resuming driving and shopping alone, using learned coping skills to manage early symptoms, and restored sleep and work all show that treatment for panic disorder with agoraphobia is working. Persistent avoidance of crowded places and medication-related nausea are areas that still need attention, and the intake history and vital signs are baseline data.

items.stem: Click to highlight the statements in the telehealth note that indicate the client is at risk of relapse to alcohol use.

highlightSegments.text: Telehealth check-in with a 52-year-old client 5 months into recovery from alcohol use disorder.
Client states, 'I stopped going to meetings 3 weeks ago; they were getting repetitive.'
Reports working 60-hour weeks since a coworker resigned.
Has started going to the bar with old drinking friends 'just for the food and to watch the game.'
Takes naltrexone daily and denies missed doses.
States, 'Honestly I think I could handle one beer now and then; I was never that bad.'
Sleeping 7 hours and exercising three times a week.
Sponsor called last week but the client did not call back.
Liver enzymes at the last visit were within normal limits.
Client's partner remains supportive.

items.rationale: Dropping out of support meetings, avoiding the sponsor, returning to high-risk people and places, mounting work stress, and minimizing the severity of past drinking with thoughts of controlled use are the classic warning signs of the relapse process, which begins well before the first drink. Adherence to naltrexone, healthy sleep and exercise, normal liver enzymes and a supportive partner are protective factors that the nurse can build on.

items.stem: The nurse reviews the trended data for a client admitted to an eating disorder unit with anorexia nervosa. Which conclusion should the nurse draw?
options: The client is medically stabilizing and the nutritional rehabilitation plan is effective
The client is developing refeeding syndrome and feeding should stop
The rising heart rate indicates anxiety that needs an anxiolytic
The weight gain is too rapid and intake should be reduced
items.rationale: Steady weight gain of about 0.2 kg per day, resolution of bradycardia toward normal, disappearing orthostatic hypotension, and completion of all prescribed meals show medical stabilization and engagement with the treatment plan. A gain of about 2 kg over 10 days is within the expected range, refeeding syndrome would present with electrolyte shifts, edema and cardiac symptoms rather than these improvements, and a heart rate returning from 44 to 64 is recovery, not anxiety.

items.stem: The nurse reviews the trended data for a client with schizoaffective disorder who became agitated on the unit. Which action should the nurse take next?
options: Ask the peer who was struck to talk with the client about the incident
Continue verbal de-escalation alone because it was partially effective at 1400
Prepare for emergency IM medication and, if needed, seclusion or restraint as the least restrictive measure that ensures safety
Place the client in four-point restraints for the rest of the shift
trendRows: Yelling at voices, banging on the door
Continues to threaten, will not accept oral medication
items.rationale: The trend shows escalation from anxiety to verbal and then physical aggression despite verbal de-escalation and offered oral medication; once a client has assaulted someone and refuses oral treatment, emergency intramuscular medication with seclusion or restraint only as long as necessary is the least restrictive option that protects everyone. Verbal techniques alone are no longer sufficient, restraint for a fixed shift-long period violates restraint standards, and involving the injured peer is unsafe.

items.stem: The nurse reviews the trended data for an 80-year-old client who had bowel surgery. Which conclusion should the nurse draw?
options: The changes are expected in an older adult after anesthesia and will resolve without intervention
The client needs a sitter and scheduled haloperidol as the primary treatment
The client has developed delirium and the nurse should assess for reversible causes such as urinary retention, pain, opioids and sleep loss
The client has undiagnosed dementia that was masked before surgery
trendRows: Picking at IV line, thinks it is 1985
Pulling at dressing, has not voided in 10 hours
items.rationale: A CAM that turns positive with new inattention, fluctuating orientation and sleep loss within days of surgery is postoperative delirium; the nurse looks for the reversible drivers already visible in the data, such as 10 hours without voiding, opioid use and sleep deprivation, and reports them. Dementia has a gradual course and would have been evident before surgery, delirium is never an expected consequence of age or anesthesia, and antipsychotics are reserved for dangerous agitation rather than being primary treatment.

items.stem: The nurse reviews the trended data for a client beginning buprenorphine induction for opioid use disorder. Which conclusion should the nurse draw?
options: The falling score means the client is becoming oversedated
The induction is proceeding as expected and withdrawal symptoms are resolving
The client is experiencing precipitated withdrawal and buprenorphine should be stopped
The client needs naloxone because the pupils have constricted
items.rationale: Starting buprenorphine at a COWS of 14 with objective signs of moderate withdrawal and observing the score fall steadily to 3 with normal pupils and comfort is the expected course of a successful induction. Precipitated withdrawal would show a sharp rise in COWS after the first dose, not a decline; resting quietly and asking for lunch indicate comfort rather than oversedation; and pupils returning to normal size reflect relief of withdrawal, not overdose.

items.stem: A client admitted after a suicide attempt is placed on suicide precautions. For each intervention, click to specify whether it is indicated or contraindicated.
matrixRows: Search belongings and remove belts, shoelaces, cords and sharp objects
Allow the client to keep a personal razor for hygiene after signing a safety agreement
Observe the client swallow each oral medication
Assign the client to a private room at the end of the hall
Ask the client directly about suicidal thoughts and plans at each shift
Avoid mentioning suicide so the client is not reminded of it
Serve meals with plastic utensils and count them afterward
items.rationale: Suicide precautions remove means, ensure medications are swallowed rather than hoarded, keep the client near staff for observation, and include direct, repeated assessment of suicidal thinking because asking does not increase risk. A personal razor and a secluded room provide means and opportunity, and no-suicide contracts have no protective value; avoiding the subject leaves risk unassessed.

items.stem: The nurse observes client behaviors on a medical unit. For each behavior, click to specify which defense mechanism it best illustrates.
matrixRows: A client who was scolded by the surgeon snaps at the nursing assistant who brings the lunch tray
A client who resents a demanding sibling brings the sibling lavish gifts and praises them constantly
A client who is angry about the diagnosis accuses the nurse of being hostile
A client who missed dialysis says, 'The unit was so busy they would not have had a chair for me anyway'
A client who fears dependence on staff tells the nurse, 'You seem to need me to need you'
A client who smokes explains, 'My grandfather smoked and lived to 95, so it can't be that bad'
items.rationale: Displacement redirects feelings from the real source to a safer target, reaction formation expresses the opposite of an unacceptable feeling, projection attributes one's own unacceptable feelings to another person, and rationalization supplies logical-sounding excuses for a behavior with a different motive. Naming the mechanism helps the nurse respond to the underlying feeling rather than the surface behavior.

items.stem: The nurse assesses a client with schizophrenia. Which findings are negative symptoms of the disorder? Select all that apply.
options: Speaking only when asked a direct question and answering in one or two words
Belief that the television is broadcasting the client's thoughts
Flat facial expression and monotone voice
Sitting alone for hours and showing no interest in activities the client once enjoyed
Not showering or changing clothes for a week despite reminders
Rapidly switching between unrelated topics
Hearing a voice commenting on the client's actions
items.rationale: Negative symptoms are deficits in normal function: affective flattening, alogia (poverty of speech), anhedonia and asociality, and avolition that shows as neglected self-care. Thought broadcasting is a delusion and hearing a commenting voice is a hallucination, both positive symptoms, and loose associations are a positive disorganized-thought symptom. Negative symptoms respond less well to antipsychotics and need structured, patient nursing support.

items.stem: The nurse follows up with a client 1 year after the death of the client's adult child. Which statements indicate the client is adapting to the loss in a healthy way? Select all that apply.
options: 'I keep her room exactly as it was and go in every night to talk to her as if she were there.'
'I joined a group for parents who have lost children and it helps to be with people who understand.'
'I think I would be better off dead so I could be with her.'
'I have not been able to go back to work or see my friends since the funeral.'
'On her birthday we planted a tree and shared stories about her.'
'I still miss her every day, but I can talk about her now without falling apart.'
items.rationale: Healthy adaptation to loss includes being able to remember and speak about the deceased with manageable sadness, seeking support from others who share the experience, and creating rituals that honor the person while continuing life. Preserving a room unchanged and speaking to the deceased as if present, prolonged withdrawal from work and friends a year later, and a wish to die to reunite with the child are signs of prolonged grief disorder and suicide risk that need referral.

items.stem: A client scheduled for surgery says, 'I cannot sign the consent until my eldest son arrives; in my family he makes the decisions about health matters.' Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?
options: 'The surgery cannot be delayed, so you will need to sign now.'
'I will let the surgeon know that you would like your son present before you sign.'
'I will have your son sign the form for you when he arrives.'
'You are the client, so legally only your decision matters here.'
items.rationale: Many cultures make health decisions collectively or defer to a designated family member, and respecting this while keeping the competent client as the legal decision-maker is culturally sensitive care; the nurse arranges for the son to be present and informs the surgeon. Insisting on individual autonomy or pressuring the client dismisses cultural values and may lead to a decision made under duress, and the son cannot sign for a competent adult.

items.stem: A client admitted 3 days ago after a fall, with a history of drinking a bottle of vodka daily, is now disoriented, tremulous, diaphoretic and terrified of 'snakes on the floor'; temperature 38.6 C (101.5 F), heart rate 138/min, blood pressure 178/104 mmHg. Complete the diagram by selecting the condition the client is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the nurse should take, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor to assess progress.
bowtieActions: Administer IV lorazepam per the CIWA-Ar protocol
Implement seizure precautions and continuous monitoring
Restrict fluids to prevent cerebral edema
Encourage the client to describe the snakes in detail
Discharge to an outpatient detoxification program
bowtieParams: CIWA-Ar score and level of consciousness
items.rationale: Disorientation, tremor, autonomic hyperactivity, fever and vivid visual hallucinations 48 to 96 hours after the last drink define delirium tremens, a life-threatening emergency; Wernicke encephalopathy causes ataxia and ophthalmoplegia without an autonomic storm, and alcoholic hallucinosis occurs with a clear sensorium. IV benzodiazepines titrated to the CIWA-Ar plus seizure precautions with continuous monitoring are the priority actions, and serial CIWA-Ar scores and vital signs show whether treatment is working. Fluid restriction, exploring the hallucinations and outpatient discharge are unsafe.

items.stem: Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A client whose home was destroyed by a fire last night arrives at the clinic unable to stop crying and says, 'I can't think, I don't know what to do first.' The nurse's first step in crisis intervention is to {{1}}, and the overall goal is {{2}}.

options: give the client a list of community agencies to contact
encourage the client to rest at home and call back in a week
assess the client's safety and perception of the event
refer the client for long-term psychotherapy
return the client to at least the pre-crisis level of functioning within about 4 to 6 weeks
teach the client to avoid discussing the fire
resolve underlying childhood conflicts
keep the client in the hospital until all housing problems are solved

items.rationale: Crisis intervention begins with assessing safety, including suicide risk, and the client's perception of the event, then moves to identifying supports and concrete next steps, because a client in crisis has temporarily lost the ability to problem-solve. The aim is short-term: to restore at least the previous level of functioning, usually within 4 to 6 weeks. Long-term therapy, handing over a list, or delaying contact do not address the acute disorganization.

items.stem: Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A college student with normal body weight reports 'eating out of control' several nights a week, and the nurse notes swollen parotid glands, dental enamel erosion and calluses on the knuckles of the right hand. The nurse suspects {{1}} and should plan to {{2}}.

options: bulimia nervosa with self-induced vomiting
binge-eating disorder without purging
anorexia nervosa, restricting type
a food allergy causing recurrent vomiting
insist the client gain 1 kg per week
restrict the client to a liquid diet
allow unsupervised bathroom use immediately after eating to preserve dignity
stay with the client for about 1 hour after meals and monitor serum potassium

items.rationale: Parotid enlargement, enamel erosion and knuckle calluses (Russell sign) result from repeated self-induced vomiting after binges, which with normal weight points to bulimia nervosa rather than anorexia or binge-eating disorder. Purging causes hypokalemia and cardiac dysrhythmias, so the nurse monitors potassium and supervises the client after meals to interrupt the cycle. Forced weight gain and liquid diets are not indicated at normal weight, and immediate unsupervised bathroom access enables purging.

items.stem: Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A resident of a memory care unit with Alzheimer disease becomes restless, tearful and tries to leave the building every day around 1700. The nurse identifies this pattern as {{1}} and should plan {{2}}.

options: delirium
an adverse reaction to evening medications
sundowning
attention-seeking behavior
a consistent late-afternoon routine with a quiet activity, bright lighting and reduced noise before dusk
keeping the resident in bed with the lights off after 1600
a scheduled dose of lorazepam at 1600
moving the resident to a room near the busy front entrance

items.rationale: Predictable late-afternoon agitation and exit-seeking in dementia is sundowning, linked to fatigue, fading light and disrupted circadian rhythm rather than acute illness or a wish for attention. Non-drug strategies such as a stable routine, calm activity, adequate lighting and less noise are first-line. Benzodiazepines worsen confusion and fall risk, a noisy entrance increases stimulation and elopement risk, and darkness with enforced bed rest intensifies disorientation.

items.stem: Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A client with generalized anxiety disorder was taught progressive muscle relaxation and diaphragmatic breathing 2 weeks ago. The nurse would evaluate the teaching as effective if the client reports {{1}} and demonstrates {{2}}.

options: needing an extra dose of the as-needed medication most days
holding the breath to stop feelings of tension
avoiding all situations that cause worry
using the techniques daily and falling asleep more easily
rapid shallow chest breathing
breathing through a straw when anxious
tensing all muscle groups at once and holding for 2 minutes
slow abdominal breathing with a relaxed jaw and shoulders

items.rationale: Regular practice with a measurable benefit such as easier sleep, plus correct technique of slow diaphragmatic breathing and sequential tensing and releasing of muscle groups, shows that relaxation training has been learned and is reducing physiological arousal. Avoidance maintains anxiety, increased reliance on rescue medication suggests the skills are not working, and breath-holding, shallow chest breathing or restricted breathing raise tension rather than relieve it.

items.stem: Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: A 76-year-old client on day 4 in the ICU, who wears glasses and hearing aids at home, is disoriented at night, startles at alarms and cannot tell day from night. The nurse recognizes {{1}} and should {{2}}.

options: sensory overload and deprivation contributing to delirium
the expected effects of the client's age
an early sign of dementia
attention-seeking behavior
sedate the client continuously so alarms are not disturbing
restrict family visits to reduce stimulation
return the glasses and hearing aids, open blinds by day, cluster care and reduce noise and light at night
keep the lights on and the television playing all night for orientation

items.rationale: Constant alarms, lights and interruptions combined with missing sensory aids create both overload and deprivation, which disrupt the sleep-wake cycle and precipitate ICU delirium. Restoring glasses and hearing aids, providing daylight cues, clustering care and creating a quiet, dark night environment re-establish orientation. Continuous light and television add overload, family presence is orienting rather than harmful, and sedation deepens delirium and is never a substitute for environmental management.

items.stem: Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: The spouse of a client with alcohol use disorder tells the nurse, 'I call in sick for him and hide the bottles so the kids don't see; I'm just keeping the family together.' The nurse recognizes this behavior as {{1}} and should {{2}}.

options: enabling, which shields the client from the consequences of drinking
a sign the spouse also has a substance use disorder
an effective way to motivate the client to stop
healthy protective parenting
advise the spouse to leave the marriage
ask the spouse to stop discussing the drinking with the children
tell the spouse to pour out all alcohol in the home
refer the spouse to a family support program such as Al-Anon and explore setting limits

items.rationale: Covering for the client and hiding evidence of drinking are enabling behaviors: they are well intentioned but remove the natural consequences that motivate change and keep the family organized around the addiction. The nurse supports the spouse's own recovery through a family program and helps them set boundaries. Advising divorce is outside the nurse's role, removing alcohol is another form of managing the client's behavior, and secrecy increases the children's confusion and shame.

items.stem: Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
items.clozeText: During the morning community meeting on an inpatient psychiatric unit, a client says, 'These meetings are pointless; I'm not coming anymore.' Applying the principles of milieu therapy, the nurse should {{1}} because the community meeting is intended to {{2}}.

options: tell the client that attendance is mandatory and privileges will be lost
excuse the client from all future meetings
invite the client to share the concern with the group and involve the group in responding
ask the client to leave the room until willing to participate
evaluate which clients are ready for discharge
give clients a shared voice in unit rules and practice problem-solving with peers
let staff announce the day's schedule without discussion
identify clients who need higher doses of medication

items.rationale: Milieu therapy uses the structured social environment of the unit as a treatment tool; community meetings let clients raise concerns, negotiate rules and practice communication and problem-solving with feedback from peers and staff. Bringing the objection to the group models exactly that process. Excusing, threatening or excluding the client abandons the therapeutic use of the community and turns a shared environment into a staff-controlled one.

items.stem: Click to highlight the statements made by the client during a private interview that indicate intimate partner violence and a need for safety planning.

highlightSegments.text: During a private interview in the urgent care clinic, a 31-year-old client with a bruised cheek says:
'We've been together 6 years and have two kids.'
'He only gets rough with me when he's been drinking, so it's really the alcohol.'
'He checks my phone every night and I'm not allowed to have money of my own.'
'I work part time at the library and my mother lives nearby.'
'Last month he took the car keys so I couldn't leave, and he said if I ever told anyone he would take the kids.'
'He is a good father when he's calm.'
'I'm scared to go home tonight because he knows I came here.'
'I don't want anyone to call the police.'
The client has no prior documented visits at this clinic.

items.rationale: Physical aggression that the client minimizes, controlling behaviors such as monitoring the phone and withholding money, preventing the client from leaving with threats about the children, and fear of going home are defining features of intimate partner violence and signal escalating danger; the nurse validates the client, assesses lethality and builds a safety plan the client controls. Relationship length, employment, family nearby, the partner's good moments and the wish not to involve police are context, not indicators of violence.

items.stem: Click to highlight the findings in the nurses' note for a client with major depressive disorder that require immediate follow-up rather than being interpreted as improvement.

highlightSegments.text: Day 16 of admission; escitalopram started on day 2.
Client showered without prompting and joined the walking group this morning.
States, 'I feel a lot more energy today, like I can finally do what I need to do.'
When asked about mood, replies, 'Still hopeless; nothing about my situation has changed.'
Ate 100% of breakfast for the first time since admission.
Called the client's brother to arrange for the brother to take the client's dog 'permanently.'
Slept 6 hours last night per night staff.
Asked the nurse whether the unit's window screens are secured.
Vital signs stable.
Scheduled for discharge planning meeting tomorrow.

items.rationale: Two weeks into antidepressant therapy, energy and motivation often return before hopelessness lifts, giving a still-suicidal client the means to act; new energy paired with persistent hopelessness, giving away a beloved pet, and probing the security of windows are cues that risk has increased, not decreased, and the nurse completes an immediate risk assessment and increases observation. Showering, walking, eating and sleeping are genuine improvements but do not offset the safety cues.

items.stem: Click to highlight the findings in the handoff report for a client with borderline personality disorder that the oncoming nurse should address first.

highlightSegments.text: 0700 handoff: 26-year-old client admitted 3 days ago after an impulsive overdose following a breakup.
Attended art therapy and completed a coping-skills worksheet.
Night nurse noted three new superficial scratches on the left forearm made with a plastic fork; client says, 'It's the only way I feel anything.'
Client told the night nurse, 'You're the only one here who actually gets me; the day staff are all fake.'
Ate dinner and slept 5 hours.
Client learned discharge is planned for tomorrow and stated, 'If you send me home I'll just do it again, and next time I'll do it right.'
Requested to call the ex-partner from the unit phone; call was declined per the treatment plan.
